## The three tiers

**Tier 1 — stateless rule modifiers (one day, one agent).** Holy Light, Mercy, Death Touch, Darkness, March, Leap. No `Position` field, no FEN, no Zobrist, no repetition, no undo, no search state. 5 files (`rules.ts`, `engine.ts`, `rules.test.ts`, `main.ts`/`index.html`, docs), ~120 engine lines, ~20 tests. The lab A/Bs them this week with `--rule kings=Mud:March`; `runAb` needs nothing new.

**Tier 2 — charges and timed marks (2–3 days).** Freeze, Ice Wall, Strike, Haste, Flight. 9 files, ~350 lines, ~32 tests. Freeze and Ice Wall first (one shape, proves the plumbing); **Haste last**, and only after `moverAt` learns about it.

**Tier 3 — captured-pieces reserve (1–2 days).** Sacrifice, which is the same hand-plus-drop seam the Squire needs. 7 files, ~200 lines, ~15 tests.

## Findings worth the parent agent's attention

- **A power activation should be a `Move`.** Then king safety, undo, LAN, replay, the search's make/unmake and the sim's counters all come free. Usable-while-in-check answers itself.
- **`Game.key()` is board + turn only.** Any tier-2 mark or counter must reach it or two different positions count as a repetition. Easiest bug to ship.
- **Haste is the dangerous one.** It changes whose turn it is at a ply no index can predict, so `moverAt(ply, rules)` cannot answer it — `PlyRecord` needs a `by` field, or LESSONS 2026-09-14 repeats itself. Also `rootTurn ^ (ply & 1)` in the search is wrong mid-haste.
- **Sacrifice needs no `Move` field**: `{from: sq, to: sq, promo: T}` plus a reserve decrement — `landed()` already does the work. And repetition needs nothing, because the reserve only changes on moves that reset `halfmove`.
- **Mercy + an enemy guard = a permanently uncapturable piece** (only a king takes a guard; a Mercy king takes nothing). Sharpest trap in the set; decision #15 recommends giving the guard capture back.
- **Kings belong in `Rules`, not a new module** — `stampOf()` hashes the whole rule set, so a king change cannot silently resume onto a mismatched control (the `pb-ab-base` void-run trap).
- **Kings stay out of FEN** (they are rules); tier-2/3 *state* goes in a seventh field and a Crazyhouse bracket, both backwards compatible since `fromFen` ignores trailing fields.

## Decisions to batch

24, each with a recommended default and a one-line reason, in §4 of the plan. The load-bearing ones: (1) March/Leap always-on for the lab as the ceiling of the counted rule; (2) firing Freeze/Ice Wall costs the whole turn; (4) "never gives check/mate" enforced on the power's own action, not on consequences; (7) a struck piece keeps its own capture rules; (12/13) Death Touch replaces the king's displacement capture and may eat defended pieces; (15) the Mercy/guard exception; (17) Sacrifice may not return a guard; (21) browser default stays no powers; (24) if only one ships, ship Death Touch — it is the only power expected to *cut* draws at zero state cost.

`src/rules/engine.ts`, directly below `makeMove` (the only other place that decides whose turn it is):

```ts
export function moverAt(ply: number, rules: Partial<Rules> = RULES): Color {
  return ((rules.secondPlayerDoubleFirstTurn && ply >= 2 ? ply - 1 : ply) & 1) as Color;
}
```

`rules` defaults to the live rule set (engine/browser). ## The table

| Asset class | Source | Licence | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| `white_tile_1.jpg`, `black_tile_1.jpg` | textures.com `FloorsCheckerboard0037` | Textures.com ToS Rev 3-21 | **Must replace** |
| `board_texture1.jpg` | same Drive folder, origin probable | same, if origin holds | **Must replace** |
| `public/models/*.json` (11) | designer's own sculpts, voxelised | © Saar Shai / Double Edged Games; Dream Catcher sculpts | Needs attribution |
| `public/sprites/*` (126) | same sculpts + his colour guides | same | Needs attribution |
| Press Start 2P, DotGothic16 (CDN) | Google Fonts | SIL OFL 1.1 | Clear |
| Google Fonts CSS request | fonts.googleapis.com | Google APIs ToS | Clear |
| three.js + build runtime in bundle | npm | MIT / Apache-2.0 / ISC / MPL-2.0 | Clear |
| DB32, Endesga 32 palettes | Lospec | free to use; a colour list is not a protected work | Clear |
| Imperator | Paul Lloyd | aggregators say "100% Free", no author EULA | Unknown — **not shipped** |

## Key findings

**The tiles are the only real problem.** Article 6.2(b) of the [Textures.com ToS](https://www.textures.com/static/terms/TexturesCom%20-%20Terms%20of%20Service%20Rev3-21.pdf) allows games and 6.1 allows modification, but 6.3(a) forbids you to "sell or distribute any Content (modified or not) by themselves". We serve three standalone JPEGs at fixed URLs; anyone can save a clean marble texture. "Modified or not" kills the downscale defence. Two more clauses bite: 6.3(k) bans releasing derivatives "under Open Source Licences" — so the repo can never go open source with these files in its history — and there is no separate free licence, just an Indie tier capped at $150k annual revenue (Art. 2.4). Attribution is required only inside a 3D-model bundle (6.2(c)), and it does not make standalone serving legal.

**Imperator is confirmed absent.** `grep -ril imperator` returns seven prose documents and zero assets; no `.ttf/.otf/.woff*` exists in `public/`, `dist/` or `src/`. # three.js r186 — Stylised Rendering Reference

**Current release: r186 (`"version": "0.186.0"`)** — verified from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mrdoob/three.js/dev/package.json

**Docs URL structure changed.** The old `threejs.org/docs/#api/en/materials/MeshToonMaterial` hash-routing scheme is gone. Canonical form is now flat: `https://threejs.org/docs/pages/<ClassName>.html`.

## 1) MeshToonMaterial + gradientMap

**Docs:** https://threejs.org/docs/pages/MeshToonMaterial.html
**Source:** https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/dev/src/materials/MeshToonMaterial.js

Extends `Material` (via `EventDispatcher`). Full property set with defaults:

| Property | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `color` | `(1,1,1)` | |
| `map` | `null` | color data → `SRGBColorSpace` |
| `gradientMap` | `null` | **non-color** → `NoColorSpace` |
| `lightMap` / `lightMapIntensity` | `null` / `1` | needs 2nd UV set; `LinearSRGBColorSpace` |
| `aoMap` / `aoMapIntensity` | `null` / `1` | red channel; needs 2nd UV set |
| `emissive` / `emissiveIntensity` / `emissiveMap` | `(0,0,0)` / `1` / `null` | emissiveMap is sRGB |
| `bumpMap` / `bumpScale` | `null` / `1` | ignored if `normalMap` set |
| `normalMap` / `normalMapType` / `normalScale` | `null` / `TangentSpaceNormalMap` / `(1,1)` | |
| `displacementMap` / `Scale` / `Bias` | `null` / `1` / `0` | (docs table says Scale `0`, source says `1` — source is authoritative: `1`) |
| `alphaMap` | `null` | green channel sampled |
| `wireframe` / `wireframeLinewidth` / `Linecap` / `Linejoin` | `false` / `1` / `'round'` / `'round'` | last three SVGRenderer only |
| `fog` | `true` | |
| `isMeshToonMaterial` | `true` | readonly type flag |

Note there is **no** `specular`/`shininess`/`roughness` — toon is Lambert-only diffuse.

### The actual GLSL

`src/renderers/shaders/ShaderChunk/gradientmap_pars_fragment.glsl.js` — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mrdoob/three.js/dev/src/renderers/shaders/ShaderChunk/gradientmap_pars_fragment.glsl.js

```glsl
#ifdef USE_GRADIENTMAP

	uniform sampler2D gradientMap;

#endif

vec3 getGradientIrradiance( vec3 normal, vec3 lightDirection ) {

	// dotNL will be from -1.0 to 1.0
	float dotNL = dot( normal, lightDirection );
	vec2 coord = vec2( dotNL * 0.5 + 0.5, 0.0 );

	#ifdef USE_GRADIENTMAP

		return vec3( texture2D( gradientMap, coord ).r );

	#else

		vec2 fw = fwidth( coord ) * 0.5;
		return mix( vec3( 0.7 ), vec3( 1.0 ), smoothstep( 0.7 - fw.x, 0.7 + fw.x, coord.x ) );

	#endif

}
```

Four load-bearing facts from this:
1. **`dotNL` is NOT clamped.** It is remapped `[-1,1] → [0,1]` via `dotNL * 0.5 + 0.5`. So the *midpoint* texel (u = 0.5) is the terminator, and the entire left half of your ramp covers surfaces facing away from the light. This is the single most common source of "my 3-band ramp only shows 2 bands" — half your texture is spent on the dark side.
2. **Only the RED channel is read**, and it is splatted to `vec3`. The gradient map is a monochrome *irradiance multiplier*, not a colour LUT. You cannot make a purple-shadow ramp this way — tint via `color`/`map` instead.
3. **`coord.y = 0.0`** — it is a 1×N sample along u only. Height must be 1.
4. The fallback (no gradientMap) is a hardcoded 2-tone `0.7 → 1.0` step with `fwidth` antialiasing at `coord.x == 0.7`.

`src/renderers/shaders/ShaderChunk/lights_toon_pars_fragment.glsl.js` — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mrdoob/three.js/dev/src/renderers/shaders/ShaderChunk/lights_toon_pars_fragment.glsl.js

```glsl
varying vec3 vViewPosition;

struct ToonMaterial {

	vec3 diffuseColor;

};

void RE_Direct_Toon( const in IncidentLight directLight, const in vec3 geometryPosition, const in vec3 geometryNormal, const in vec3 geometryViewDir, const in vec3 geometryClearcoatNormal, const in ToonMaterial material, inout ReflectedLight reflectedLight ) {

	vec3 irradiance = getGradientIrradiance( geometryNormal, directLight.direction ) * directLight.color;

	reflectedLight.directDiffuse += irradiance * BRDF_Lambert( material.diffuseColor );

}

void RE_IndirectDiffuse_Toon( const in vec3 irradiance, const in vec3 geometryPosition, const in vec3 geometryNormal, const in vec3 geometryViewDir, const in vec3 geometryClearcoatNormal, const in ToonMaterial material, inout ReflectedLight reflectedLight ) {

	reflectedLight.indirectDiffuse += irradiance * BRDF_Lambert( material.diffuseColor );

}

#define RE_Direct				RE_Direct_Toon
#define RE_IndirectDiffuse		RE_IndirectDiffuse_Toon
```

Critical: `RE_Direct_Toon` **replaces** the usual `dotNL` multiply — the ramp value *is* the irradiance. But `directLight.color` already has the light's intensity and distance attenuation folded in, so a `PointLight` with high intensity will blow the banded result past 1.0 and flatten your bands after tone mapping. And `RE_IndirectDiffuse_Toon` is plain Lambert — **ambient light is not banded**, it just lifts everything uniformly.

### Building a gradient map in code

**Correction to your assumption: it is `NoColorSpace`, not `SRGBColorSpace`.** Verbatim from the docs:

> "Gradient map for toon shading. It's required to set `Texture#minFilter` and `Texture#magFilter` to `NearestFilter` when using this type of texture. `gradientMap` represents non-color data. Any texture assigned must have `texture.colorSpace = NoColorSpace` (default)."

`NoColorSpace` is already the default, so the correct action is to **not touch `colorSpace`**. Setting `SRGBColorSpace` would make three.js request an `SRGB8_ALPHA8` internal format and apply an sRGB→linear decode to your ramp values, non-linearly crushing your band positions.

`DataTexture` docs: https://threejs.org/docs/pages/DataTexture.html — signature:

```js
new DataTexture( data, width, height, format, type, mapping, wrapS, wrapT, magFilter, minFilter, anisotropy, colorSpace )
```

**`DataTexture` already defaults both `magFilter` and `minFilter` to `NearestFilter`** (unlike base `Texture`, which defaults to Linear-family). So for a hand-built ramp the filters are correct out of the box — set them explicitly anyway for self-documentation and to survive a refactor to `TextureLoader`.

Working snippet:

```js
import * as THREE from 'three';

// N-band toon ramp. Returns a 1-row DataTexture usable as MeshToonMaterial.gradientMap.
function makeGradientMap( bands ) {
	const data = new Uint8Array( bands );
	for ( let i = 0; i < bands; i ++ ) {
		data[ i ] = Math.round( i / ( bands - 1 ) * 255 );  // 0 .. 255 inclusive
	}
	const tex = new THREE.DataTexture( data, bands, 1, THREE.RedFormat );
	tex.minFilter = THREE.NearestFilter;   // hard bands, no blending
	tex.magFilter = THREE.NearestFilter;
	tex.generateMipmaps = false;           // 1px-tall texture: mips are meaningless
	tex.wrapS = THREE.ClampToEdgeWrapping; // default, but explicit: never repeat a ramp
	tex.wrapT = THREE.ClampToEdgeWrapping;
	// colorSpace intentionally left at NoColorSpace (the default) — non-color data
	tex.needsUpdate = true;                // REQUIRED after constructing from a raw array
	return tex;
}

const material = new THREE.MeshToonMaterial( {
	color: 0xff6b35,
	gradientMap: makeGradientMap( 4 )
} );
```

`RedFormat` + `Uint8Array` is the minimal pairing (1 byte/texel) and matches the shader, which reads `.r`. `UnsignedByteType` is the default `type` and is what `Uint8Array` requires.

**Band count behaviour** — remember the `[-1,1] → [0,1]` remap means half the texels serve the unlit hemisphere:

- **2 texels** — pure lit/unlit split exactly at the terminator (`dotNL == 0`). Hardest possible look.
- **3 texels** (`0, 128, 255`) — texel 0 covers `dotNL ∈ [-1, -0.33]`, texel 1 covers `[-0.33, 0.33]`, texel 2 covers `[0.33, 1]`. Gives shadow / mid / light. This is the classic cel look and what `threeTone.jpg` approximates.
- **4 texels** — adds a second shadow step; reads as a soft core shadow plus terminator.
- **5 texels** (`fiveTone.jpg`) — approaches a smooth ramp; bands become subtle and read more as "stylised soft shading" than cel.

Because of the remap, for a strongly-lit look you often want a **non-linear** ramp that spends few texels on the dark half. Just write the array by hand: `new Uint8Array([ 0, 0, 0, 90, 200, 255, 255, 255 ])` gives a deep flat shadow, a tight terminator, and a flat highlight.

### The shipped gradient maps

Both confirmed present in the repo:

- `examples/textures/gradientMaps/threeTone.jpg` (11,040 bytes) — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mrdoob/three.js/dev/examples/textures/gradientMaps/threeTone.jpg
- `examples/textures/gradientMaps/fiveTone.jpg` (11,054 bytes) — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mrdoob/three.js/dev/examples/textures/gradientMaps/fiveTone.jpg

Directory listing: https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/tree/dev/examples/textures/gradientMaps

Canonical load code, verbatim from `docs/scenes/material-browser.html`:

```js
const gradientMaps = ( function () {

	const threeTone = textureLoader.load( '../../examples/textures/gradientMaps/threeTone.jpg' );
	threeTone.minFilter = THREE.NearestFilter;
	threeTone.magFilter = THREE.NearestFilter;

	const fiveTone = textureLoader.load( '../../examples/textures/gradientMaps/fiveTone.jpg' );
	fiveTone.minFilter = THREE.NearestFilter;
	fiveTone.magFilter = THREE.NearestFilter;

	return {
		none: null,
		threeTone: threeTone,
		fiveTone: fiveTone
	};

} )();
```

Note it sets **only** the two filters — no `colorSpace`, confirming the `NoColorSpace` default is intended. Caveat: these are **JPEGs**, so they carry compression ringing at the band edges. For clean bands, build a `DataTexture` instead; the shipped files are convenience assets for the demos.

### Official example pages

- **https://threejs.org/examples/#webgl_materials_toon** — page `<title>` is "three.js webgl - materials", subtitle **"Toon Material with OutlineEffect"**. Direct: https://threejs.org/examples/webgl_materials_toon.html
- Source: https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/dev/examples/webgl_materials_toon.html

**`webgl_materials_variations_toon` no longer exists** — it was renamed to `webgl_materials_toon`. Confirmed against https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mrdoob/three.js/dev/examples/files.json, which lists only `webgl_materials_toon` (plus a WebGPU sibling `webgpu_materials_toon`). Use the new name.

This example is doubly useful: it builds gradient maps procedurally **and** demonstrates `OutlineEffect`:

```js
const colors = new Uint8Array( alphaIndex + 2 );

for ( let c = 0; c <= colors.length; c ++ ) {

	colors[ c ] = ( c / colors.length ) * 256;

}

const gradientMap = new THREE.DataTexture( colors, colors.length, 1, THREE.RedFormat );
gradientMap.needsUpdate = true;
```

**Do not copy this loop verbatim — it has two bugs.** `c <= colors.length` writes one past the end (silently dropped by the typed array), and `* 256` combined with dividing by `colors.length` rather than `length - 1` means the ramp never reaches 255. My snippet above is the corrected form. It iterates 6 alpha steps (`stepSize = 1.0 / 5`), so it produces ramps of 2–7 texels.

Same file, the outline half:

```js
import { OutlineEffect } from 'three/addons/effects/OutlineEffect.js';
// ...
effect = new OutlineEffect( renderer );
// in the render loop, replacing renderer.render():
effect.render( scene, camera );
```

## 2) Inverted-hull outline

### OutlineEffect.js — confirmed, it IS an inverted hull

**Path confirmed:** `examples/jsm/effects/OutlineEffect.js`
**Source:** https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/dev/examples/jsm/effects/OutlineEffect.js
**Raw:** https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mrdoob/three.js/dev/examples/jsm/effects/OutlineEffect.js
**Docs:** https://threejs.org/docs/pages/OutlineEffect.html
**Import:** `import { OutlineEffect } from 'three/addons/effects/OutlineEffect.js';`

Self-described as "An outline effect for toon shaders". **WebGLRenderer only — it cannot be used with WebGPURenderer.**

Verified inverted hull: `createMaterial()` returns `side: BackSide`, and the vertex shader flips and extrudes along the normal.

```js
function createMaterial() {
	return new ShaderMaterial( {
		type: 'OutlineEffect',
		uniforms: UniformsUtils.merge( [
			UniformsLib[ 'fog' ],
			UniformsLib[ 'displacementmap' ],
			uniformsOutline
		] ),
		vertexShader: vertexShader,
		fragmentShader: fragmentShader,
		side: BackSide
	} );
}
```

**Parameters** (constructor: `new OutlineEffect( renderer, parameters )`):

| Parameter | Default |
|---|---|
| `defaultThickness` | `0.003` |
| `defaultColor` | `[ 0, 0, 0 ]` |
| `defaultAlpha` | `1.0` |
| `defaultKeepAlive` | `false` |

`defaultKeepAlive: false` means the internal cache of generated outline materials is **purged every frame for objects not rendered that frame**. If you have many objects entering and leaving the frustum you will thrash shader compilation — set `defaultKeepAlive: true` to trade memory for stable frame times.

Per-material override is via `userData`, not constructor args:

```js
mesh.material.userData.outlineParameters = {
	thickness: 0.01,
	color: [ 0, 0, 0 ],
	alpha: 1.0,
	visible: true,
	keepAlive: true
};
```

Read by `updateUniforms()`:

```js
function updateUniforms( material, originalMaterial ) {
	const outlineParameters = originalMaterial.userData.outlineParameters;
	material.uniforms.outlineAlpha.value = originalMaterial.opacity;

	if ( outlineParameters !== undefined ) {
		if ( outlineParameters.thickness !== undefined )
			material.uniforms.outlineThickness.value = outlineParameters.thickness;
		if ( outlineParameters.color !== undefined )
			material.uniforms.outlineColor.value.fromArray( outlineParameters.color );
		if ( outlineParameters.alpha !== undefined )
			material.uniforms.outlineAlpha.value = outlineParameters.alpha;
	}

	if ( originalMaterial.displacementMap ) {
		material.uniforms.displacementMap.value = originalMaterial.displacementMap;
		material.uniforms.displacementScale.value = originalMaterial.displacementScale;
		material.uniforms.displacementBias.value = originalMaterial.displacementBias;
	}
}
```

Note `outlineAlpha` is seeded from `originalMaterial.opacity` **before** the override is applied — a transparent material gets a transparent outline unless you set `alpha` explicitly.

**Thickness space — this is the important answer: neither view space nor world space. It is clip space, scaled by `pos.w`, which makes it effectively screen-space / NDC-proportional.** The full vertex shader:

```glsl
uniform float outlineThickness;

vec4 calculateOutline( vec4 pos, vec3 normal, vec4 skinned ) {
	float thickness = outlineThickness;
	const float ratio = 1.0;
	vec4 pos2 = projectionMatrix * modelViewMatrix * vec4( skinned.xyz + normal, 1.0 );
	vec4 norm = normalize( pos - pos2 );
	return pos + norm * thickness * pos.w * ratio;
}

void main() {
	#include <uv_vertex>
	#include <beginnormal_vertex>
	#include <morphnormal_vertex>
	#include <skinbase_vertex>
	#include <skinnormal_vertex>
	#include <begin_vertex>
	#include <morphtarget_vertex>
	#include <skinning_vertex>
	#include <displacementmap_vertex>
	#include <project_vertex>

	vec3 outlineNormal = - objectNormal;
	gl_Position = calculateOutline( gl_Position, outlineNormal, vec4( transformed, 1.0 ) );

	#include <logdepthbuf_vertex>
	#include <clipping_planes_vertex>
	#include <fog_vertex>
}
```

Reading it precisely: it projects `position + normal` to clip space, takes the normalised clip-space *difference* as the offset direction, then multiplies by `pos.w`. Since the perspective divide later divides by `w`, **the `* pos.w` cancels the divide — the outline width in NDC is constant regardless of distance from camera.** That is why the default is a tiny `0.003`: it is roughly a fraction of screen height, not a world-space distance. This also means a distant object gets an outline as thick as a near one, which can look wrong for large scenes — it is a deliberate stylistic choice (matching MMD/cel convention), not a bug.

Note `vec3 outlineNormal = - objectNormal;` negates the normal, then `normalize( pos - pos2 )` negates again — the two cancel, producing outward extrusion. It handles skinning, morph targets, and displacement maps correctly by running the standard chunks first.

Fragment shader is trivially flat:

```glsl
uniform vec3 outlineColor;
uniform float outlineAlpha;

void main() {
	#include <clipping_planes_fragment>
	#include <logdepthbuf_fragment>
	gl_FragColor = vec4( outlineColor, outlineAlpha );
	#include <tonemapping_fragment>
	#include <colorspace_fragment>
	#include <fog_fragment>
	#include <premultiplied_alpha_fragment>
}
```

Because it includes `<tonemapping_fragment>` and `<colorspace_fragment>`, a pure-black outline stays black, but a coloured outline will be tone-mapped — set `renderer.toneMapping = NoToneMapping` if you need exact outline colours.

### Rolling your own (the lazy path — no new class)

`onBeforeCompile` on a plain `MeshBasicMaterial` is the shortest thing that works, and avoids OutlineEffect's per-frame material cache entirely:

```js
function addOutline( mesh, thickness = 0.02, color = 0x000000 ) {
	const mat = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial( { color, side: THREE.BackSide } );
	mat.onBeforeCompile = ( shader ) => {
		shader.uniforms.uThickness = { value: thickness };
		shader.vertexShader = 'uniform float uThickness;\n' + shader.vertexShader
			.replace(
				'#include <begin_vertex>',
				'vec3 transformed = position + objectNormal * uThickness;'
			);
	};
	const outline = new THREE.Mesh( mesh.geometry, mat );  // shares geometry, no extra VRAM
	mesh.add( outline );
	return outline;
}
```

This is **object-space** thickness: the outline scales with the mesh and gets thinner as the camera pulls away (the opposite tradeoff to `OutlineEffect`). For constant screen-space width, extrude in clip space instead:

```glsl
// after #include <project_vertex>, gl_Position is in clip space
vec3 clipNormal = normalize( ( projectionMatrix * vec4( normalMatrix * objectNormal, 0.0 ) ).xyz );
gl_Position.xy += clipNormal.xy * uThickness * gl_Position.w;
```

Placement matters: `objectNormal` is only defined after `#include <beginnormal_vertex>`, which is why replacing `<begin_vertex>` (which runs after it) works and replacing anything earlier does not.

### Pitfall list

1. **Hard/split normals tear the hull open.** This is the number one failure. A cube, or any model with flat-shaded faces, has 3–4 *different* normals at each corner vertex position. Extruding along each one separately pulls the corner apart into disconnected face-quads, leaving visible gaps at every hard edge. **Fix:** weld positions and average normals before building the hull:
   ```js
   import { mergeVertices } from 'three/addons/utils/BufferGeometryUtils.js';
   const hullGeo = mergeVertices( mesh.geometry );  // welds coincident positions
   hullGeo.computeVertexNormals();                  // averages across the weld
   ```
   Use `hullGeo` for the outline only and keep the original geometry for the beauty pass so you do not lose your hard-edge shading. `mergeVertices` accepts a tolerance argument if your exporter emitted slightly-offset duplicates. Docs: https://threejs.org/docs/pages/BufferGeometryUtils.html
   For a cube specifically, welded+averaged normals point along the corner diagonals, so the hull becomes a rounded-corner cube — acceptable for outlines, but if you need a crisp silhouette store the smoothed normals in a **second attribute** (e.g. `aSmoothNormal`) and read that in the outline shader while the beauty pass keeps the real normals.

2. **Thickness scaling with distance** — pick your space deliberately. Object/world-space extrusion (`position + normal * t`) shrinks with distance and is correct for "the outline is a physical rim". Clip-space extrusion with `* gl_Position.w` (what `OutlineEffect` does) is constant on screen and is correct for "the outline is an ink line". Mixing the two across a scene looks inconsistent. Also: **non-uniform object scale breaks object-space extrusion** — a mesh scaled `(1, 1, 5)` gets a 5× thicker outline on one axis. Either normalise scale or extrude in view space using `normalMatrix`.

3. **Backface culling must be inverted, and depth must still be written.** `side: THREE.BackSide` is the whole trick — you draw only the far side of an inflated shell, so the original mesh punches through it and only the rim survives. If you also set `depthWrite: false` or `transparent: true` you will get the outline drawing over the object or z-fighting with it. Keep the outline opaque and depth-writing.

4. **Open/single-sided geometry has no backface to draw.** Planes, cloth, and ripped-open meshes produce no outline (or an inverted one). Inverted hull fundamentally needs a closed manifold.

5. **Multi-mesh GLTF models outline every child separately**, producing internal lines where parts touch. From the discourse thread on exactly this: merge the children into one geometry with `BufferGeometryUtils.mergeGeometries()` **for the outline only**, keeping the original hierarchy for rendering. Do this once at load time — merging at selection time is, quoted from the thread, "terribly slow". Cost is doubled triangle count. https://discourse.threejs.org/t/unsure-of-correct-approach-to-apply-outline-shader/68515

6. **It does not draw interior lines.** Inverted hull gives you silhouette only. Creases, folds, and detail edges need a post-process (see the Sobel / RenderPixelatedPass options below) — the two techniques are complements, not alternatives.

7. **Skinned meshes** need the extrusion applied *after* skinning, or the outline will detach during animation. `OutlineEffect` handles this by ordering `<skinning_vertex>` before `calculateOutline`. A naive `onBeforeCompile` replacing `<begin_vertex>` also works, because skinning transforms `transformed` afterwards — but then the thickness is in pre-skin space. Watch for this on heavily-deformed limbs.

## 3) RenderPixelatedPass

**Path:** `examples/jsm/postprocessing/RenderPixelatedPass.js`
**Source:** https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/dev/examples/jsm/postprocessing/RenderPixelatedPass.js
**Raw:** https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mrdoob/three.js/dev/examples/jsm/postprocessing/RenderPixelatedPass.js
**Docs:** https://threejs.org/docs/pages/RenderPixelatedPass.html
**Example page:** https://threejs.org/examples/#webgl_postprocessing_pixel
**Example source:** https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/dev/examples/webgl_postprocessing_pixel.html
**Import:** `import { RenderPixelatedPass } from 'three/addons/postprocessing/RenderPixelatedPass.js';`

### Constructor

```js
constructor( pixelSize, scene, camera, options = {} )
```

```js
const renderPixelatedPass = new RenderPixelatedPass( 6, scene, camera );
composer.addPass( renderPixelatedPass );
```

| Param | Type | Default | Range used by the official example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pixelSize` | number | — (required) | `.min(1).max(16).step(1)` |
| `scene` | Scene | — | |
| `camera` | Camera | — | |
| `options.normalEdgeStrength` | number | `0.3` | `.min(0).max(2).step(0.05)` |
| `options.depthEdgeStrength` | number | `0.4` | `.min(0).max(1).step(0.05)` |

Defaults use `||`, not `??`: `this.normalEdgeStrength = options.normalEdgeStrength || 0.3;`. **Passing `0` therefore silently becomes the default.** To disable an edge type at construction you must set the property afterwards: `pass.normalEdgeStrength = 0;`. Both are plain public properties read fresh every `render()`, so runtime mutation works (which is how the GUI binds directly to `renderPixelatedPass`, not to `params`).

`setPixelSize( pixelSize )` is the correct way to change pixel size at runtime — it re-runs `setSize` to resize the internal targets. Assigning `.pixelSize` directly does nothing until the next resize.

### Render targets

```js
this._beautyRenderTarget = new WebGLRenderTarget();
this._beautyRenderTarget.texture.minFilter = NearestFilter;
this._beautyRenderTarget.texture.magFilter = NearestFilter;
this._beautyRenderTarget.texture.type = HalfFloatType;
this._beautyRenderTarget.depthTexture = new DepthTexture();

this._normalRenderTarget = new WebGLRenderTarget();
this._normalRenderTarget.texture.minFilter = NearestFilter;
this._normalRenderTarget.texture.magFilter = NearestFilter;
this._normalRenderTarget.texture.type = HalfFloatType;
```

Both `NearestFilter` (so the upscale to screen stays blocky and the neighbour taps land on exact texels), both `HalfFloatType` (needed to survive tone mapping without banding), and the beauty target carries a `DepthTexture` for the depth edge test. The normal target has **no** depth texture — depth is read from the beauty target in both cases.

Sizing, verbatim:

```js
setSize( width, height ) {

	this._resolution.set( width, height );
	this._renderResolution.set( ( width / this.pixelSize ) | 0, ( height / this.pixelSize ) | 0 );
	const { x, y } = this._renderResolution;
	this._beautyRenderTarget.setSize( x, y );
	this._normalRenderTarget.setSize( x, y );
	this._fsQuad.material.uniforms.resolution.value.set( x, y, 1 / x, 1 / y );

}
```

So **pixelated size = resolution / pixelSize, floored via `| 0`**. The `resolution` uniform is a `Vector4` packing `(w, h, 1/w, 1/h)` — the `.zw` half is the texel size used for neighbour offsets, precomputed on the CPU to avoid a per-fragment divide.

The normal buffer is produced by `scene.overrideMaterial`, with correct save/restore:

```js
renderer.setRenderTarget( this._beautyRenderTarget );
renderer.render( this.scene, this.camera );

const overrideMaterial_old = this.scene.overrideMaterial;
renderer.setRenderTarget( this._normalRenderTarget );
this.scene.overrideMaterial = this._normalMaterial;
renderer.render( this.scene, this.camera );
this.scene.overrideMaterial = overrideMaterial_old;
```

`_normalMaterial` is a plain `MeshNormalMaterial`, so normals arrive **view-space, encoded `[-1,1] → [0,1]`**. That is a full second scene draw — the pass costs 2× geometry throughput.

### Edge detection, exactly

Neighbour sampling — a 4-tap **von Neumann** neighbourhood (N/S/E/W only, no diagonals), one pixelated-texel out:

```glsl
float getDepth(int x, int y) {

	return texture2D( tDepth, vUv + vec2(x, y) * resolution.zw ).r;

}

vec3 getNormal(int x, int y) {

	return texture2D( tNormal, vUv + vec2(x, y) * resolution.zw ).rgb * 2.0 - 1.0;

}
```

`resolution.zw` is `(1/w, 1/h)` at the *pixelated* resolution, so `vec2(1,0) * resolution.zw` steps exactly one low-res texel. `getNormal` decodes `[0,1] → [-1,1]`.

**Depth edges** — sums only the *positive* differences, i.e. only neighbours that are **further away** than this fragment. That means the test fires on the **near side** of a depth discontinuity, so the outline is drawn on the silhouette of the closer object rather than smeared across both:

```glsl
float depthEdgeIndicator(float depth, vec3 normal) {

	float diff = 0.0;
	diff += clamp(getDepth(1, 0) - depth, 0.0, 1.0);
	diff += clamp(getDepth(-1, 0) - depth, 0.0, 1.0);
	diff += clamp(getDepth(0, 1) - depth, 0.0, 1.0);
	diff += clamp(getDepth(0, -1) - depth, 0.0, 1.0);
	return floor(smoothstep(0.01, 0.02, diff) * 2.) / 2.;

}
```

The tail `floor(smoothstep(0.01, 0.02, diff) * 2.) / 2.` **quantises the result to exactly three levels: `0.0`, `0.5`, `1.0`.** This is deliberate — a continuous edge value would produce anti-aliased grey fringes and destroy the pixel-art look. The `0.01/0.02` thresholds are on raw non-linear depth-buffer values, which is why this pass is tuned for the example's `near: 0.1, far: 10` orthographic camera; with a perspective camera and a large far plane, non-linear depth compresses hard at distance and distant edges stop being detected.

**Normal edges** — a dot-product angle test, gated by depth so only one side of the edge lights up:

```glsl
float neighborNormalEdgeIndicator(int x, int y, float depth, vec3 normal) {

	float depthDiff = getDepth(x, y) - depth;
	vec3 neighborNormal = getNormal(x, y);

	// Edge pixels should yield to faces who's normals are closer to the bias normal.
	vec3 normalEdgeBias = vec3(1., 1., 1.); // This should probably be a parameter.
	float normalDiff = dot(normal - neighborNormal, normalEdgeBias);
	float normalIndicator = clamp(smoothstep(-.01, .01, normalDiff), 0.0, 1.0);

	// Only the shallower pixel should detect the normal edge.
	float depthIndicator = clamp(sign(depthDiff * .25 + .0025), 0.0, 1.0);

	return (1.0 - dot(normal, neighborNormal)) * depthIndicator * normalIndicator;

}

float normalEdgeIndicator(float depth, vec3 normal) {

	float indicator = 0.0;

	indicator += neighborNormalEdgeIndicator(0, -1, depth, normal);
	indicator += neighborNormalEdgeIndicator(0, 1, depth, normal);
	indicator += neighborNormalEdgeIndicator(-1, 0, depth, normal);
	indicator += neighborNormalEdgeIndicator(1, 0, depth, normal);

	return step(0.1, indicator);

}
```

Three multiplied factors:
- `(1.0 - dot(normal, neighborNormal))` — the raw angular difference. `0` for coplanar, `1` for perpendicular, `2` for opposed. This is the actual edge magnitude.
- `depthIndicator` — `sign(depthDiff * .25 + .0025)` clamped to `[0,1]`. Only the **shallower** (nearer) pixel of the pair reports the edge, so a crease produces a 1px line, not a 2px double line. The `+.0025` bias makes coplanar-but-equal-depth pixels count as "shallower" so flat creases still register.
- `normalIndicator` — the `normalEdgeBias` of `vec3(1,1,1)` is an arbitrary tie-breaker direction. When two faces meet, only the one whose normal points more towards `(1,1,1)` draws the highlight, again avoiding double lines. The source comment concedes `// This should probably be a parameter.` — it is hardcoded, so **your edge highlights have a fixed directional preference baked in**, which is visible as asymmetric highlighting when you orbit. If you need symmetric edges, fork the shader and expose this.

`step(0.1, indicator)` makes the final normal edge strictly **binary** — on or off, no gradient.

**Combination** — this is the neat part. Depth edges *darken*, normal edges *lighten*, and depth wins ties:

```glsl
void main() {

	vec4 texel = texture2D( tDiffuse, vUv );

	float depth = 0.0;
	vec3 normal = vec3(0.0);

	if (depthEdgeStrength > 0.0 || normalEdgeStrength > 0.0) {

		depth = getDepth(0, 0);
		normal = getNormal(0, 0);

	}

	float dei = 0.0;
	if (depthEdgeStrength > 0.0)
		dei = depthEdgeIndicator(depth, normal);

	float nei = 0.0;
	if (normalEdgeStrength > 0.0)
		nei = normalEdgeIndicator(depth, normal);

	float Strength = dei > 0.0 ? (1.0 - depthEdgeStrength * dei) : (1.0 + normalEdgeStrength * nei);

	gl_FragColor = texel * Strength;

}
```

The ternary is exclusive: if a depth edge exists at all (`dei > 0.0`), the fragment is **multiplied down** toward black (silhouette/outline); otherwise a normal edge **multiplies up** toward white (a lit crease highlight). Because it is a multiply on `texel`, the effect is a tint of the existing colour, not a flat ink line — it preserves hue. That is also why `depthEdgeStrength` maxes at `1` (at `1.0` with `dei == 1.0`, `Strength` reaches `0` = pure black) while `normalEdgeStrength` maxes at `2` (brightening has no natural ceiling).

Both branches are guarded by `if (strength > 0.0)`, so zeroing a strength genuinely skips the taps.

### Camera snapping — confirmed NOT handled by the pass

**Verified: `RenderPixelatedPass` contains no snapping logic whatsoever.** Its entire `render()` is the two scene draws plus the fullscreen quad, quoted above. There is no frustum manipulation, no position quantisation, no rotation snapping.

**All snapping lives in the example HTML**, not the pass. This is the standard gotcha: drop the pass into your project and moving the camera will make the pixel grid *swim* — pixels crawl across surfaces because the low-res grid is fixed in screen space while geometry slides continuously beneath it. You must implement snapping yourself. The example's implementation, verbatim from `webgl_postprocessing_pixel.html`:

```js
function pixelAlignFrustum( camera, aspectRatio, pixelsPerScreenWidth, pixelsPerScreenHeight ) {
  const worldScreenWidth = ( ( camera.right - camera.left ) / camera.zoom );
  const worldScreenHeight = ( ( camera.top - camera.bottom ) / camera.zoom );
  const pixelWidth = worldScreenWidth / pixelsPerScreenWidth;
  const pixelHeight = worldScreenHeight / pixelsPerScreenHeight;
  const camPos = new THREE.Vector3(); camera.getWorldPosition( camPos );
  const camRot = new THREE.Quaternion(); camera.getWorldQuaternion( camRot );
  const camRight = new THREE.Vector3( 1.0, 0.0, 0.0 ).applyQuaternion( camRot );
  const camUp = new THREE.Vector3( 0.0, 1.0, 0.0 ).applyQuaternion( camRot );
  const camPosRight = camPos.dot( camRight );
  const camPosUp = camPos.dot( camUp );
  const camPosRightPx = camPosRight / pixelWidth;
  const camPosUpPx = camPosUp / pixelHeight;
  const fractX = camPosRightPx - Math.round( camPosRightPx );
  const fractY = camPosUpPx - Math.round( camPosUpPx );
  camera.left   = - aspectRatio - ( fractX * pixelWidth );
  camera.right  =   aspectRatio - ( fractX * pixelWidth );
  camera.top    =   1.0 - ( fractY * pixelHeight );
  camera.bottom = - 1.0 - ( fractY * pixelHeight );
  camera.updateProjectionMatrix();
}
```

That is the key one: rather than quantising the camera *position* (which would make motion visibly stutter), it shifts the **frustum** by the sub-pixel fractional remainder, so the camera moves smoothly while the pixel grid stays locked to world space. Only works on an `OrthographicCamera`.

```js
function pixelAlignCamera( camera, target, rotationIncrementDegrees, zoomIncrement ) {
  if ( rotationIncrementDegrees > 0 ) {
    const increment = THREE.MathUtils.degToRad( rotationIncrementDegrees );
    const offset = new THREE.Vector3().subVectors( camera.position, target );
    const spherical = new THREE.Spherical().setFromVector3( offset );
    spherical.theta = Math.round( spherical.theta / increment ) * increment;
    spherical.phi   = Math.round( spherical.phi   / increment ) * increment;
    spherical.makeSafe();
    offset.setFromSpherical( spherical );
    camera.position.copy( target ).add( offset );
    camera.up.set( 0.0, 1.0, 0.0 );
    camera.lookAt( target );
  }
  if ( zoomIncrement > 0 ) {
    camera.zoom = Math.max( zoomIncrement, Math.round( camera.zoom / zoomIncrement ) * zoomIncrement );
    camera.updateProjectionMatrix();
  }
}
```

Example GUI defaults for these: `snapping: true, pixelAlignedPanning: true, pixelAlignedObjects: true, rotationSnap: 15, cameraRotationSnap: 9, cameraZoomSnap: 0.1` (rotation snaps in degrees, `.min(0).max(90).step(1)`; zoom `.min(0).max(1).step(0.05)`).

The animate loop uses a **save / mutate / render / restore** pattern, which is the part most people miss — the snapped values are used *only* for the render, then reverted so `OrbitControls` keeps operating on smooth un-snapped state:

```js
const cameraPosition = camera.position.clone();
const cameraQuaternion = camera.quaternion.clone();
const cameraZoom = camera.zoom;

if ( snapping && ( params[ 'cameraRotationSnap' ] > 0 || params[ 'cameraZoomSnap' ] > 0 ) ) {
  pixelAlignCamera( camera, controls.target, params[ 'cameraRotationSnap' ], params[ 'cameraZoomSnap' ] );
}

if ( snapping && params[ 'pixelAlignedPanning' ] ) {
  pixelAlignFrustum( camera, aspectRatio, pixelsPerScreenWidth, pixelsPerScreenHeight );
} else if ( camera.left != - aspectRatio || camera.top != 1.0 ) {
  camera.left = - aspectRatio; camera.right = aspectRatio;
  camera.top = 1.0; camera.bottom = - 1.0;
  camera.updateProjectionMatrix();
}

// ... pixelAlignObject / snapObjectRotation on crystalMesh ...

composer.render();

crystalMesh.position.copy( crystalPosition );
crystalMesh.rotation.copy( crystalRotation );
camera.position.copy( cameraPosition );
camera.quaternion.copy( cameraQuaternion );
camera.zoom = cameraZoom;
camera.updateProjectionMatrix();
```

Grid size is derived independently of the pass: `Math.floor( rendererSize.x / params['pixelSize'] )` — note you must keep this in sync with the pass's own `| 0` flooring or the grid will drift.

The example's camera and texture helper:

```js
camera = new THREE.OrthographicCamera( - aspectRatio, aspectRatio, 1, - 1, 0.1, 10 );

function pixelTexture( texture ) {
  texture.minFilter = THREE.NearestFilter;
  texture.magFilter = THREE.NearestFilter;
  texture.generateMipmaps = false;
  texture.colorSpace = THREE.SRGBColorSpace;
  return texture;
}
```

Note `SRGBColorSpace` **is** correct here — these are colour maps, unlike gradient maps.

## 4) Other examples, docs, and low-res rendering

### Relevant official examples (verified present in `examples/files.json`)

| Example | Page | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Toon material + OutlineEffect | https://threejs.org/examples/#webgl_materials_toon | https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/dev/examples/webgl_materials_toon.html |
| Pixelated render pass | https://threejs.org/examples/#webgl_postprocessing_pixel | https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/dev/examples/webgl_postprocessing_pixel.html |
| Sobel edge detection | https://threejs.org/examples/#webgl_postprocessing_sobel | https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/dev/examples/webgl_postprocessing_sobel.html |
| Selective outline (OutlinePass) | https://threejs.org/examples/#webgl_postprocessing_outline | https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/dev/examples/webgl_postprocessing_outline.html |

WebGPU siblings also exist for all four: `webgpu_materials_toon`, `webgpu_postprocessing_pixel`, `webgpu_postprocessing_sobel`, `webgpu_postprocessing_outline`. Relevant if you ever move off WebGLRenderer — remember `OutlineEffect` does **not** work on WebGPURenderer.

There is no `webgl_postprocessing_edge` or any `cel` example.

**Sobel setup** (note it is a *luminance* edge detector — it finds edges in the rendered image, so it will trace texture detail and lighting gradients as well as geometry, which is usually not what you want for clean cel outlines; `RenderPixelatedPass`'s depth+normal approach is geometrically correct):

```js
import { SobelOperatorShader } from 'three/addons/shaders/SobelOperatorShader.js';
import { LuminosityShader } from 'three/addons/shaders/LuminosityShader.js';
import { ShaderPass } from 'three/addons/postprocessing/ShaderPass.js';

const effectGrayScale = new ShaderPass( LuminosityShader );
composer.addPass( effectGrayScale );

const effectSobel = new ShaderPass( SobelOperatorShader );
effectSobel.uniforms[ 'resolution' ].value.x = window.innerWidth * window.devicePixelRatio;
effectSobel.uniforms[ 'resolution' ].value.y = window.innerHeight * window.devicePixelRatio;
composer.addPass( effectSobel );
```

The `resolution` uniform must be updated in your resize handler or edges will be the wrong width.

### EffectComposer

**Docs:** https://threejs.org/docs/pages/EffectComposer.html
**Source:** https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/dev/examples/jsm/postprocessing/EffectComposer.js
**Import:** `import { EffectComposer } from 'three/addons/postprocessing/EffectComposer.js';`

```js
new EffectComposer( renderer : WebGLRenderer, renderTarget : WebGLRenderTarget )
```

`renderTarget` optional (auto-created). Methods: `addPass( pass )`, `render( deltaTime )`, `setSize( width, height )` (resizes internal buffers **and every pass**, honouring pixel ratio), `setPixelRatio( pixelRatio )`. The last enabled pass is rendered to screen automatically.

Related: `Pass` / `FullScreenQuad` at https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/dev/examples/jsm/postprocessing/Pass.js — `FullScreenQuad` is what `RenderPixelatedPass` uses and is the right base for a custom fullscreen effect.

### OrthographicCamera

**Docs:** https://threejs.org/docs/pages/OrthographicCamera.html

```js
new OrthographicCamera( left = -1, right = 1, top = 1, bottom = -1, near = 0.1, far = 2000 )
```

`.zoom` defaults to `1`. Any change to frustum planes or zoom requires `.updateProjectionMatrix()`. Ortho is effectively mandatory for pixel-art snapping — `pixelAlignFrustum` above manipulates `left/right/top/bottom` directly and has no perspective equivalent.

### Low-res rendering — the canonical approaches

There are two, and they are for different jobs.

**(a) Low-res canvas, CSS upscale** — cheapest, no render targets, but pixelates the *entire* output including any UI drawn into the canvas, and gives you no depth/normal buffers for edge detection.

```js
const SCALE = 4;
renderer.setPixelRatio( 1 );                                        // ignore devicePixelRatio
renderer.setSize( window.innerWidth / SCALE, window.innerHeight / SCALE, false );
```

The `false` third argument is the load-bearing part. Verbatim from the docs:

> ".setSize( width : number, height : number, updateStyle : boolean ) — Resizes the output canvas to (width, height) with device pixel ratio taken into account, and also sets the viewport to fit that size, starting in (0, 0). Setting `updateStyle` to false prevents any style changes to the output canvas."

So `false` sets the canvas *backing store* to the low resolution while leaving the CSS size alone — the browser then stretches it. Pair with CSS to keep the upscale blocky rather than bilinear:

```css
canvas { width: 100%; height: 100%; image-rendering: pixelated; }
```

Also call `renderer.setPixelRatio( 1 )` — otherwise `setSize` multiplies your already-reduced size by the device pixel ratio and a retina display quietly undoes the effect. Docs: https://threejs.org/docs/pages/WebGLRenderer.html

**(b) `WebGLRenderTarget` at low resolution + `NearestFilter`** — the correct approach when you need the depth/normal buffers (i.e. any edge detection), or want the pixelation composited under crisp UI. This is what `RenderPixelatedPass` does internally.

```js
const rt = new THREE.WebGLRenderTarget( width / SCALE, height / SCALE, {
	minFilter: THREE.NearestFilter,   // MUST override — default is LinearFilter
	magFilter: THREE.NearestFilter,   // the one that actually controls the upscale
	type: THREE.HalfFloatType,        // survives tone mapping without banding
	depthBuffer: true
} );
```

`RenderTarget` constructor defaults, verbatim from `src/core/RenderTarget.js`:

```js
options = Object.assign( {
	generateMipmaps: false,
	internalFormat: null,
	minFilter: LinearFilter,
	depthBuffer: true,
	stencilBuffer: false,
	resolveColorBuffer: true,
	resolveDepthBuffer: true,
	resolveStencilBuffer: true,
	storeMultisampledColorBuffer: true,
	storeMultisampledDepthBuffer: true,
	storeMultisampledStencilBuffer: true,
	depthTexture: null,
	samples: 0,
	count: 1,
	depth: 1,
	multiview: false,
	useArrayDepthTexture: false
}, options );
```

Two traps here: **`minFilter` defaults to `LinearFilter`** so you must override it (and `magFilter`, which is inherited from `Texture`'s `LinearFilter` default and is the one that matters for upscaling); and **`samples` defaults to `0`** — do not raise it, MSAA anti-aliases exactly the hard pixel edges you are trying to create.

Docs: https://threejs.org/docs/pages/WebGLRenderTarget.html and https://threejs.org/docs/pages/RenderTarget.html

For a stylised pipeline, (b) via `EffectComposer` is the right default — `composer.setSize()` then propagates the resize to every pass for you.

---

## Summary of corrections to your assumptions

1. **Current release is r186**, not r18x-generic.
2. **Docs URLs changed** to `threejs.org/docs/pages/<Class>.html`; the `#api/en/...` hash form is obsolete.
3. **gradientMap must be `NoColorSpace`, not `SRGBColorSpace`** — it is non-color data. It is already the default, so set nothing. This is the opposite of the colour maps in the pixel example, which correctly use `SRGBColorSpace`.
4. **`webgl_materials_variations_toon` no longer exists** — renamed to `webgl_materials_toon`.
5. **`OutlineEffect` thickness is clip-space × `pos.w`**, i.e. constant in screen space — neither view nor world space as commonly assumed.
6. **`DataTexture` already defaults to `NearestFilter`** on both filters, unlike `WebGLRenderTarget`, which defaults to `LinearFilter` and must be overridden.
7. **`RenderPixelatedPass` confirmed to have zero camera snapping** — all of it is in the example file and you must port it yourself.
8. The `gradientMap` lookup is on **unclamped** `dotNL` remapped from `[-1,1]`, so half your ramp texels serve the unlit hemisphere.

**Strongest findings** (all replicated across the two sweeps' *different* engines; `sweep-p2` 9 600 games / 60 ranks primary, `sweep-d3` 4 000 / 100 ranks replication):

1. **Pace is army value, not fairy count.** `armyValue` (measured pawns of the 7 non-king pieces) correlates −0.79 with mean plies and −0.69 with draw rate — beating `fairyCount` (+0.66, +0.54). The pool holds exactly seven standard pieces, so `QRRBBNN` at 32.00 pawns is the *only* all-standard army; every fairy piece makes the army lighter (range 30.48 → 16.48). Fairy count 2→6: draws 0.221→0.438, plies 109→180.
2. **Queen = −10.8 draw points, −27 plies.** One queen is worth ~two fairy slots of pace.
3. **Guards wall the game — H10 confirmed.** 0→2 guards: +10.0 draw points (replication +14.0), survival 0.966. Guard effects on *balance* do not replicate.
4. **The paladin is the only fairy piece that sharpens** (−6 draw points) and it fires: survives 7% of games, captures in 89% (H5 predicted >30% never capture — it's 11%).
5. **Balance is flat.** No rank feature beats noise in both samples; between-rank spread ≈ 9 Elo.

**Dead weight:** the **beast** — utilisation 0.45 (a pawn is 0.43), never leaves its start square in 20% of games (31% from a-file, 30% from h), captures in 45%, chains ≥2 only 8.3% of the time. The **guard captures nothing in 13 120 games** (`guardCaptures:'none'`): immortal, inert, and 7.6% of promotions buy one anyway. **Placement:** a centre archer shoots 5.4× as often as an h-file archer (4 431 vs 827); corner archers/beasts are 2–8× more likely to be furniture. Sliders and knights are indifferent to their start file.

**Interest axis warning:** `nS` correlates −0.77 with interest because the +0.20 `minFairyUse` term is a *minimum*, and one beast drags it to 0.45. Strip that term and residualise on draw rate and the across-rank spread collapses from ±0.10 to ±0.019 against ~0.008 noise — **no back rank is distinguishable on interest right now.** Don't rank arrangements on it until the beast is fixed.

**Pilot (the one 100-game run, permitted):** value-matched court `AAGMMQN` (23.86 pawns) beat horde `SSLQBBG` (23.76) **0.790 ± 0.041** — ~+225 Elo where matched values predict zero, despite the horde holding more conventional material. The 1.70-pawn band floor badly overprices beast and guard in company.

**Batch 3:** 29 specs, 69 300 games, ~3.9 h at 5 games/s, ordered by information gain — the first four (50 min) separate army value from fairy count (`b3-val-*`, `b3-iso-*`), isolate the guard via the A→G swap at fixed value (`b3-guard0/1/2`), and certify the five uncertifiable ranks at 500 games (`b3-deep5`). ## 2026-09-13T15:06:08.236Z source line 311

# Empirical fairy-piece valuation — research notes

**Source-quality warning up front:** almost all of Muller's methodology exists only as forum posts (chess.com, TalkChess, GitHub issues) written by him. They are primary (his own words) but not peer-reviewed and never collected into one paper. I verified every quote below by fetching the page and grepping the raw text, except where marked `[unverified]`.

---

## 1. H.G. Muller — the asymmetric-material self-play method

**The core method, in his words** (chess.com, post #10, Jan 2018) — https://www.chess.com/forum/view/chess960-chess-variants/variant-pieces-values
> "Computer self-play from materially imbalanced positions. E.g. if you replace the Queen of one player by a Chancellor, and play a few hundred games, the side with the Queen will score about 58%. If you then delete an extra Pawn for the Queen side, the Chancellor wins by ~58%. So Q is halfway between C and C+P. You repeat that with all kind of other combinations."

Same thread, post #12 — the full protocol:
- "I mostly do this under opening conditions: start from a FIDE setup, and replace or delete a few of the pieces, to get material balanced to within ~1.5 Pawns."
- On why openings not endgames: endgame positions "often are already decided, so that scores are close to 100%, 50% or 0%, and not a continuous range that you could use to quantify the difference."
- Game diversity: "The engine randomizes the first four moves, by adding a random score of about 0.5 Pawn to each move in the root… If I want to do really large numbers of games, I start from a number of different positions that permute the backrank pieces in a Chess960-like way. And of course I always average results with reversed colors, to eliminate any first-move advantage."
- Triangulation across imbalances: "if replacing a Queen by a Chancellor in the standard FIDE opening position makes the score drop to 42%, I also test how well a Queen does against 2 Rooks… **To be consistent the score should always drop by ~8% when you replace Q by C in an opening position.**"

**Parallel worked example with different numbers** (Archbishop), https://www.chess.com/forum/view/chess-variants/how-can-i-figure-out-the-relative-piece-values-in-variants-i-come-up-with:
> "replace the Queen of one player by an Archbishop in the FIDE setup, and have the program play, say, 400 games against itself starting from that position. (To average out the first-move advantage, you can alternately replace the white and the black Queen.) The Queen will win such a match with a score of around 62%. But if you then delete the f-Pawn for the Queen side in addition, the Archbishop will score about 54%." → concludes Q = A + 0.75P.

Also from that page: **"Never believe piece values obtained by calculation, no matter how advanced. They are usually off by a large amount."**

## 2. Sample size and statistical error — actual numbers

- **The one concrete error bar I found.** https://www.chess.com/forum/view/chess960-chess-variants/hgmuller---would-like-your-help (Telepath test): "After the Queen vs Telepath test ended in about 59% advantage for the Queen after 500 games, I did the ultimate test by handicapping the Queen side by another Pawn, and playing **800 games from 16 different start positions** (also those whith Knights and Bishops swapped for white, black or both) to create more game diversity. The Telepath won this by 56%. **The statistical error in this is about 1.4%.**" → Telepath ≈ 8.9 when Q = 9.5.
- **Minimum for quarter-pawn resolution.** https://www.chess.com/forum/view/chess-variants/experiment-to-find-the-relative-value-of-variant-pieces: "To determine value difference to within a quarter of a Pawn needs at least 100 games, though." Same thread: his demo games ran "40 moves per minute, where a game lasts about 3 min", and he notes "Stockfish is developed using 10-second games, and would do 1800 games in that time."
- **General rule.** https://www.chess.com/forum/view/chess960-chess-variants/establishing-the-value-of-a-chess-piece: "The only way to know for sure is to play a couple of hundred materially unbalanced games, between equally strong opponents (i.e. self-play of a Chess engine)"; "You will need several hundreds of games to get the statistical error acceptably small."
- **Conversion (my arithmetic, not his):** he states classical pawn odds ≈ "65-68% score", i.e. 1 P ≈ 15-18% score. So 1.4% SE at 800 games ≈ **±8-9 cP ≈ ±0.09 Pawn**. At 100 games SE ≈ 4% ≈ ±25 cP, which matches his "quarter of a Pawn needs at least 100 games" exactly. Consistent, but I never found him state the cP-per-game scaling directly.
- Elsewhere he cites corpora of "tens of thousands of computer games" (https://www.chess.com/forum/view/chess-variants/fairy-chess-piece-values) and 64,957 games in a B-vs-N imbalance study (https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?t=45321).
- Keeping the experiment in the linear zone: "the sides that has the Bishops or Knights should be given additional Pawn odds… to get you in the score range where result score is approximately linearly dependent on material value."

## 3. Muller's findings on piece-value effects

**Measured 8x8 table** (two versions, ~6 years apart — note the revision):

| | 2018 (cP) | 2024 (pawns) |
|---|---|---|
| P | 100 | 1 |
| N | 325 | 3.25 |
| B | 325, **pair 700** | 3.25, **+0.50 pair bonus** |
| R | 500 | 5 |
| Q | 950 | 9.5 |
| BN (Archbishop/Princess) | 875 | 8.75 |
| RN (Chancellor/Empress) | 925 | **9.00** |

2018: https://www.chess.com/forum/view/chess960-chess-variants/variant-pieces-values (post #8). 2024: https://www.chess.com/forum/view/chess-variants/values-of-fairy-pieces (post #4) — "as determined by analyzing tens of thousands of GM games and (for the fairy pieces) tens of thousands of computer-computer games". The RN value moved 9.25 → 9.00; treat the last digit as soft.

- **Bishop pair = 50 cP, independently confirmed.** Same 2024 thread: "According to the statistics in GM games that Larry Kaufman investigated, the B-pair should be 50cP. This is the same conclusion I got from comp-comp games: an imbalance of B-pair vs N-pair in the initial position results in a winning percentage for the B that exactly reverses when you handicap those by deleting one of the Pawns."
- **Synergy/cooperation is large and is NOT mainly colorboundness.** Same thread: "The Princess indeed shows remarkable synergy between the B and N moves. Breaking the color binding of the Bishop cannot be the whole story; a Bishop with a single extra orthogonal non-capture step is not color bound, but a pair of those doesn't gain very much value compared to a normal Bishop pair… **My best guess is that it is the number of orthogonal contacts between the move patterns that provides most of the synergy.**" (B 3.25 + N 3.25 = 6.5 vs measured 8.75 → ~+2.25 pawns of synergy.)
- **Short-Range Leaper Law.** value(cP) = α·[30N + 0.625N²], N = squares attacked; later refits 31.5N+0.66N², then 33N+0.69N² / "33*N+0.7*N*N". α ≈ 1.0 on the classical N=300 scale, 1.1 on the Kaufman N=325 scale. Muller's own gloss: https://www.chess.com/forum/view/chess960-chess-variants/formula-to-estimate-a-leaping-piece-s-value — "'Short range' here means up to two King steps away. So pieces like Camel are not included. **The formula was derived by fitting empirical values measured on an 8x8 board**". He accepted the name "the Short-range leaper law". Note the law is **superlinear in N** — that is the synergy effect baked into a fit.
- **Colorbound / restricted-range pieces.** Camel (1,3 leaper) "next to worthless on 8x8… opening value of the Camel about 250", dropping as the board empties (forking power only). Alfil/Dabbaba "nearly worthless; less than a FIDE Pawn". A pair of Ferzes tested "~25cP weaker than a Knight" (https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?t=67776). Two Xiangqi Horses ≈ one FIDE Knight (lameness penalty).
- **Board size matters a lot.** "Board size strongly affects the piece values. On 8x8 a lone Bishop and a lone Knight are about equal in value; on 10x8 they already differ by half a Pawn." Also "Nightriders are worth about half a Pawn more than Rooks. On an 8x8 board." (chess.com "How can I figure out…" thread.)
- **Value depends on the opponent's material — "levelling" / "elephantiasis".** The name *Levelling Effect* is **Betza's**, not Muller's: https://www.chessvariants.com/d.betza/pieceval/levelling.html — "Chess has a democratic tendency that tends to make all pieces become more nearly equal in value; I call it the Levelling Effect." Muller quantified it. His mechanism (https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?t=45321): "You can never stray on a square under attack by an inferior piece, no matter how well you control that square, because it will always at least give the opponent a favorable trade." Applied to 10x8 (https://www.chess.com/forum/view/chess-variants/chess-variants-chess-variants-gothic-chess-4?page=2): "in orthodox Chess a Queen is much better than Rook + Knight… But it is not true when C and A are still on the board. Then R+N is significantly stronger than Q… R+N strongly hinder the remaining C and A, which have to avoid being traded for them." The label "elephantiasis effect" is attributed to Muller by the Chess Programming Wiki (https://chessprogramming.org/Point_Value) — I could not find him using that term in his own prose.
- **Additivity fails.** https://talkchess.com/forum3/viewtopic.php?t=72726: Archbishop "beats Rook + Knight (two separate pieces) more often than not"; and on calculation-based methods generally — "Its evaluation algorithm for piece values is proprietry, but it is unlikely to go much beyond the calculation of some weigthed average of mobility. Which is a very unreliable method."
- **Move-type weights, derived empirically** (https://www.chess.com/forum/view/chess960-chess-variants/hgmuller---would-like-your-help): "captures contributed about twice as much to the value as non-captures… and that forward moves contribute about twice as much as sideway or backward moves." Also: "On a Bishop the power to jump to the 2nd square turned out to be worth as much as all moves beyond it; on a Queen it was worth as much as all moves beyond the third."

## 4. Engine strength and time control

This is the question where Muller's answer is most counterintuitive and most useful to you:

- **A weak engine still measures correctly, and a *wrong* seed value still works** (variant-pieces-values #12): "The engine is a normal alpha-beta searcher, with very basic evaluation: just piece values, a bonus for centralizing some of the pieces… No neural networks. To get realistic play, you have to put in a approximately correct piece value, **although this is not very critical**. E.g. if you play the games with an engine that believes the Chancellor is worth more than a Queen, the Chancellor will still lose, probably by a differerence of even more than 8%."
- **But there is a failure mode — the seed must not invert an exchange.** "**if I will set the value of an Archbishop to below that of a Rook, it will never discover how strong an Archbishop really is**, because it is strong enough to always force a trade for a Rook (which it will believe to be a gain), no matter how much the Rooks will try to avoid it." → his fix: **iterate** — "I just do a scond iteration of the experiment, with the value deduced from the result of the first."
- **Time control is a throughput knob, not a correctness knob.** He recommends Fairy-Max over slower tools because it is "a lot stronger, so that you can use faster time control to get the same quality of play." No claim that measured values shift systematically with TC.

## 5. Muller's engines

- **Fairy-Max** — purpose-built for exactly this. Docs: https://home.hccnet.nl/h.g.muller/CVfairy.html and https://www.chessvariants.com/index/msdisplay.php?itemid=MSfairy-max. Table-driven pieces via `fmax.ini`, boards up to 12x8; piece movement model (leaper/slider/hopper/alternator bits) documented at https://home.hccnet.nl/h.g.muller/fairy.html. Warning in the docs: "Fairy-Max is not smart enough to figure this out by itself. If you tell it an immensely powerful piece like a Queen is only worth half a Pawn, it will happily trade it for one!"
- **Joker80** (10x8 Capablanca/Gothic): https://home.hccnet.nl/h.g.muller/joker80.html — candidly "I did not spend any real effort on the evaluation yet… values for Archbishop and Chancellor had to be invented." Not a measurement tool.
- **Correction to your brief: Sjaak / SjaakII is not Muller's.** It is Evert Glebbeek's (https://chessprogramming.org/Sjaak_(Glebbeek)). Muller recommends it as an alternative measuring engine alongside NebiyuAlien.
- **Spartan Chess:** Fairy-Max supports it via "delocalized royalty" (negative piece values encode royalty; https://manpages.ubuntu.com/manpages/trusty/man6/maxqi.6.html). He also references his own Spartan engine "Spartacus". I found **no published Spartan piece-value table** — only the draw-rate figure below.

## 6. Ralph Betza — "About the Values of Chess Pieces" (1996)

Contents/index: https://www.chessvariants.com/d.betza/pieceval/ (note: chessvariants.com 403s to most fetchers; a browser User-Agent works).

- **Intro** (https://www.chessvariants.com/d.betza/pieceval/intro.html): opens by contrasting STANDARD (P1/N3/B3/R5/Q9), SPIELMANN (R4.5/Q8.5) and PROGRAM (N3.3/B3.3/R5/Q9.5) tables — "the difference between the correct values and the values used by most players is large enough that you can use it to win games!"
- **The "crowded board" discount is his central method** (https://www.chessvariants.com/d.betza/pieceval/betterway.html): don't average mobility on an *empty* board — weight each slider step by the probability the intervening squares are empty. Rook on a1 "is certain of being able to reach a2 but has only a 50% chance of getting to a3, one chance in 4 to reach a4…". Result: R 6.0, B 4.75, Q 10.75 — which he immediately says are "much too low", because "the board doesn't stay 50% full for long". The emptiness probability is the free parameter: "The probability that a square is empty is the key to it all."
- **The five factors** (https://www.chessvariants.com/d.betza/pieceval/forward.html): "Mobility, Forwardness, Distance, Colorboundness, and Capture seem to be the five main factors."
  - Forwardness: "multiplying the number of forward moves times the mobility of those moves times the square root of the distance of those moves produces a number with some predictive power, but it seems so *ad hoc*." He credits forwardness for Q > R+B: "Forwardness must be the main reason why the Queen is worth more than the sum of the values of Rook and Bishop. More directions of movement, more forking power."
  - Colorboundness: acknowledged as a penalty, explicitly **not quantified** — "how to quantify it?"
- **Betza also ran self-play, at scale, in the 1990s** (https://www.chessvariants.com/d.betza/pieceval/moredata.html): Waffle (W+A) replacing Knights — "after **5256 games**, White's winning rate was **0.457002** (for reference, White's winning rate in standard chess was **0.49227 after 13842 games**)." Opening permuted 6 ways (Ra1/Nb1/Bc1, Ra1/Bb1/Nc1, …); "One machine can crank out 36 games in four hours." He is blunt about validity: "The results are reproducible, but their meaning is unclear" — K vs N measured 0.37 win rate until he found a better strategy for the King side that made it >50%. Summary page (https://www.chessvariants.com/d.betza/pieceval/sum01.html): "I described a way of testing values empirically, which gives **very precise results of dubious meaning**."
- **Mating potential / "safe checks"** appears as *Can-Mate* in his factor list (https://www.chessvariants.com/d.betza/pieceval/p7-01.html): "The WD is a lot weaker than the HFD, but the Pawnless endgame of K+WD versus K is a win, and the endgame of K+HFD versus K is only a draw." Same page lists Center Control, Carpet Bombing, Pawn Cooperation, Rank, Role, Location, Restrictions on Being Captured, Occupation, Stealth, Sociability. These are named, not quantified.
- **Hoppers**: Cannon/Grasshopper mobility is computable under the same emptiness-probability framework (https://www.chessvariants.com/d.betza/pieceval/p7-02.html).

### Betza's "Ideal and Practical Values" series — yes, it exists (6 parts)
All under https://www.chessvariants.com/piececlopedia.dir/ : `ideal-and-practical-values.html`, `-2.html` (Atomic Pieces and Subatomic Movements), `-3.html` (The Rider Problem), `-4.html` (Odds and Ends), `-5.html` (Modified Jumpers), `-6.html` (A Case Study in Piece Values).

**This is the "atoms" formula you were after, and it is far simpler than his 1996 work:**
- Part 1: "the ideal values of simple one-step pieces are absurdly simple: **however many different moves it can make, that's its ideal value.** An Alfil moves to 4 different squares, so it is ideally worth half as much as a Knight, which moves to 8." Combine any 2 half-knight atoms (W, F, A, D, Crab, Barc, …) → Knight/Bishop value; any 3 → Rook; 4 → Archbishop; 5 → Queen; 7 → Amazon.
- The **ideal vs practical split** is the key idea: "each piece has two values… the practical value of that particular piece, considering all its specific weaknesses and strengths; and the **ideal value** of that piece, the abstract value that the piece has when combining the moves of two pieces masks the weaknesses of both." Masking rule: "adding W or Crab to a colorbound piece nearly always does the trick."
- Part 2 subdivides atoms into directional "subatomic movements" (a Ferz = 4 move + 4 capture directions), and warns the ideal value collapses for pieces with many non-capturing moves, capture-only moves, or lopsided forwardness.
- Part 3 gives his on-board probability formula explicitly: for an (x,y) jump on a w×h board, P = ((w−x)(h−y))/(w·h); ×8 directions gives the Knight's 5.25 average moves on 8x8. He concedes the rider case is unsolved: "The probability that a square is empty varies… so there isn't one perfect number for the average mobility of a rider."

## 7. Fairy-Stockfish

- **Custom piece definition** — `variants.ini` (https://github.com/fairy-stockfish/Fairy-Stockfish/blob/master/src/variants.ini), slots `customPiece1`…`customPiece25`, e.g. `customPiece1 = p:mfWcfF`, using a documented **subset** of Betza notation (it links https://www.gnu.org/software/xboard/Betza.html).
- **Per-variant piece values ARE settable** (variants.ini lines 109-118, verbatim):
  > `### Piece values` / "The predefined and precalculated piece values can be overridden by specifying the pieceValueMg and pieceValueEg options, e.g., `pieceValueMg = p:150 n:800` / `pieceValueEg = p:200 n:900`. For orientation, the internal predefined piece values can be found in types.h. A suitable piece for gauging the piece values is the rook, which internally has: `pieceValueMg = r:1276` / `pieceValueEg = r:1380`"
- **Published FSF value table** — `src/types.h` lines 365-400 (https://github.com/fairy-stockfish/Fairy-Stockfish/blob/master/src/types.h). Internal scale, P=126/208 Mg/Eg:

  `Pawn 126/208 · Knight 781/854 · Bishop 825/915 · Rook 1276/1380 · Queen 2538/2682 · Fers 420/450 · Alfil 350/330 · FersAlfil 700/650 · Silver 660/640 · Aiwok 2300/2700 · Bers 1800/1900 · Archbishop 2200/2200 · Chancellor 2300/2600 · Amazon 2700/2850 · Knibis 1100/1200 · Biskni 750/700 · Kniroo 1050/1250 · Rookni 800/950 · ShogiPawn 90/100 · Lance 400/240 · ShogiKnight 420/290 · Gold 720/700 · DragonHorse 1550/1550 · Cannon 800/700 · JanggiCannon 800/600 · Soldier 200/270 · Horse 520/800 · Elephant 300/300 · JanggiElephant 340/350 · Banner 3400/3500 · Wazir 400/350 · Commoner 700/900 · Centaur 1800/1900`

  **Worth flagging for your project:** normalize by Rook=500 and FSF gives Archbishop ≈ 862, Chancellor ≈ 901, Queen ≈ 994 — close to Muller's 875/925/950, but FSF puts A further below C than Muller does.
- **How they were derived: mostly hand-set, admittedly under-tuned.** Fichter (`ianfab`) in https://github.com/fairy-stockfish/Fairy-Stockfish/issues/135 — "Piece values in Fairy-SF are **not as heavily tuned** (since they need to be a good compromise for all variants) as in Seirawan-SF, so it is very possible that they might be slightly off." On TalkChess (https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?t=72754&start=10): "In Fairy-Stockfish the base piece values are the same for all variants, they are only adjusted for a few rules"; drop variants scale by `v_max/(v_max+v)` with `v_max` ≈ 3×Queen.
- **Variant adaptation is computed but largely unused — Muller found the bug.** https://github.com/fairy-stockfish/Fairy-Stockfish/issues/968 was opened by **HGMuller** (2026-01-08): adapted values go into `CapturePieceValue`/`EvalPieceValue`, not `PieceValue`. Fichter's reply: "The PieceValue entries are very sensitive for the standard chess pieces, therefore I was very hesitant to dynamically change them… because it affects basically all games, **testing is very difficult**… I never arrived at a conclusion." So FSF's per-variant/board-size adjustment reaches SEE and (partly) eval, but not the main material term.
- **The board-size scaling that does exist** is in `src/psqt.cpp` (comment: `// Scale slider piece values with board size`), blending leaper-step count and slider-direction count: `score * (lc*leaper + r1*slider) / (lc*leaper + r0*slider)`. https://github.com/fairy-stockfish/Fairy-Stockfish/blob/master/src/psqt.cpp
- SPSA tuner exists as a separate repo (https://github.com/fairy-stockfish/spsa) but I found **no public record of piece values being SPSA-tuned** — the evidence points to inherited Stockfish constants + hand-chosen fairy constants + formulaic adjustment. Related open issue: https://github.com/fairy-stockfish/Fairy-Stockfish/issues/1036 ("variants.ini pieceValue never reaches material, SEE or move ordering").

## 8. Chess960 per-position balance, and Capablanca drawishness

**Chess960 — Barthelemy, "Not all Chess960 positions are equally complex"** (arXiv 2512.14319, submitted 2025-12-16, revised 2026-03-09). Abstract: https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.14319 · full text: https://arxiv.org/html/2512.14319. Numbers below are grepped from the HTML, **not** from a summarizer — two separate WebFetch passes returned mutually inconsistent figures (#333/#774/+0.28), so trust only these:
- Stockfish 17.1, **depth 30**, NNUE, single thread, 1GB hash, all 960 positions.
- Mean initial eval **⟨E⟩ = +0.297 ± 0.136 pawns** (abstract rounds to +0.30 ± 0.14); **σ = 0.14**.
- **956 of 960 (99.6%)** evaluate positive for White. "Only four position achieve exact or close to balance."
- Most White-favourable: **#279 (NRBKNRQB), +0.83** — "approximately 2.8 times the mean".
- Closest to balance: **#535 (RNBKQNRB), −0.09** (infinitesimal Black edge).
- Standard chess **#518 = +0.30, 47th percentile** — "statistically typical within the Chess960 landscape."
- Author's own caveat: "these results depend on the engine and search depth. While specific outliers may shift, the overall distribution and its statistics remain robust."
- Separate complexity result: most complex #226 (BNRQKBNR), simplest #316, most balanced on both axes #198 (QNBRKBNR); #518 sits at the 91st percentile of *asymmetry* (Black carries the harder decisions) but its σ swallows the effect.
- Popular coverage: https://physicsworld.com/a/chess960-still-results-in-white-having-an-advantage-finds-study/ · https://en.chessbase.com/post/complexity-chess960-marc-barthelemy

**Capablanca/Gothic is LESS drawish, not more** — Muller, https://www.chess.com/forum/view/chess960-chess-variants/decreasing-draws-result:
> "There is no reason at all to assume adding a medium-strength piece will have any effect on draw rate. In general such games will keep a **~32% draw rate**, just like orthodox Chess. Games that reduce draw rate typically add a number of super-pieces, which enhance the probability that the game ends in the middle-game by a devastating mate attack (**Capablanca/Gothic Chess, which has 16% draw rate**). Or variants where white and black have a completely different set of pieces, so that symmetric end-games (which tend to be the most drawish ones) are impossible. **Spartan Chess has only a 26% draw rate.**"

He also states the mechanism for why adding a *medium* piece does nothing: "Games like Chess have a draw margin, and the initial position lies deep within the draw zone… the presence of a medium-valued piece just doesn't change the 'diffusion rate' of the score very much." **Caveat: forum post, no game counts, engine, or TC given for the 32/16/26% figures.** Treat as an order-of-magnitude claim, not a measurement you can cite.

---

## What this implies for a King Down balance protocol

1. Copy Muller's harness literally: FIDE-like opening, swap one piece, mirror colors, randomize the first ~4 plies with ±0.5 pawn root noise, permute the back rank Chess960-style, keep the imbalance inside ~1.5 pawns so the score stays in the linear zone.
2. Budget **~800 games per measurement** for ±1.4% ≈ ±0.09 pawn; ~100 games only buys ±0.25 pawn.
3. **Iterate the seed value.** One pass with a wrong seed can be systematically blind — specifically when the seed inverts a plausible exchange.
4. Bracket rather than point-estimate: measure X vs Y, then X vs Y+P, and interpolate.
5. Don't trust any additive/mobility formula for a compound piece — Muller measures ~+2.25 pawns of unexplained synergy on the Archbishop alone, and his own leaper law is superlinear in N for the same reason.
6. Two gaps I could not close: no primary Muller text quantifying a *generic* colorbound penalty (only per-piece measurements), and no published Spartan Chess piece-value table.

**Root cause is not the style — it is four measured faults:**

- Pieces render at **34.7 virtual px** on desktop and **18.9 on a phone** (portrait sizes the ortho camera by `size/aspect`, blowing the view to 14.5 units); target is 48–64. At **0.96 px per model voxel**, the 37-voxel sculpts are pure aliasing.
- `RenderPixelatedPass` ends `gl_FragColor = texel * Strength` — a multiply. It **structurally cannot outline the dark army**.
- Indigo on a dark tile is **1.01 : 1** contrast.
- DB32 nearest-colour matching speckles single surfaces across unrelated hues.

**Tested offline** against `public/sprites/`: 56 px + 4 toon bands + bespoke per-material ramps + a 1 px contrast rim reads as hand-made pixel art. Gain order: **rim > ramps > resolution** — the two cheapest changes are the biggest.

**Recommendation:** toon-pixel hybrid (`MeshToonMaterial` 4-band + inverted-hull outline + `pixelSize` 2 desktop / 1 phone). Of the three sprite schemes on disk use **ivory-charcoal**; `blue-red` puts both armies at the same luminance (1.11 : 1).
