# 32-bit isometric pre-rendered sprites: verified technical reference

## 1. Diablo 1 (Blizzard North / Condor, 1996)

**Pipeline & directions — primary source, the 1994 Condor pitch doc** ([full text, archive.org](https://archive.org/stream/diablo_pitch/diablo_pitch_djvu.txt)):
> "We intend for the game to operate in Super VGA mode (640x480 pixels). The three-quarter perspective requires eight directions of movement, three of which can sometimes be flipped. Each monster will have multiple graphic deaths and will require at least 50 frames of animations."

- Shipped engine confirms **8 facings**: `enum class Direction { South, SouthWest, West, NorthWest, North, NorthEast, East, SouthEast, NoDirection }` — [devilutionX/Source/engine/direction.hpp](https://github.com/diasurgical/devilutionX/blob/master/Source/engine/direction.hpp). CL2 multi-group files store one frame group per facing.
- **3D Studio for Diablo 1: UNVERIFIED.** I found no primary source naming the tool. It *is* verified for Diablo II (below). Don't assert it for D1.

**Sprite dimensions (verified, from devilutionX's data tables — these are the original game's values):**

Player sprite widths, [assets/txtdata/classes/*/sprites.tsv](https://github.com/diasurgical/devilutionX/blob/master/assets/txtdata/classes/warrior/sprites.tsv):

| class | stand | walk | attack | bow | swHit | block | lightning | fire | magic | death |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| warrior | 96 | 96 | 128 | 96 | 96 | 96 | 96 | 96 | 96 | 128 |
| rogue | 96 | 96 | 128 | 128 | 96 | 96 | 96 | 96 | 96 | 128 |
| sorcerer | 96 | 96 | 128 | 128 | 96 | 96 | 128 | 128 | 128 | 128 |
| monk (Hellfire) | 112 | 112 | 130 | 130 | 98 | 98 | 114 | 114 | 114 | 160 |

- **Monster widths: only three values exist across all 112 monster rows** — 96 px (9 rows), 128 px (69), 160 px (34). [assets/txtdata/monsters/monstdat.tsv](https://github.com/diasurgical/devilutionX/blob/master/assets/txtdata/monsters/monstdat.tsv)
- Frame **heights** are derived from decoded pixel count ÷ supplied width in `Cl2ToClx`, not stored in CL2 — so "96×96 square" is the common assumption but is **unverified** from spec.
- Warrior frame counts ([animations.tsv](https://github.com/diasurgical/devilutionX/blob/master/assets/txtdata/classes/warrior/animations.tsv)): idle 10, walk 8, sword attack 16 (action frame 9), axe 20 (10), bow 16 (11), block 2, death 20, cast 20 (14), recovery 6, town idle 20, town walk 8.

**Tile geometry** ([MIN-TIL.md](https://github.com/savagesteel/d1-file-formats/blob/master/PC-Mac/MIN-TIL.md)):
- Base CEL frame for levels = **32×32 px**; floor/wall-bottom types split into two 32×16 halves ([CEL.md](https://github.com/savagesteel/d1-file-formats/blob/master/PC-Mac/CEL.md))
- Subtile ground layer = **64×32 px**; full subtile = **64×160** (10 frames) for dungeon/catacombs/caves/nest/crypt, **64×256** (16 frames) for Town and Hell
- TIL megatile = **128×192** (Town/Hell 128×288)

**Palette handling:**
- PAL = **768 bytes, 256 colours, 3 bytes RGB**; `COLOR PALETTE OFFSET = 3 * PALETTE INDEX` ([PAL.md](https://github.com/savagesteel/d1-file-formats/blob/master/PC-Mac/PAL.md))
- TRN = **256 bytes, one index→index remap per entry** ([TRN.md](https://github.com/savagesteel/d1-file-formats/blob/master/PC-Mac/TRN.md))
- **TRN is Diablo's "team colour" analogue.** Monster colour variants are the *same CL2 art* + a different 256-byte remap: Zombie / Ghoul / Rotting Carcass / Black Death all use `zombie\zombie` with trn `—`, `zombie\bluered`, `zombie\grey`, `zombie\yellow`. Fallen One / Carver / Dark One share `falspear` art with `falspear\fallent`, `\dark`, `\blue`. Skeletons: `skelaxe\white`, `skelaxe\skelt`, `skelaxe\black`. (monstdat.tsv, column `trnFile`)
- **Lighting is also palette remapping**: 16 light levels, each a 256-entry index table — `constexpr char LightsMax = 15; constexpr size_t LightTableSize = 256; constexpr size_t NumLightingLevels = LightsMax + 1;` ([lighting_defs.hpp](https://github.com/diasurgical/devilutionX/blob/master/Source/engine/lighting_defs.hpp), [light_tables.hpp](https://github.com/diasurgical/devilutionX/blob/master/Source/engine/light_tables.hpp))
- **Colour cycling is confined to the low indices** ([Source/engine/palette.cpp](https://github.com/diasurgical/devilutionX/blob/master/Source/engine/palette.cpp)):
  - caves: `CycleColors(1, 31)`
  - crypt: lava `CycleColorsReverse(1, 15)` every other frame + glow `CycleColorsReverse(16, 31)` every frame — *"Lava has 15 colors and the glow 16, so the full animation has 240 frames before it loops"*
  - hive: `CycleColorsReverse(1, 8)` + `CycleColorsReverse(9, 15)` every 3rd frame — *"Bubles have 8 colors and waves 7, so the full animation has 56 frames before it loops"*
  - `lighting_color_cycling()` rotates **indices 1–31** inside every light table ([lighting.cpp](https://github.com/diasurgical/devilutionX/blob/master/Source/lighting.cpp))
- CL2 encoding ranges ([CL2.md](https://github.com/savagesteel/d1-file-formats/blob/master/PC-Mac/CL2.md)): `[0x01,0x7F]` transparent run, `[0x80,0xBE]` repeated index, `[0xBF,0xFF]` literal run. Frame header = 5 WORDs pointing at 32-pixel-line blocks.

**Diablo II, for pipeline comparison** — [Game Developer postmortem](https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/postmortem-blizzard-s-i-diablo-ii-i-): *"Almost all of Diablo II's in-game and cinematic art was constructed and rendered in 3D Studio Max"*; *"An in-house tool would render the files from many different angles (eight for all monsters, 16 for player characters)"*; 640×480, 8-bit colour.

---

## 2. Fallout 1 / 2 (Interplay)

**FRM format** — [fodev.net FRM docs](https://fodev.net/files/fo2/frm.html) (current, derived from Fallout 2 CE) and [Falltergeist wiki](https://github.com/falltergeist/libfalltergeist/wiki/Frm-file-format):
- Header is **always 0x3E bytes**: `version`, `fps`, `action_frame`, `frames_per_direction`, `int16 x_offsets[6]`, `int16 y_offsets[6]`, `uint32 data_offsets[6]` (relative to 0x3E), `frame_area_size`
- Frame record: `uint16 width`, `uint16 height`, `uint16 size`, `int16 x`, `int16 y`, then `size` bytes of **palette indices** (1 byte/pixel)
- **6 directions.** Rotation numbering per the engine: *"Rotations use six directions: 0 northeast, 1 east, 2 southeast, 3 southwest, 4 west, and 5 northwest"* ([fodev MAP docs](https://fodev.net/files/fo2/map.html)). Directional critter art also splits into `.fr0`–`.fr5`.
- Anchor: *"The logical anchor of an FRM is normally the center of the bottom edge of the visible frame."* Per-frame x/y are **motion deltas**, not crop origins — that's how feet stay planted as the bounding box changes.
- Equal consecutive `data_offsets` = that rotation reuses the previous rotation's frames (the engine's cheap mirroring/dedup).

**Tile size = 80×36 px — verified from engine source, not a wiki.** [fallout2-ce/src/tile.cc](https://github.com/alexbatalov/fallout2-ce/blob/main/src/tile.cc), `squareTileToScreenXY()`:
```c
*coordX += 48 * v8;  *coordY -= 12 * v8;   // one diagonal step
*coordX += 32 * v9;  *coordY += 24 * v9;   // the other
```
48 + 32 = **80** across, 12 + 24 = **36** down. Corroborated by the per-tile lighting buffer being 80 wide: `_intensity_map[160 + 80 * row]`, `static int _intensity_map[3280]` (= 80 × 41).

**Grid:** each elevation has a **200×200 hex grid for objects** and a **100×100 square grid for floor/roof tiles** ([fodev MAP](https://fodev.net/files/fo2/map.html)). The isometric tile grid and the hex movement grid are separate systems.

**Palette — [fodev colour sheet](https://fodev.net/files/fo2/fo_colors.html)** (the page ships the actual cycling tables in its own JS):
- 256 entries, **index 0 is transparent**, index 255 = black
- Animated/cycled ranges (RGB for 229–255 in `color.pal` is stubbed to 0xFF and the real values live in the exe):

| indices | count | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 229–232 | 4 | green — radioactive waste / slime |
| 233–237 | 5 | blue — computer screens/monitors |
| 238–242 | 5 | fire #1 (orange/red/yellow) |
| 243–247 | 5 | fire #2 |
| 248–253 | 6 | brown — shores / water |
| 254 | 1 | #200000 (not marked animated on that sheet) |

- Lighting is a 2D LUT: `intensityColorTable[colorIndex][intensity >> 9]` (tile.cc).
- **No team/player colour system in Fallout.** Nothing is reserved for faction tint.

**3D pipeline: UNVERIFIED, and probably *not* 3D Studio.** The NMA thread [What Was The Technology Behind Fallout (1 & 2)'s Graphics?](https://www.nma-fallout.com/threads/what-was-the-technology-behind-fallout-1-2-s-graphics.218299/) reports walls, scenery, tiles, items and critters were built in 3D with **Lightwave** and touched up in Photoshop. The page returns 403 to direct fetch, so treat that as second-hand until you can read the thread yourself.

---

## 3. Baldur's Gate 1/2 (BioWare, Infinity Engine)

**BAM v1** — [IESDP bam_v1](https://gibberlings3.github.io/iesdp/file_formats/ie_formats/bam_v1.htm):
- 20-byte header: `"BAM "`/`"V1  "`, frame count (word @0x08), cycle count (byte @0x0a, **max 255 cycles**), **compressed colour index** (byte @0x0b), then dwords to frame entries / palette / frame lookup table
- Frame entry: `width` (word), `height` (word), **`centre X` (signed word), `centre Y` (signed word)**, data offset dword where bit 31 = uncompressed flag
- Palette = **256 RGBQUADs in BB GG RR AA order**; alpha unused in classic, meaningful in BGEE
- Transparency: *"The transparency index is set to the first occurence of RGB(0,255,0). If RGB(0,255,0) does not exist in the palette then transparency index is set to 0"*
- RLE: any byte ≠ transparent index is literal; transparent index followed by `x` = `x+1` transparent pixels
- **Frame size cap: BG2 will only display frames up to 256×256** (BG1/IWD unknown; PST > 256×256). Actual character-sprite pixel sizes are per-frame variable — **no fixed avatar dimension; unverified**.

**Directions: 9 stored → 16 rendered.** *"Most modern animation types use 9 base directions (S, SSW, SW, WSW, W, WNW, NW, NNW, N) with eastern directions calculated by the engine through mirroring"*; some older types store 8 unmirrored orientations plus separate `*E.BAM` files. [IESDP ini_anim](https://gibberlings3.github.io/iesdp/file_formats/ie_formats/ini_anim.htm)

**COLOUR RANGES — the exact index map (this is the big one).** From NearInfinity's `SpriteDecoder`, the reference implementation of IE false-colour ([source](https://github.com/Argent77/NearInfinity/blob/master/src/org/infinity/resource/cre/decoder/SpriteDecoder.java)):

```java
protected int getColorOffset(int locationIndex) {
  if (locationIndex >= 0 && locationIndex < 7) retVal = 4 + locationIndex * 12;
}
...
final int srcOfs = 4;  final int dstOfs = 88;
final int srcLen = 12; final int dstLen = 8;
...
palette[2] = 0xFF000000;
palette[3] = 0xFF000000;
```

- **7 colour locations, 12 palette entries each**, starting at index 4:
  `4–15`, `16–27`, `28–39`, `40–51`, `52–63`, `64–75`, `76–87`
- **Indices 88–255 are auto-generated blend ranges**: every pair of the 7 base ranges (21 pairs) gets an 8-entry interpolated ramp — 88 + 21×8 = 256 exactly. This is why IE characters read cleanly where two dyed materials meet.
- **Indices 2 and 3 are forced to opaque black** (shadow).

**Which location is which** — IESDP opcode 51 location values ([opcodes](https://gibberlings3.github.io/iesdp/opcodes/bgee.htm)):
`00` belt buckle (armour) / amulet (robes) — entire body on some animations · `01` **minor colour** · `02` **major colour** · `03` skin · `04` strap (armour) / minor trim (robes) · `05` armour colour (+ major trim on robes) · `06` hair.
Equipment layers have their own location blocks: weapon `16–22` (16 quillons, 20 grip, 21 blade), shield `32–40` (32 hub, 33 interior, 34 panelling, 37 rim), helmet `48–54` (48/49/50 ornamentation, 52 face, 53 main covering).

**Where the values live:** CRE v1 header bytes — `0x2c` metal, `0x2d` minor, `0x2e` major, `0x2f` skin, `0x30` leather, `0x31` armor, `0x32` hair ([cre_v1](https://gibberlings3.github.io/iesdp/file_formats/ie_formats/cre_v1.htm)). Each byte selects one **gradient** from the engine's gradient table: 256 gradient ids, `00h–73h` (0–115) valid in all versions, `74h–77h` differ between classic and EE, `78h–FFh` EE-only ([Colour Gradients appendix](https://gibberlings3.github.io/iesdp/appendices/colourgradients.htm)).

**Backgrounds:** TIS tilesets — **64×64 px tiles**, *each tile carries its own 256-colour palette*, **5120 bytes per tile** (1024 palette + 4096 indices), *"Index 0 is hardcoded to be the transparent index"* ([tis_v1](https://gibberlings3.github.io/iesdp/file_formats/ie_formats/tis_v1.htm)). IE areas are painted backdrops cut into a 64px grid, not a tiled isometric ground — worth saying explicitly in your report.

---

## 4. Age of Empires II (Ensemble, SLP) + Definitive Edition

**PLAYER COLOUR PALETTE INDEXES — the detail you flagged.** [openage slp-files.md](https://github.com/SFTtech/openage/blob/master/doc/media/slp-files.md), verbatim:
> "In AoK and SWGB, blue player colors begin at index 16 in the palette, red at index 32, green at index 48, yellow at index 64, orange at index 80, cyan/teal at index 96, purple at index 112, and grey at index 128."
> "The real palette index is `player_color_palette_index + player * 16`, where `player` is the player ID you're drawing for (1-8)."

So: **indices 16–143 are eight contiguous 16-entry player blocks.** The SLP stores only a **0–15 offset within the block** — the artist paints a 16-step ramp, the engine picks the base. (AoE1 DE uses separate palettes with indices 0x00–0x7F.)

Relevant SLP commands (same doc):
- `0x06` **player colour draw** (`0bXXXX0110`), count = `command >> 4` or next byte if 0
- `0x0A` **fill player colour** (`0bXXXX1010`)
- `0x0B` **shadow draw**; shadow pixels use a **shadow palette that is a darkened variant of the graphics palette (50500)**
- `0x4E` **Outline 1** — `palette_index = player_index = player * 16`. *"the outline that surrounds a unit and is seen when a unit is obstructed, such as when it is behind a building or tree… Its color is determined by the team color of the player."* **This is the single most important legibility mechanism in the format.**
- `0x6E` **Outline 2** — `palette_index = 243` (SWGB shields)

**Directions & frames:**
> "each animation has 10 keyframes and 5 directions. The other 3 directions are generated later by flipping the sprite on the y axis. One SLP stores one animation -> 50 frames per SLP."
> "Arrows and projectiles have 35 keyframes and 5 directions… -> 175 frames per SLP."

So **5 rendered angles → 8 displayed**, exactly as you suspected.

**Frame header:** `slp_frame_info` stores int32 `width`, `height`, `hotspot_X`, `hotspot_Y` (sprite centre). Sizes are per-frame variable — there is no single "unit sprite size".

**Tile size — correct your 96×48 assumption.** [openage terrain.md](https://github.com/SFTtech/openage/blob/master/doc/media/terrain.md) gives a rhombus of **97 px across × 49 rows** (its ASCII diagram annotates the widest row `<| 97 pixels, 25th row`, i.e. the 25th of 49 rows is the centre). Note the doc's own prose labels are transposed — it writes "Tile image height = 97px / Tile image width = 49px", which contradicts its diagram. Frame selection: `frame_id = (x % tc) + ((y % tc) * tc)`, `tc = sqrt(tilecount) = 10` for the 100-tile terrains. terrain.drs holds **27 SLPs, one per terrain type**, mostly 100 tiles each.

**Original sprite scale:** the only dev figure I can source is *~"100 pixels high"* for original AoE2 units, from the AoE2 DE team ([Game Developer: Rebuilding a classic in Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition](https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/rebuilding-a-classic-in-i-age-of-empires-ii-definitive-edition-i-)). Exact per-unit dimensions: **unverified**.

**AoE2 DE re-render:**
- Same article: *"Literally every asset in the game had to be remade. In the HD editions, all the graphics were the original graphics."* · *"We didn't have any of the original assets. Those were all lost. So we literally had no choice but to make everything from scratch."* · about **four times the fidelity** of the ~100px originals, working from the old sprites as reference to preserve silhouettes · *"This game is still 2D. A lot of people think it's 3D now, but it's actually 2D sprites because we really wanted to keep that old feel."*
- **SMX** (launch format) — [openage smx-files.md](https://github.com/SFTtech/openage/blob/master/doc/media/smx-files.md): up to 3 layers per frame (main graphic, shadow, outline), `frame_type` bitfield selects them, per-frame `palette_number`, layer header has width/height/hotspot. Still palette-indexed.
- **SLD** (build 66692 onward) — [openage sld-files.md](https://github.com/SFTtech/openage/blob/master/doc/media/sld-files.md): **abandons indexed palettes entirely.** DXT1/BC1 for main graphics + damage mask, DXT4/BC4 for shadow + **player colour mask**. Up to 5 layers: main, shadow, `???`, damage mask, playercolor mask. Player colour is now *"an index for a playercolor value in each pixel… technically greyscale images… treated as an index for looking up the actual player color value from a palette."* Frames define a square canvas with a hotspot (doc's worked example: 200×200 canvas; files of 721 / 961 frames).
- **32 directions**: that figure comes from the **AoE1 DE** blog ([Forgotten Empires: Is it a 3D or a 2D game?](https://www.forgottenempires.net/age-of-empires-definitive-edition-is-it-a-3d-or-a-2d-game)) — *"we're creating all our units, buildings and trees as 3D models, but then render them out as 2D images"*, *"Where the original units would only turn in 8 directions, units now… 32 directions"*, *"every asset in the game has been rendered 3 times"* for HD→4K. **Whether AoE2 DE also uses 32 directions: unverified** — don't transfer the claim.

---

## 5. Heroes of Might & Magic III (New World Computing) — DEF

**First: HoMM3's adventure map is not isometric.** It's a square **32×32 px** grid (VCMI draws road halves as `Rect(0, 16, 32, 16)` / `Rect(0, 0, 32, 16)` — [MapRenderer.cpp](https://github.com/vcmi/vcmi/blob/develop/client/mapView/MapRenderer.cpp)). Battles are a flat hex stage. Say so, or the comparison misleads.

**DEF palette = 256 RGB triplets**, read 3 bytes per entry ([CDefFile.cpp](https://github.com/vcmi/vcmi/blob/develop/client/render/CDefFile.cpp)). Per-sprite header (`SSpriteDef`) carries `format`, `width`, `height`, `fullWidth`, `fullHeight`, `leftMargin`, `topMargin` — so **sprite dimensions are per-frame variable; no fixed creature size (unverified)**.

**RESERVED PALETTE INDEXES — exact.** [VCMI clientsdl2/render/ScalableImage.cpp](https://github.com/vcmi/vcmi/blob/develop/clientsdl2/render/ScalableImage.cpp), comment *"First 8 colors in def palette used for transparency"*:

| idx | magic RGB baked into the DEF | what the engine substitutes |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | (0, 255, 255) | full transparency (a = 0) |
| 1 | (255, 150, 255) | shadow border, a = 64 — battle & adventure-map DEFs |
| 2 | (255, 100, 255) | shadow border, a = 64 — fog-of-war DEFs |
| 3 | (255, 50, 255) | shadow body, a = 128 — fog-of-war DEFs |
| 4 | (255, 0, 255) | shadow body, a = 128 — battle & adventure-map DEFs |
| 5 | (255, 255, 0) | **selection / owner flag colour** |
| 6 | (180, 0, 255) | shadow body below selection, a = 128 — battle DEFs |
| 7 | (0, 255, 0) | shadow border below selection, a = 64 — battle DEFs |

Indices 2 and 3 are only remapped *if the DEF's actual colour matches* the magic value (`colorsSimilar()`), so authors can reuse them as real colours.

**PLAYER COLOUR = indices 224–255.** [Graphics.cpp](https://github.com/vcmi/vcmi/blob/develop/client/render/Graphics.cpp):
```cpp
SDL_SetPaletteColors(targetPalette, palette, 224, 32);   // 32-entry player block
...
SDL_SetPaletteColors(targetPalette, &color, 5, 1);       // single flag colour at index 5
```
- The 32 colours come from `DATA/PLAYERS.PAL`: **8 players × 32 colours**, 4 bytes per entry (4th byte is a flags byte, *not* alpha), starting at file offset **24**. Unowned objects use `config/NEUTRAL.PAL` (32 colours).
- The 8 flat player colours: red `ff0000`, blue `3152ff`, tan `9c7352`, green `429429`, orange `ff8400`, purple `8c29a5`, teal `099ca5`, pink `c67b8c`; neutral grey `848484`.

So HoMM3 = **32 reserved indices for the owner ramp + 1 reserved index for the flag/selection**, on top of **8 reserved indices for transparency and a two-level shadow**.

**3ds Max pipeline: UNVERIFIED.** The best retrospective I found ([Game Developer: Remembering Erathia, 15 Years Later](https://www.gamedeveloper.com/production/heroes-of-might-magic-iii-remembering-erathia-15-years-later)) names the team — lead artist Phelan Sykes, assistant lead Rebecca Riel, illustrator George Almond, lead animator Adam McCarthy — and *"over 10,000 pieces of artwork"*, but names no software, no resolutions, no frame counts.

---

## 6. Disciples II (Strategy First, 2002)

Weakest evidence set of the six; also the weakest structural fit (battle view is a flat 2D stage, strategic map a 2D grid — not units on a tiled isometric ground).

- **3ds Max pre-render: UNVERIFIED.** [GameSpot Designer Diary #9](https://www.gamespot.com/articles/disciples-ii-dark-prophecy-designer-diary-9/1100-2801857/) is the right primary source and search snippets from it say units were modelled in 3D Studio Max with no polygon budget because they ship as pre-rendered animation, but the page returns 403 to fetch. Read it directly before citing.
- **Sprite dimensions, frame counts, palette depth, team colour: all unverified.** Assets live in `.ff` archives (`Faces.ff` etc.). Tools: [Disciples2-ROTE-Editor](https://github.com/Vanosz/Disciples2-ROTE-Editor-Releases) (Media → Resource Explorer), [D2ModdingToolset](https://github.com/VladimirMakeev/D2ModdingToolset) (has `batimagesloader.h`, `batunitanim.h`, `factoryimageanim.h` if you want to reverse the numbers). [Spriters Resource: Disciples II](https://www.spriters-resource.com/pc_computer/disciplesii/) if you just need reference sheets.

---

## 7. Cross-game synthesis: how units stay legible on a tiled ground

**Verified mechanisms, by strength of evidence:**

1. **A dedicated outline layer drawn in the owner's colour.** AoE2's SLP command `0x4E` draws the silhouette with `palette_index = player * 16` when the unit is behind a building or tree; SMX and SLD both keep outline as a first-class layer. This is the only mechanism in the set that is *explicitly documented as a readability feature*. ([slp-files.md](https://github.com/SFTtech/openage/blob/master/doc/media/slp-files.md), [smx-files.md](https://github.com/SFTtech/openage/blob/master/doc/media/smx-files.md))
2. **A dedicated shadow channel that grounds the sprite.** AoE2: command `0x0B` + a shadow palette that is a darkened copy of palette 50500; SMX/SLD carry a DXT4 shadow layer. HoMM3: shadow is baked into palette indices 1/2/3/4 as 25%/50% black, so the artist paints shadow *as index* and the engine controls opacity.
3. **Team colour as a reserved ramp, never a single colour.** AoE2 reserves 8 × 16 = 128 indices (16–143); HoMM3 reserves 32 (224–255) + 1 flag index (5); Infinity Engine reserves 7 × 12 = 84 base indices (4–87) plus 168 auto-blended (88–255). In all three the artist paints a *gradient of one hue* and the engine substitutes the ramp — which is why these sprites keep full shading under any team colour.
4. **Lighting by index remap, not per-pixel maths.** Diablo: 16 light levels × 256-byte tables. Fallout: `intensityColorTable[color][intensity >> 9]`. Both keep contrast bands quantised, which preserves silhouette edges at small size.
5. **Silhouette preservation across a remaster.** AoE2 DE artists worked from the ~100px originals specifically so players still identify *"that unit as being a camel… 20 years later"* ([Game Developer](https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/rebuilding-a-classic-in-i-age-of-empires-ii-definitive-edition-i-)).
6. **Angle counts, as a table** — Diablo 1 **8** (pitch doc allowed 3 mirrored, shipped game stores 8); Fallout **6** (hex grid); AoE2 **5 rendered → 8 shown**; Infinity Engine **9 rendered → 16 shown**; Diablo II **8 monsters / 16 players**; AoE1 DE **32**; AoE2 DE unverified.

**Explicitly NOT verified:** top-lighting conventions, fixed key-light angles, outline-width rules, or any written silhouette guideline from any of these teams. I found no primary source stating a lighting direction. Do not invent one — the per-direction sprite sets *imply* a fixed camera and fixed light, but no document I reached says it.

---

Fandom wikis (`falloutmods.fandom.com` etc.) are behind Cloudflare and returned 402/403 throughout — the `fodev.net` docs are a better and more current substitute for everything Fallout.

# Research B: ML / Self-Play Frameworks That Can Learn New Rules

All GitHub metadata verified via `gh api` on **2026-09-13**. Where I could not verify something, it is flagged.

## Headline

There is **one mature, proven pipeline for teaching a strong engine brand-new fairy rules** — Fairy-Stockfish + `variant-nnue-pytorch` — and it is a realistic single-GPU project. But it has two hard blockers for *your five specific mechanics*, and one that likely kills in-browser NNUE. Read §2 before anything else.

---

## 1. Leela Chess Zero — dead end for rules

[LeelaChessZero/lc0](https://github.com/LeelaChessZero/lc0) is healthy: GPL-3.0, 3,209 stars, last push **2026-09-12**, 20 commits in 90 days, stable **v0.32.1 (2025-11-23)**, **v0.33.0-rc0 (2026-09-05)**.

**It does not support variants.** A code search for `UCI_Variant` in the repo returns **0 hits**; `UCI_Chess960` is present (`src/chess/uciloop.cc`, `src/selfplay/game.cc`), and the 0.33 notes mention *"Fixed castling move display for FRC"*. So: Chess960/FRC only, hardcoded 8x8 chess otherwise.

- [Issue #1563 "Please create Fairy-LC0"](https://github.com/LeelaChessZero/lc0/issues/1563) — closed **2021-06-20**; the sole comment says variant support *"currently just isn't happening"* and redirects to CrazyAra.
- [Issue #2336 "LC0 supporting chess variants"](https://github.com/LeelaChessZero/lc0/issues/2336) — opened 2025-11-01, **still open, zero maintainer replies**.
- The [GSoC 2026 ideas page](https://lczero.org/contribute/gsoc/2026/) lists 12 projects, **none** about variants. (It does list a *"JavaScript/WebAssembly backend for browser play"*.)

**No variant forks exist.** `gh search repos` for "lc0 variant chess" and "leela chess variant" both return `[]`; scanning lc0's recently-pushed forks shows only vendor mirrors and personal clones, all 0–1 stars. [frpays/lc0-js](https://github.com/frpays/lc0-js) (Emscripten) last pushed 2024-04-27 — dead.

*Caveat: lc0's 2026 stance is inferred from the 2021 closure plus silence on #2336, not from a current maintainer statement.*

**Still useful:** lc0's net architecture as a reference, and [hunterchen7/play-lc0](https://github.com/hunterchen7/play-lc0) as working prior art for running lc0-format nets in-browser via onnxruntime-web in a Web Worker.

### The real lc0-shaped answer: CrazyAra

[QueensGambit/CrazyAra](https://github.com/QueensGambit/CrazyAra) — GPL-3.0, 292 stars, **v1.0.6 released 2026-03-02**, but only **9 commits since 2025-01-01** (semi-maintained). It is an AlphaZero-style MCTS+NN *chess variant* engine, and critically its [`.gitmodules`](https://github.com/QueensGambit/CrazyAra/blob/master/.gitmodules) pulls in **Fairy-Stockfish** as a submodule, with CMake options:

```
option(MODE_BOARDGAMES  "Build with Fairy-Stockfish environment support for board games" OFF)
option(MODE_OPEN_SPIEL  "Build with open_spiel environment support" OFF)
option(USE_RL           "Build with reinforcement learning support" OFF)
```

It has `engine/src/rl/selfplay.cpp` and ONNX-based inference backends (TensorRT/Torch/OpenVINO; 24 code hits for `onnx`). **This is the only existing bridge from a Fairy-Stockfish `variants.ini` to an AlphaZero self-play loop *and* an ONNX net you can ship to a browser.**

---

## 2. Fairy-Stockfish NNUE pipeline — the proven path, with two blockers

**Repos:** [Fairy-Stockfish](https://github.com/fairy-stockfish/Fairy-Stockfish) (GPL-3.0, 905★, pushed **2026-09-06**) → [variant-nnue-tools](https://github.com/fairy-stockfish/variant-nnue-tools) (data gen, GPL-3.0, pushed **2026-09-11**, tracks FSF master; last *tag* 2022-04-26) → [variant-nnue-pytorch](https://github.com/fairy-stockfish/variant-nnue-pytorch) (trainer, **no LICENSE file at all** — `gh api .../contents/LICENSE` 404s and the API reports `license: null`).

> ⚠️ Fairy-Stockfish's last *GitHub release* is `fairy_sf_14_0_1_xq` from **2021-11-19**. Development is entirely on master. Build from source.

**The trainer does not need to know your rules.** Per the [wiki Introduction](https://github.com/fairy-stockfish/variant-nnue-pytorch/wiki/Introduction): *"the training code is variant-agnostic and other than those minor adaptations has no knowledge of the rules of the variants."* You edit only `variant.h`/`variant.py` (`FILES`, `RANKS`, `PIECE_TYPES`, `PIECE_COUNT`, `KING_SQUARES`, `DATA_SIZE`, `PIECE_VALUES`) — and the data generator writes those files for you via `trainer_config yourvariant /target/dir`. Arch is HalfKAv2 with **L1=512, L2=16, L3=32** ([model.py](https://github.com/fairy-stockfish/variant-nnue-pytorch/blob/master/model.py)).

**Concrete compute numbers** (from [Training-data-generation](https://github.com/fairy-stockfish/variant-nnue-pytorch/wiki/Training-data-generation) and [NNUE-training](https://github.com/fairy-stockfish/variant-nnue-pytorch/wiki/NNUE-training)):

- *"Usually at least 100M positions should be used to get decent results."*
- *"Depths 4-5 usually already give quite good results"* (the example command uses `depth 2 count 10000000`).
- *"One epoch is 20M positions"* → 200M positions ≈ `--max_epochs 10`.
- The [Kaggle guide](https://github.com/fairy-stockfish/variant-nnue-pytorch/wiki/Training-through-Kaggle-GPU) says Kaggle's free **30 GPU-hr/week** is *"quite enough for NNUE training."* That is your compute envelope — an RTX 4090/5090 is comfortably sufficient. **Data generation on CPU, not training, is the long pole.**
- Deps pin `pytorch-lightning==1.9.5`, and a **`requirements-CUDA128.txt`** exists → Blackwell/RTX 5090 supported. (The wiki FAQ's *"lightning version <1.5.0"* is stale — contradicted by `requirements.txt`.)
- Limitations: **`bin` format only, no binpack**; *"Many of the helper scripts… are not maintained and likely broken."*

**It demonstrably works on exotic fairy rules.** The [network list](https://fairy-stockfish.github.io/nnue/) has **146 published nets**, 35 of them trained in 2025 (newest 2025-10-31), mostly by two or three individuals. Elo gains over classical eval: chak **+2062**, antiantichess **+1309**, elimination **+1303**, crossderby **+1186**, xiangfu **+1102**. Nets dated 2026+ are CC0.

### ⛔ Blocker 1 — 4 of your 5 mechanics aren't expressible in `variants.ini`

I grepped the full 2,126-line [`variants.ini`](https://github.com/fairy-stockfish/Fairy-Stockfish/blob/master/src/variants.ini), which embeds the complete option documentation. Results:

| Your mechanic | Expressible? |
|---|---|
| Rifle capture (capture without moving) | **No** — zero hits for `rifle` in the whole repo |
| Kamikaze (capturer removes itself) | **No** — closest is `petrifyOnCaptureTypes` (capturer → *wall square*) or `blastOnCapture` (atomic). Different semantics. (`[kamikazerooks]` is an extinction-goal variant, unrelated.) |
| Uncapturable, non-capturing | **Half** — non-capturing movement is Betza-expressible (`m` prefix, e.g. `mQ`); true uncapturability is not (`blastImmuneTypes` is blast-only, `mutuallyImmuneTypes` is same-type-only) |
| Swap with friendly | **No** — zero hits for `swap` |
| Chain capture | **No** — `mustCapture` is *mandatory* capture, not multi-leg within a turn |

Also note only a **subset of Betza** is supported (base atoms, directional modifiers, W/R + F/B + N riders, `pR/pB/gR/gB` hoppers, `nN/nA/nZ/nD` lame leapers).

**So expect to patch Fairy-Stockfish C++** (move generation + `do_move`/`undo_move` + legality) for four mechanics. That is the real cost of this path — but it buys you *everything downstream for free*, including CrazyAra's `MODE_BOARDGAMES`.

### ⛔ Blocker 2 — your NNUE would be ~94 MB

The [FAQ](https://github.com/fairy-stockfish/variant-nnue-pytorch/wiki/FAQ) gives `FILE_SIZE_IN_BYTE >= SQUARES * KING_SQUARES * PIECE_TYPES * 2080`, and warns nets **>80 MB** need the large-board build.

| Config | Size |
|---|---|
| Standard chess (6 types) | 51.1 MB |
| **KDC: 6 standard + 5 fairy = 11 types** | **93.7 MB** |
| If fairy pieces reuse types (8) | 68.2 MB |

A 94 MB download is a non-starter for a web game. **Either run the engine server-side, or ship Fairy-Stockfish WASM with classical eval only** (still a strong opponent), or go the small-net AlphaZero route (§3).

---

## 3. AlphaZero-style frameworks, current status

| Project | Last push / release | ★ | License | Pluggable rules? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **[rlglab/minizero](https://github.com/rlglab/minizero)** | 2026-08-18 | 142 | Apache-2.0 | **Best fit** — see below |
| [google-deepmind/open_spiel](https://github.com/google-deepmind/open_spiel) | v2.0.2, 2026-08-12 | 5,478 | Apache-2.0 | Yes |
| [google-deepmind/mctx](https://github.com/google-deepmind/mctx) | 2026-09-10 | 2,662 | Apache-2.0 | Search only — you supply `recurrent_fn` |
| [opendilab/LightZero](https://github.com/opendilab/LightZero) | 2026-08-28 | 1,647 | Apache-2.0 | Yes; bundles EfficientZero/Gumbel MuZero/UniZero |
| [AlphaZero.jl](https://github.com/jonathan-laurent/AlphaZero.jl) | v0.5.5, 2025-12-12 | 1,334 | MIT | Yes (Julia) |
| [jcbmrshll/turbozero](https://github.com/jcbmrshll/turbozero) | 2026-08-09 | 112 | Apache-2.0 | Yes (JAX) |
| [KataGo](https://github.com/lightvector/KataGo) | v1.18.2, 2026-08-30 | 5,107 | MIT-ish | **No** — Go-specific board layer |
| [suragnair/alpha-zero-general](https://github.com/suragnair/alpha-zero-general) | **2025-01-01** | 4,513 | MIT | Dormant; use [cestpasphoto fork](https://github.com/cestpasphoto/alpha-zero-general) (2026-05-01) |
| [werner-duvaud/muzero-general](https://github.com/werner-duvaud/muzero-general) | **2024-09-03** | 2,869 | MIT | Dormant |
| [sotetsuk/pgx](https://github.com/sotetsuk/pgx) | **v2.6.0, 2025-03-06** | 648 | Apache-2.0 | Abandoned — 20 open PRs, none merged since |
| facebookresearch/Polygames | **archived 2021** | — | — | Dead |

**minizero is the recommendation.** Maintained, Apache-2.0 (commercially safe, unlike GPL FSF/lc0), C++ MCTS + PyTorch training, implements AlphaZero *and* Gumbel AlphaZero/MuZero, and already ships 20+ games including breakthrough, amazons, linesofaction, surakarta. Its [`BaseEnv`](https://github.com/rlglab/minizero/blob/main/minizero/environment/base/base_env.h) is a ~25-method virtual interface returning `std::vector<Action> getLegalActions()` — **dynamic move lists**, so chain-capture needs no fixed-shape gymnastics. `breakthrough.cpp` is ~14 KB: a realistic size target for your port.

**pgx** does have `chess` and `gardner_chess`, and is fast (~**500K chess steps/s**, batch 1024, single A100 — [paper](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2303.17503) Fig. 3, *values read off a plot*). But everything must be `jit`/`vmap`-clean on fixed shapes. Rifle, kamikaze and swap are fine; **chain-capture is the hard one** (variable-length sequence → bounded `lax.while_loop` or a "continue the chain" sub-turn). Combined with abandonment, hard to recommend.

**OpenSpiel** has a genuine Python-only path: implement in `open_spiel/python/games/` and call `pyspiel.register_game()` — no C++ build. Its AlphaZero has been **rewritten in JAX/Flax** (`model_linen.py`, `model_nnx.py`), though [`docs/alpha_zero.md`](https://github.com/google-deepmind/open_spiel/blob/master/docs/alpha_zero.md) still describes the old TF1 version. Standing caveat from the docs: *"it is not designed to scale to superhuman performance in Go or Chess."* Python games are ≥1 order of magnitude slower than C++. Good for a 2-week prototype; port to C++ (or minizero) for the real run.

**KataGo** — copy the *techniques*, not the code ([KataGoMethods.md](https://github.com/lightvector/KataGo/blob/master/docs/KataGoMethods.md)): playout cap randomization, forced playouts + policy target pruning, auxiliary heads (your analogue: material-differential / piece-survival), policy surprise weighting, dynamic variance-scaled cPUCT. Its [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.10565) claims a **50× reduction in computation**, and the README states *"a training run using only a single top-end consumer GPU could possibly train a bot from scratch to superhuman strength within a few months."*

**Realistic single-GPU datapoints:**
- 9x9 Hex, near-perfect play, **single RTX 2080 Ti, <3 hours** ([Scaling Scaling Laws with Board Games](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2104.03113)); also **~500 Elo per 10× compute**.
- Connect Four, RTX 2070: **1–2 h/iteration × 15 iterations ≈ 15–30 h** ([AlphaZero.jl tutorial](https://jonathan-laurent.github.io/AlphaZero.jl/stable/tutorial/connect_four/)).
- alpha-zero-general on chess: **1–2 min per self-play episode** at 100 sims ([discussion #210](https://github.com/suragnair/alpha-zero-general/discussions/210)) — Python-loop MCTS is the bottleneck, not the GPU. Avoid.

Budget **a few days to ~2 weeks of 4090 time** for a genuinely strong 8x8 variant agent, assuming a fast C++ rules engine. A TypeScript rules engine in the self-play loop will not work — port to C++ (or expose it to minizero/OpenSpiel).

---

## 4. Maia — not applicable, but worth stealing later

- [CSSLab/maia-chess](https://github.com/CSSLab/maia-chess) — GPL-3.0, 1,237★, pushed 2026-05-24, **0 commits in 90 days**.
- [CSSLab/maia2](https://github.com/CSSLab/maia2) — MIT, v0.11.0 (2026-07-15). Its README now says: *"Maia-3 is recommended for new projects."*
- [CSSLab/maia3](https://github.com/CSSLab/maia3) — **AGPL-3.0**, 173★, created 2026-05-22, [paper arXiv:2605.19091](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.19091).

**Relevance to King Down Chess: essentially zero.** Maia's entire premise is supervised learning on millions of human Lichess games to predict *human* moves at a target Elo. You have no human corpus, so there is nothing to train on. Note also the **AGPL-3.0** on maia3 — a serious hazard for a hosted web game.

The idea worth copying **once you have player data**: conditioning on skill level to produce a beatable, human-feeling opponent — far better UX than a depth-limited engine. Also, [maia-platform-frontend](https://github.com/CSSLab/maia-platform-frontend) uses `onnxruntime-web ^1.23.0` client-side, confirming the deployment pattern.

---

## 5. Browser inference in 2026

**onnxruntime-web** — npm `latest` **1.29.0, published 2026-08-24**; GitHub tagged **v1.30.0 on 2026-09-10** (not yet npm latest). Critical gotcha: **the default import still gives you JSEP, not the native WebGPU EP.** Per [JSEP_Deprecation.md](https://github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime/blob/main/docs/JSEP_Deprecation.md) you must `import 'onnxruntime-web/webgpu'`. The [1.29.0 notes](https://github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime/releases/tag/v1.29.0) state: *"onnxruntime-web has announced the deprecation of WebGL and JSEP. The native WebGPU EP is the recommended path going forward."* JSEP removal is unscheduled; **WebGL is deprecated — do not use it.**

**Workers:** WebGPU needs no canvas and works in dedicated workers (Chrome 113+/144 full, Firefox 141 dedicated-only, Safari 26). Two traps: ORT's own `env.wasm.proxy` **cannot be combined with WebGPU** (*"a GPU buffer is not transferable"*) — spawn your own worker; and service workers still fail ([#20876](https://github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime/issues/20876), open since 2024).

**WASM:** SIMD is mandatory (only `ort-wasm-simd-threaded.*` ships). Threads require **COOP+COEP / `crossOriginIsolated`**; without them it silently drops to single-threaded SIMD.

**TensorFlow.js — treat as unmaintained.** `@tensorflow/tfjs` latest is **4.22.0, published 2024-10-21** (verified via registry); `next` 4.23.0-rc.0 from 2025-01-08 was never promoted. Repo not archived, but [issue #8719 "Is this project deprecated?"](https://github.com/tensorflow/tfjs/issues/8719) (opened 2026-06-10) has **no maintainer reply**. Weekly downloads: tfjs 366k vs onnxruntime-web 3.20M. *No official deprecation statement exists — the absence is the finding.*

**transformers.js** — 4.2.0 (2026-04-22), very active, but it's a wrapper that pins an older ORT-web. Irrelevant for a small policy/value net; use `onnxruntime-web/webgpu` directly.

### Sizing: dispatch overhead dominates, not FLOPs

[arXiv:2604.02344](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.02344) (2026-02-09) measured per-dispatch cost: **32.8 µs** Chrome/RTX 5090, **31.7 µs** Safari/M2, **66.5 µs** Intel iGPU — but **~1,037 µs on Firefox** (both Metal and D3D12). [Follow-up](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08730): *"dispatch overhead, not kernel quality, is the bottleneck at batch size 1"*; fusing 876→564 dispatches gave **+53% throughput**.

Practical consequences:
- Chrome/Safari give you **~75–150 dispatches inside a 5 ms budget**. A 6–10 block resnet post-fusion is ~60–120 — right at the cliff.
- **Firefox is unusable for tiny nets on WebGPU** (5 dispatches ≈ 5 ms). Gate it off.
- At batch 1, **WASM SIMD frequently beats WebGPU**: EfficientNet measured **~80 ms WASM vs ~1100 ms WebGPU** on an RTX 4090 ([gpuweb #5292](https://github.com/gpuweb/gpuweb/discussions/5292)).
- **Recommendation: default to WASM SIMD in a dedicated worker; use WebGPU only if you batch MCTS leaf evaluations** — batching is the only thing that makes WebGPU win. Target **4–6 blocks × 64 channels** on 8x8 to stay under ~5 ms.

### You may not need to build a browser engine at all

Fairy-Stockfish already ships browser builds, both published **2026-08-26**:

- **[`fairy-stockfish-nnue.wasm@1.1.12`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/fairy-stockfish-nnue.wasm)** — GPL-3.0, 1.7 MB unpacked, *"WebAssembly port of Fairy-Stockfish with NNUE support, optimized via WASM SIMD"*. Its [emscripten Makefile](https://github.com/fairy-stockfish/fairy-stockfish.wasm/blob/nnue/src/emscripten/Makefile) sets `-msimd128`, `USE_PTHREADS=1`, `PROXY_TO_PTHREAD=1`, `ENVIRONMENT=web,worker,node`, `FILESYSTEM=1` — so **COOP/COEP headers are required**. Already used by pychess.org for client-side analysis.
- **[`ffish` / `ffish-es6@0.7.10`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/ffish)** — GPL-3.0, with TypeScript typings (`ffish.d.ts`) exposing `loadVariantConfig(variantInitContent: string)`, `Board.legalMoves()`, `isGameOver()`. **You can load a custom `variants.ini` from a JS string at runtime in the browser.** Also `pyffish` 0.0.90 (2026-08-26) for Python.

NPS reference point (dated, 2020): [lichess-org/stockfish.wasm#21](https://github.com/lichess-org/stockfish.wasm/pull/21) reports *"1000 knps wasm master / 10 knps wasm nnue / **60 knps wasm nnue with `-msimd128`**"* vs 1000 knps native NNUE.

---

## ⚠️ Licensing

Fairy-Stockfish, lc0, CrazyAra, the WASM builds and `ffish` are all **GPL-3.0**; maia3 is **AGPL-3.0**. For a closed-source commercial web game this is a real constraint — GPL WASM shipped to clients is distribution. `variant-nnue-pytorch` has **no license file at all**. minizero, OpenSpiel, LightZero and mctx are **Apache-2.0**, and the cestpasphoto alpha-zero-general fork is MIT — that's the permissive lane if licensing matters.

## Could not verify

- **No community-reported GPU-hours** for variant NNUE training. The only Fairy-Stockfish discussion on the topic ([#789](https://github.com/fairy-stockfish/Fairy-Stockfish/discussions/789), 2024-08-04) has **zero replies**. My compute figures come from the wiki's own guidance, not user reports.
- No published batch-1 latency benchmark for a 1–20M-param convnet under onnxruntime-web WebGPU; **no published NPS for browser MCTS**.
- lc0's current official stance on variants (inferred, not stated).
- pgx throughput figures are read off a plot, not a table.
- CrazyAra's `MODE_BOARDGAMES` is confirmed present in CMake and `.gitmodules`, but **I did not verify anyone has actually driven a *user-defined* `variants.ini` game through its self-play loop.** Validate this early — it's the linchpin of the cheapest end-to-end path.

## Suggested path

1. **Implement the 5 mechanics in Fairy-Stockfish C++** (~4 of 5 need real move-gen work). This single investment unlocks: a strong classical engine, the NNUE pipeline, CrazyAra self-play, and `ffish` browser move-gen/validation that cross-checks your TypeScript rules.
2. **Ship `ffish` + `fairy-stockfish-nnue.wasm` (classical eval) in the browser now** for a playable opponent, behind COOP/COEP headers.
3. **For a stronger/smaller net, go minizero** (Apache-2.0, dynamic move lists) → small resnet → ONNX → `onnxruntime-web` WASM-SIMD in a dedicated worker. Skip the 94 MB NNUE for browser delivery.
4. Revisit Maia-style skill conditioning only after you have real player games.

**Dead / not applicable:** `facebookresearch/Polygames` is now [facebookarchive/Polygames](https://github.com/facebookarchive/Polygames) — **archived, last push 2021-10-12**. [YeWR/EfficientZero](https://github.com/YeWR/EfficientZero) last push 2023-12-20; [EfficientZeroV2](https://github.com/Shengjiewang-Jason/EfficientZeroV2) 2024-08-09 — both stale; LightZero carries EfficientZero/Sampled EfficientZero/Stochastic MuZero/Gumbel MuZero/UniZero/ReZero under one roof. [Ludeme/Ludii](https://github.com/Ludeme/Ludii) pushed 2026-05-31, Java, non-OSI license.

**Ludax is the tempting trap.** Its README claims "tens of millions of steps per second" and the [paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.22609v1) benchmarks on a **4090** vs PGX and Ludii (up to ~55x over Ludii on Pente; PGX still wins at large batch on Hex/Reversi). But it "currently supports a relatively narrow class of games: two-player, perfect-information board games played by placing, capturing, and flipping pieces," explicitly excluding "games requiring piece movement (e.g. Amazons)" and "games with multiple piece types (e.g. Checkers)." Chess variants are out of scope.

## B. pgx

**Chess: yes** — `chess` and `gardner_chess` (5x5), plus shogi, animal_shogi, go_9x9/19x19, backgammon, othello, hex, connect_four, 2048, poker variants, MinAtar ([`pgx/core.py` EnvId](https://github.com/sotetsuk/pgx/blob/main/pgx/core.py)).

**Throughput** ([paper](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2303.17503), Fig. 3, batch 1024, single A100): tic-tac-toe ~2M steps/s, Connect Four ~1.5M, **chess ~500K**, Go 19x19 ~400K; "at least 10x faster throughputs than other existing Python libraries" (OpenSpiel, PettingZoo), ~100x with eight A100s. *(Figure values are approximate — read off the plot, not a table.)*

**Adding a game:** subclass `pgx.Env` and implement `_init(key)`, `_step(state, action, key)`, `_observe(state, player_id)`, plus `id`/`version`/`num_players` properties. `State` carries `current_player, observation, rewards, terminated, truncated, legal_action_mask, _step_count`. Note `EnvId` is a closed `Literal` and `make()` is a hardcoded if/elif chain — you cannot *register*, but you can instantiate your subclass directly, so it's not blocking.

**The pain is JAX, not pgx.** Everything must be `jit`/`vmap`-clean on fixed shapes: no dynamic move lists, no Python branching on board state. Rifle capture and kamikaze are fine (pure array edits). **Swap-with-friendly is fine.** **Chain-capture is the hard one** — a variable-length capture sequence must become either a fixed-bound `jax.lax.while_loop`/`scan` or a multi-step "continue the chain" sub-turn encoded in state. Doable; expect this to dominate the port.

**Effectively abandoned: yes.** Last commit *and* v2.6.0 both 2025-03-06; **20 open PRs, none merged since**, last merged PR is #1303 (the v2.6.0 release). Unmerged contributions include `go_13x13`, Domineering, and a batch of June-2026 perf fixes. The code works; nobody is driving.

## C. OpenSpiel

⭐5478, pushed 2026-08-31, v2.0.2 2026-08-12, Apache-2.0. **Python-only path exists**: implement in `open_spiel/python/games/` and call `pyspiel.register_game()`, which makes `pyspiel.load_game` find it — no C++ build, no CMake edits. The C++ path is an 11-step copy-tic-tac-toe-and-rename recipe ([developer_guide.md](https://openspiel.readthedocs.io/en/latest/developer_guide.html)). Python games are markedly slower (C++ Kuhn poker beats Python by ≥1 order of magnitude); for self-play at volume you'd eventually port to C++.

**AlphaZero ships and is maintained** — note the docs are stale: [`docs/alpha_zero.md`](https://github.com/google-deepmind/open_spiel/blob/master/docs/alpha_zero.md) still describes a TF1 implementation, but the actual directory now contains `model_linen.py` and `model_nnx.py` — it has been **rewritten in JAX/Flax**. A C++ LibTorch version lives at `open_spiel/algorithms/alpha_zero_torch/`. The standing caveat: "although it can handle games like Connect Four, it is not designed to scale to superhuman performance in Go or Chess."

**Chess**: full C++ implementation (`chess.cc`, `chess_board.cc`, `chess960_starting_positions.cc`) — a realistic base to fork for a variant.

## D. KataGo as reference

Claimed speedup: **"50x reduction in computation over comparable methods"**, using **fewer than 30 GPUs** and **19 days** to surpass ELF OpenGo's final model ([arXiv 1902.10565](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.10565)). The [README](https://github.com/lightvector/KataGo) adds: "a training run using only a *single* top-end consumer GPU could possibly train a bot from scratch to superhuman strength within a few months."

**Copy these** ([KataGoMethods.md](https://github.com/lightvector/KataGo/blob/master/docs/KataGoMethods.md)) — nearly all are game-agnostic: playout cap randomization; forced playouts + policy target pruning; auxiliary value/score/ownership targets (your analogue: material-differential and piece-survival heads); policy surprise weighting; shaped Dirichlet noise; root policy softmax temperature (1.1–1.25); dynamic variance-scaled cPUCT; subtree value bias correction; nested-bottleneck resnets; fixup init.

**Code is Go-specific.** `cpp/game/` is `board.cpp`, `boardhistory.cpp`, `rules.cpp` — all Go. The *techniques* transfer; the engine doesn't. KataGomo demonstrates the realistic path is fork-and-rewrite-the-board-layer, not configuration.

## E. Realistic single-GPU numbers

- **Hex, single RTX 2080 Ti** ([Scaling Scaling Laws with Board Games](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2104.03113)): near-perfect 9x9 Hex in "a little under 3 hours"; whole paper ~500 GPU-hours training + ~100 eval. Scaling laws: minimum compute for perfect play "increases 7× for each increment in board size"; **"500 Elo per order of magnitude increase in compute"**; "for each additional 10× of train-time compute, about 15× of test-time compute can be eliminated."
- **Connect Four, RTX 2070 8GB + i5-9600K** ([AlphaZero.jl tutorial](https://jonathan-laurent.github.io/AlphaZero.jl/stable/tutorial/connect_four/)): 15 iterations, **1–2 h per iteration** (~15–30 h total), 5000 self-play games and 600 MCTS sims/move per iteration. Beat a depth-5 minmax baseline; still imperfect vs a solver.
- **Chess in alpha-zero-general is a known dead end** — ~1–2 min per self-play episode at 100 sims on an RTX 2070 ([discussion #210](https://github.com/suragnair/alpha-zero-general/discussions/210)). Python-loop MCTS is the bottleneck, not the GPU.

**Could not verify:** AlphaZero-Edu's ([arXiv 2504.14636](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.14636)) hardware/hours — the abstract names 9x9 Gomoku and 19x19 Go but no GPU-hours; a secondary source says single RTX 3090 with 3.2x speedup at 8 processes. A "Quoridor trained in 24h on one consumer GPU" claim appeared only in a search snippet with no primary source reached. Exact Ludax steps/s tables and pgx Figure-3 values are read off plots.

**Bottom line for this project:** **minizero** is the closest match — maintained (2026-08-18), Apache-2.0, C++ MCTS + PyTorch training, and its [`BaseEnv`](https://github.com/rlglab/minizero/blob/main/minizero/environment/base/base_env.h) is a ~25-method virtual interface returning `std::vector<Action> getLegalActions()`, i.e. **dynamic move lists** — no fixed-shape tensor gymnastics for chain-capture. It already ships 20+ games including breakthrough, amazons, linesofaction and surakarta (breakthrough.cpp is ~14 KB, a realistic size target), and implements AlphaZero *and* Gumbel AlphaZero/MuZero. Second choice: OpenSpiel's Python `register_game` for a fast prototype, then its C++ chess as the port target. pgx only pays off if you're willing to write JAX-jittable rules and accept an unmaintained upstream.

## 1. onnxruntime-web

**Versions.** npm `latest` = **1.29.0, published 2026-08-24T19:17:15Z** (`https://registry.npmjs.org/onnxruntime-web` `time` field); `dev` = `1.31.0-dev.20260911`. GitHub tagged **v1.29.0 on 2026-08-12** and **v1.30.0 on 2026-09-10** — 1.30.0 is **not yet on npm as `latest`** as of today. ([releases](https://github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime/releases))

**WebGPU EP: recommended, not yet default.** The 1.29.0 notes say verbatim: *"onnxruntime-web has announced the deprecation of WebGL and JSEP. The native WebGPU EP is the recommended path going forward"* ([v1.29.0 notes](https://github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime/releases/tag/v1.29.0), PRs [#29716](https://github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime/pull/29716), [#31683](https://github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime/pull/31683)). But which implementation you get is a **build-time choice baked into the import path** ([docs/JSEP_Deprecation.md](https://github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime/blob/main/docs/JSEP_Deprecation.md)):

| import | WebGPU impl | wasm artifact |
|---|---|---|
| `onnxruntime-web` (default), `/all` | **JSEP** | `…jsep.wasm` |
| `onnxruntime-web/webgpu`, `/jspi` | **native WebGPU EP** | `…asyncify.wasm` / `…jspi.wasm` |

So **you must import `onnxruntime-web/webgpu`** to get the native EP today. JSEP is *"Status: deprecated… bug fixes and security fixes only"*, removal planned, **timeline explicitly not fixed**. The [migration doc](https://github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime/blob/main/docs/design/onnxruntime_web_jsep_to_webgpu_ep_migration.md) states *"Only Phase 0 is scheduled"* (Phase 1 flips the default, Phase 2 deletes JSEP).

**WebGL:** deprecated, deletion planned ([remove-webgl design doc](https://github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime/blob/main/docs/design/onnxruntime_web_remove_webgl_backend.md)); still shipped as `./webgl` in 1.29.0. Docs call it *"in maintenance mode"* ([web.html](https://onnxruntime.ai/docs/get-started/with-javascript/web.html)). Do not use it.

**Workers.** WebGPU compute needs no canvas. `WorkerNavigator.gpu` is supported in **Chrome 113 (partial) / 144 (full), Firefox 141 (dedicated workers only, *not* service workers), Safari 26** ([MDN BCD](https://github.com/mdn/browser-compat-data/blob/main/api/WorkerNavigator.json)). Safari 26 shipped WebGPU on macOS/iOS/iPadOS ([WebKit](https://webkit.org/blog/16993/news-from-wwdc25-web-technology-coming-this-fall-in-safari-26-beta/)). Two caveats: (a) ORT's own `env.wasm.proxy` worker **cannot be combined with WebGPU** — *"a GPU buffer is not transferable"* ([env flags](https://onnxruntime.ai/docs/tutorials/web/env-flags-and-session-options.html)); run ORT inside **your own** worker instead. (b) Service workers still fail (`import() is disallowed on ServiceWorkerGlobalScope`) — [#20876](https://github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime/issues/20876), open since 2024. Firefox's *"[meta] Re-enable WebGPU in worker threads"* ([bug 1818042](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1818042)) is still **NEW**.

## 2. WASM backend

**SIMD is mandatory, not optional.** Every published wasm artifact in 1.29.0 is `ort-wasm-simd-threaded.*` — there is no non-SIMD binary ([npm package exports](https://registry.npmjs.org/onnxruntime-web/1.29.0)). **Threads require cross-origin isolation.** Docs: *"Only when the browser supports WebAssembly multi-threading and `crossOriginIsolated` mode is enabled, multi-threading will be enabled"*; default `numThreads` is `min(hardwareConcurrency/2, 4)`. Without COOP+COEP/SharedArrayBuffer it **silently falls back to single-threaded SIMD wasm** (same binary, 1 thread).

## 3. TensorFlow.js — confirmed stale, no official announcement

**@tensorflow/tfjs 4.22.0, published 2024-10-21T18:51:42.166Z — verified exactly** via the registry. `next` is `4.23.0-rc.0` from **2025-01-08**, never promoted. `@tensorflow/tfjs-backend-webgpu` is on the same 4.22.0/2024-10-21. The repo is **not archived**, but default-branch commits are a single chore on 2026-04-06, and before that 2025-06-06 (`gh api repos/tensorflow/tfjs/commits`). Issue [#8719 "Is this project deprecated?"](https://github.com/tensorflow/tfjs/issues/8719) (opened 2026-06-10) is **still open, labelled `stat:awaiting tensorflower`, with no maintainer reply**. **I could not find any official statement** of maintenance mode or deprecation from the TF.js team — the absence of one is itself the finding. Weekly downloads: tfjs 366k vs onnxruntime-web 3.20M vs @huggingface/transformers 2.07M (npm downloads API, week ending 2026-09-11). Treat tfjs as unmaintained-in-practice.

## 4. transformers.js

**@huggingface/transformers 4.2.0, published 2026-04-22T16:28:41Z**; repo very active (commits through 2026-09-07). It **pins `onnxruntime-web@1.26.0-dev.20260416`** ([packages/transformers/package.json](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.js/blob/main/packages/transformers/package.json)) — i.e. it is a wrapper *around* ORT-web, one to two minors behind. WebGPU via `device: 'webgpu'`, but docs still say *"The WebGPU API is still experimental in many browsers"* ([docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers.js/en/index)). **Irrelevant for you** — it buys tokenizers, processors and pipelines you don't need, and pins an older ORT. Use `onnxruntime-web/webgpu` directly. (I found no explicit statement that it *refuses* arbitrary ONNX; the practical blocker is its config/processor layer.)

## 5. Measured numbers

**Dispatch overhead (the number that matters for tiny nets).** Maczan, *Characterizing WebGPU Dispatch Overhead…*, [arXiv:2604.02344](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.02344) (2026-02-09), [full text](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.02344v1), per-dispatch cost:

| Runtime | Backend | µs/dispatch |
|---|---|---|
| Chrome / RTX 5090 Linux | Vulkan | **32.8** |
| Chrome / RTX PRO 2000 Win | D3D12 | **58.7** |
| Chrome / Intel iGPU Win | D3D12 | **66.5** |
| Safari / M2 | Metal | **31.7** |
| **Firefox / M2** | Metal | **1038.7** |
| **Firefox / RTX PRO 2000** | D3D12 | **1036.7** |
| Dawn native / RTX 5090 | Vulkan | 23.8 |

Follow-up [arXiv:2608.08730](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08730) (2026-08-09): *"dispatch overhead, not kernel quality, is the bottleneck at batch size 1"*; fusing 876→564 dispatches gave **+53% throughput**.

**Small-model WebGPU-vs-WASM.** [gpuweb discussion #5292](https://github.com/gpuweb/gpuweb/discussions/5292): EfficientNet **~80 ms WASM vs ~1100 ms WebGPU** on an RTX 4090; WebGPU maintainer Kangz (2025-09-01): *"Most likely some operators are not implemented for WebGPU and fallback to software."* Per [sitepoint](https://www.sitepoint.com/webgpu-vs-webasm-transformers-js/) (403 to direct fetch; via search snippet only, treat as weak): all-MiniLM-L6-v2 batch-1 at **8–12 ms on WASM**, M2 MacBook Air, with WASM matching or beating WebGPU at batch 1.

**Chess-specific.** [hunterchen7/play-lc0](https://github.com/hunterchen7/play-lc0) is the closest prior art: Lc0 nets, ONNX Runtime Web, `executionProviders: ["webgpu","wasm"]`, `env.wasm.numThreads = 4`, inference in a Web Worker (`src/engine/inference.ts`); nets from 16×2 (~1.1 MB) to BT4-1024×15 (473 MB). **It publishes no latency numbers.** [Maia's platform frontend](https://github.com/CSSLab/maia-platform-frontend) uses `onnxruntime-web ^1.23.0` client-side. [frpays/lc0-js](https://github.com/frpays/lc0-js) exists (Emscripten + tfjs) but last pushed **2024-04-27** — treat as dead. Stockfish NNUE in wasm, [lichess-org/stockfish.wasm#21](https://github.com/lichess-org/stockfish.wasm/pull/21) (2020, dated): *"1000 knps wasm master branch / 10 knps wasm nnue / 60 knps wasm nnue with `-msimd128`"* vs 1000 knps native NNUE — i.e. NNUE cost ~16× the classical eval even with SIMD. Multi-threaded Stockfish wasm still *"requires proper CORS headers"*.

**Could not verify:** no published batch-1 latency benchmark for a 1–20M-param convnet under onnxruntime-web WebGPU; no published NPS for browser MCTS.

## 6. Sizing guidance (derived, not cited)

From the dispatch table: in Chrome you get **~75–150 GPU dispatches inside a 5 ms budget** before kernels do any work; Safari similar; **Firefox is unusable for tiny nets on WebGPU** (5 dispatches ≈ 5 ms). A 6–10 block resnet is ~60–120 dispatches post-fusion — right at the cliff. My arithmetic for WASM SIMD (assume 5–15 GFLOP/s single thread): a 6-block × 64-channel 8×8 resnet is ~57 MFLOP ⇒ ~4–11 ms; **4 blocks × 64ch or 6 × 32ch lands comfortably under 5 ms**. Conclusion for a batch-1 chess policy/value net: **default to WASM SIMD in a dedicated worker**, offer WebGPU only if you batch MCTS leaf evaluations (batching is what makes WebGPU win), and gate WebGPU off on Firefox.

---

# A) PS1 / LO-FI 3D ("PSX style")

## Hardware facts (verified)

| Trait | Reality |
|---|---|
| Vertex jitter | Rasterizer accepts **integer screen coords only** — no subpixel precision. Vertices round to the pixel grid, so polygons snap rather than slide. |
| Affine texture warping | Depth is discarded after projection; UVs interpolate linearly across 2D screen positions. Warping is worst on large polygons near the camera. Devs fought it with **polygon subdivision + LOD + manual mipmaps** (multiple texture resolutions stored on disc). |
| No z-buffer | An **Ordering Table** (linked list) sorted by *average polygon depth*. Hence per-polygon pop-through, not per-pixel z-fighting. |
| Colour | 24-bit capable, but display was usually cut to **15-bit (5 bits/channel)**. Hardware **ordered dithering** masked the banding. |
| Dither control | **Per-polygon, not global** — GPU register `GP0`, command `$E1`. Reads as a **2×2 checkerboard** smeared over textures and Gouraud surfaces. |
| Texture pages | Capped at **256×256**; 4bpp (16-colour) and 8bpp (256-colour) CLUT modes. FF8 characters cited at **128×128**. |
| Lighting | **Gouraud only** — one colour per vertex, interpolated. No per-pixel light. |
| Memory | 2 MB RAM, 1 MB VRAM (framebuffer *and* textures share it). |
| Resolutions | 256×240, 320×240, 512×240 common. |

- https://pikuma.com/blog/how-to-make-ps1-graphics (best single source)
- https://www.david-colson.com/2021/11/30/ps1-style-renderer.html
- https://gamingdoc.org/technical-documentation/consoles/sony-playstation/independent/video/dithering/
- https://danielilett.com/2021-11-06-tut5-21-ps1-affine-textures/ (affine shader)
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordered_dithering + https://github.com/tromero/BayerMatrix (4×4 Bayer PNGs, ready to drop in)

Colson's vertex-snap snippet (the whole trick):
```glsl
vec2 grid = targetResolution.xy * 0.5;
snapped.xy = floor(grid * snapped.xy) / grid;
```

**Ready-made implementations:** https://github.com/bonenaut7/gdx-psx (snap strength, affine, built-in Bayer matrices, colour reduction, downscale) · https://godotshaders.com/shader/ps1-shader/ · https://menacingmecha.itch.io/godot-psx-style-demo · https://romanliutikov.com/blog/ps1-style-graphics-in-threejs · Blender: https://fawkek.gumroad.com/l/psx-retro-tools

## FINAL FANTASY TACTICS (the closest analogue to your project)

Verified from the FFHacktics `SPR` format docs (https://ffhacktics.com/wiki/SPR_Spritesheet — Cloudflare blocks direct fetch; figures via indexed snippets):

- Decompressed unit spritesheet: **256 × 488 px**
- **4 bpp** — each nibble is a palette index
- **16 palettes × 16 colours** (512 bytes). **First 8 palettes = the unit, second 8 = the portrait.**
- Colour format: 2 bytes = **1 semi-transparency bit + 5 bits each B,G,R** — i.e. native PS1 15-bit
- Lower half of the sheet is compressed from offset `0x9200` (row 288)
- `SHP` files assemble frames from the sheet; `SEQ` sequences them (https://ffhacktics.com/wiki/SHP_&_Graphic_info_page)
- **Individual frame pixel dimensions: unverified** — FFT composes frames from sub-rectangles rather than a fixed grid, so there is no single "sprite size". Anyone quoting 32×32 for FFT is extrapolating.

So the readability formula is: **a unit is 16 colours max, on a 15-bit-colour 3D map.** That extreme palette scarcity per unit is exactly *why* units pop off the map — the map has far more colours and far lower contrast than any single unit.

**Team identification is done by palette swap.** Factions get their own palette index (e.g. palette 4 = Corpse Brigade / Baert Company). Directly transferable to chess: same sprite, two of the eight unit palettes = white/black side. (https://www.nexusmods.com/finalfantasytacticstheivalicechronicles/mods/43 documents per-faction palette sets.)

**Camera** (https://ffhacktics.com/wiki/How_the_Battle_Camera_Works):
- Yaw rotates on L1/R1; **if a target yaw would land orthogonal, the game adds 45° so the map always sits diagonal.** Rotation is a smooth tween to the new angle, not a jump.
- Pitch on R2; **three zoom values** on L2.
- Map also **auto-rotates when a tile is obscured**.
- Units are **flat quad polygons with transparent textures, transformed by the 3D camera** — billboards. Sprite art is drawn for fixed facings; the sprite does not re-pitch with the camera.

**Vagrant Story** — same team as FFT, and the technique worth stealing: environments shaded by **baking light into vertex colours** that multiply the texture (no lighting engine at all), and pseudo-shadows made by **layering two differently-shaded copies of the character model**. (https://threadreaderapp.com/thread/1226610123000467457.html)

**Tactics Ogre (PSX)** — battle sprites are tiny with few frames (**~28 frames** for a base battle sprite); isometric needs 4 facings but **front/back mirror, so only 2 are drawn**. PSP version billboards sprites over a 3D map of upscaled 32×32 tiles. *Medium confidence — forum-sourced* (https://steamcommunity.com/app/1451090/discussions/0/594016530242505538/).

## Modern PSX revival — readability notes

| Game | What's documented |
|---|---|
| **Signalis** (rose-engine) | Low-poly 3D **plus 2D sprites**, blended for a "pixel-perfect" look. Texture resolutions **unverified** — no dev breakdown found. http://rose-engine.org/press/Presskit_SIGNALIS.html |
| **Crow Country** (SFB Games) | Happy accident: a shader made real-time 3D read like **pre-rendered PS1 backgrounds** — but the camera rotates, revealing it isn't. Characters: defined joints, **smooth shading, high-contrast lighting**, deliberately evoking pre-rendered sprites. |
| **Dread Delusion** (James Wragg) | Readability *argument*, not spec: PS1 games are "unashamedly games" — it is always obvious what is interactable. https://www.videogamesgood.com/post/pax-west-2024-dread-delusion-james-wragg-interview-retro-ps1-rpg |
| **LUNACID** | Heavily pixelated, **repeated** textures; distant detail collapses into silhouette. Renders the PS1 look **"as it appears in memory"** — no jagged edges, no texture warping — with optional crunchier-PS1 / VHS / vaporwave filters on top. https://www.pcgamer.com/lunacid-brings-fromsoftwares-original-rpg-series-into-the-21st-century/ |
| **Paratopic** (Jessica Harvey) | Not about fidelity — about the low-poly look's "hauntological potentials". https://www.gamesradar.com/exploring-the-resurgence-of-the-low-fi-3d-visual-style-of-the-ps1-era/ |
| **Fear the Spotlight** | VHS-like retro visuals (Cozy Game Pals / Blumhouse, 2024). No art-tech detail found. |
| **Murder House** | **Nothing found.** Unverified. |

**The honest summary of the revival:** these games *gesture* at PS1 limits without respecting them — polygon counts far exceed anything the console could draw, and they use texture resolutions that were technically legal but practically unaffordable in 1997. (https://polycount.com/discussion/226167/ — 403s to fetchers, reachable in a browser.)

**Outlines:** PS1 hardware had none, and no PSX-revival title found uses them. Outlines in this space are a *modern 3D-pixel-art* convention, not a PSX one — see section C.

---

# B) HIGH-RES HAND-PAINTED PIXEL ART

| Game | Verified numbers | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Owlboy** (D-Pad Studio) | **640×360 base res; Otus is 39 px tall.** Scales 2×/3×/6× to 720p/1080p/4K with pixels intact. | Coined/popularised **"Hi-Bit"**. Palette size unverified — explicitly *unrestricted* palettes, hand-illustrated. https://www.gog.com/news/read_about_the_future_of_pixel_art_according_to_the_creators_of_owlboy |
| **Dead Cells** (Motion Twin) | **Characters ~50 px tall in-game.** | **The single most relevant reference for you.** See below. |
| **Blasphemous** (The Game Kitchen) | Fixed **360 px virtual frame height**, width from aspect ratio. | Penitent One sprite dims **unverified** (a forum asked "is it 64×64?" — never answered). Pixel art by **Andrey Gogiya** (https://www.behance.net/gallery/85604481/Pixel-arts-and-animations-for-game-Blasphemous), design Juan Miguel López Barea. Pure hand-made, pixel by pixel. B2 adds frames for fluidity. |
| **Hyper Light Drifter** | Dimensions/palette **unverified** | Method is documented: **flat colour as the base, then large gradients + vignette over the top** (from Superbrothers: S&S EP). Essentially **no per-sprite outlines** — silhouette and flat-colour blocking do the work. https://www.gamedeveloper.com/business/the-ultra-modern-stylings-of-hyper-light-drifter |
| **Eastward** (Pixpil) | Dimensions **unverified** | Pipeline is the interesting part: Aseprite assets are **split by natural structure, rebuilt in a 3D environment, and bump/normal maps hand-painted per part** so 2D pixel art responds correctly to a 3D lighting system. Artist Hong Moran. https://www.gamedeveloper.com/art/eastward-s-creators-share-insights-on-making-pixel-art-adventures |
| **The Last Night** (Odd Tales) | **Unverified** | "**Low-fi assets, hi-fi rendering.**" Hand-drawn sprites + **real 3D floor geometry**, normal maps on 2D sprites, DOF, bokeh, reflections. https://medium.com/retronator-magazine/the-future-of-pixel-art-with-the-last-night-a9a4eb61e824 (403s to fetchers) |
| **Children of Morta** | **Unverified** | "High resolution pixel art"; per-character move sets forced very large frame counts. https://techraptor.net/gaming/previews/how-dead-mage-created-art-for-children-of-morta |
| **Chasm** (Bit Kid) | **Unverified** | Artists Dan Fessler, Tony Redmer, Glauber Kotaki. |
| **Iconoclasts** (Joakim "Konjak" Sandberg) | **Unverified** — one Retronator note says "640px anti-aliased"; low confidence | Heavy anti-aliasing, coloured outlines. |
| **Vanillaware** (Odin Sphere / Dragon's Crown / Unicorn Overlord / 13 Sentinels) | Dragon's Crown native **1080p** | **Not pixel art.** Hand-painted high-res parts, each limb/piece animated separately, composited in a **layered 3D space with strong backlights** for depth. Frame counts/resolutions unverified. https://blog.playstation.com/2020/08/10/how-atlus-x-vanillaware-bring-2d-art-to-life-in-13-sentinels-aegis-rim/ |

## Dead Cells' 3D→pixel pipeline (read this first)

https://www.gamedeveloper.com/production/art-design-deep-dive-using-a-3d-pipeline-for-2d-animation-in-i-dead-cells-i- and https://www.gameanim.com/2018/01/31/dead-cells-3d-pipeline-2d-animation/

- 3DS Max → `.fbx` → **"a little homebrew program … renders the mesh at a very small size and without antialiasing."**
- Characters land at **~50 px** in-game height.
- **Cel shading** on low-res models; each frame exported as PNG **plus a normal map**, so the toon shader restores volume in-engine.
- **No documented palette quantisation or colour cap** — the pixel look comes from small render size + AA off, not from indexing.
- Honest downsides they state: **flickering pixels had to be hand-cleaned** (never solved), and *"the disappointing level of detail is and always will be an issue"* — they chose animation fluidity over sprite detail.
- Motivation: one artist for the first year. The pipeline is a **labour** decision before it is an aesthetic one.

## Pixel-art authority: outlines, ramps, colour counts

**Pixel Logic — Michael Azzi (Michafrar)** — https://michafrar.gumroad.com/l/pixel-logic. The only source found that gives page-cited rules:
- **"Readability is the #1 priority when choosing colours."** (p.79)
- **Limit main colours to 2–3 per character** for recognisability (p.104)
- **Black outlines** read well but go muddy in dense designs (p.31); **coloured outlines** (hue-matched to surroundings) blend with backgrounds (p.33)
- **Avoid pure black** — dark brown/purple/grey instead (p.72). Stylistic, not technical.
- **Silhouette must show head, limbs, cloth** (p.103); keep visual **spacing** between features or they fuse (p.106)
- **AA helps small sprites but eats pixels** — use moderately (p.111)
- **Dithering hurts small sprites and hinders animation** (p.117) — reserve for large backgrounds
- Worked example: 25 → 15 colours held up; **below 10 it degraded** (pp.81–82)
- **Selective outline = a shaded outline.** Reads as a broken line on light backgrounds; works far better on **dark** ones. Cross-ref Subpixeling p.197.
- Chapters: Introduction, Line art, Anti-aliasing, Colours (60–85), Readability (86–113), Dithering, Game perspectives, Clean-up, Subpixeling, Animation.

**Pedro Medeiros / saint11** — https://saint11.art/pixel_art_articles/article6/ (Medium mirror: https://medium.com/pixel-grimoire/how-to-start-making-pixel-art-6-a74f562a4056)
- **"Instead of a simple value ramp, use a hue-shifting and saturation-shifting ramp"** — shadow **colder, bluer, less saturated**; light **warmer, yellower, more saturated**.
- Avoid 100% saturation (eye strain). **Large low-sat areas + small high-sat details.**
- Keep hue variety limited or the image gets busy.
- **Gives no numbers on purpose** — "flexible guides, not immutable rules." Anyone citing saint11 for a colour count is inventing it.

**For a 32–64 colour 3D-rendered chess game, the structural picks are Apollo (uniform 6×6 ramps) and Vinik24 (shared shadow/highlight endpoints), not the biggest palettes.** Uniform ramp length is what lets you index by luminance instead of nearest-colour matching.

## Hue shifting

- **saint11 art.6** (above) — the canonical statement of cool/desaturated shadow, warm/saturated light
- Lospec's tutorial index: https://lospec.com/pixel-art-tutorials/tags/hueshifting — ENDESGA quicktip (2018) https://twitter.com/ENDESGA/status/971690827482202112 · GDquest "Picking Strong Colors with Hue Shifting" https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RL_5va7jEx8 · Solar Lune https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yRCTL0PA4X0
- *Pixel Logic* p.67 — conventional shift is yellow (bright) → purple (dark)
- Generators for ramps: https://www.wayline.io/color-ramp-generator · https://spritory.com/tools/color-ramp/

## Palette as LUT for 3D rendering

**The exact-swap LUT (Yanrishatum)** — https://gist.github.com/Yanrishatum/86794e9e663a7e343f9ef66e8b0f38ae
Flattens the RGB888 cube into a 2D atlas (blue channel = slice index), sampled as a post-process. **Read this for the failure modes, which are the valuable part:**
- **Semi-transparency breaks** — applying the LUT as a post-process destroys transparent elements
- **Requires exact colour matches** — `#343434` vs `#343435` silently fails. This kills it for anti-aliased or lit 3D output.
- **VRAM cost** — a full-precision LUT is a 4K texture
- **Double-LUT** (colour → index → palette texture) cuts the footprint and gives you free palette swapping — *directly useful for your two chess sides*

**Nearest-colour quantisation LUT (the one you actually want for 3D)** — https://markolainen.itch.io/godot-o1-color-quantization-shader-and-lut-creator-software
Bakes nearest-colour matches in **Oklab** (perceptually uniform — matters enormously, RGB distance picks visually wrong neighbours in dark ramps) into a LUT so runtime is **O(1)** per pixel instead of a per-pixel loop over the palette.

**Preserving value ramps — the key technique:** don't quantise by colour distance at all. Give **each material its own hand-authored ramp**, bake the ramps into LUT rows, and **index by lighting luminance**. Nearest-colour matching in any colour space will happily jump a shadow pixel into a different hue family and destroy the ramp; luminance-indexed per-material ramps cannot. See https://github.com/unitycoder/LutLight2D.

**Pro/con of palette-mapping 3D renders:**
- **Pro:** pixelation + quantisation are **deterministic render passes**, so animation stays coherent across every frame and every camera angle (https://rigbake.com/features/pixel-art-from-3d/). For a chess game — 6 piece types × 2 colours × N rotations — this is the whole argument.
- **Pro:** apply **ordered dithering before quantisation** to reclaim apparent colour depth (https://www.artstation.com/artwork/X1m423), the same trick the PS1 GPU did in hardware.
- **Con:** anti-aliased edges quantise into speckle. Dead Cells' answer was **turn AA off entirely**, and they *still* hand-cleaned flickering pixels.
- **Con:** LUTs are post-process, so they run after transparency and after any effect you wanted left alone.

## Pixel-stable 3D rendering (most important finding for your project)

**David Holland, "3D Pixel Art Rendering"** — https://www.davidhol.land/articles/3d-pixel-art-rendering/
- Renders at **640×360**
- **1-pixel outlines** from screen depth + normals edge detection with a 4-tap kernel (up/down/left/right only — that's what keeps them 1 px). Depth texture gives object outlines, normals give interior edges; **convex edges isolated by the cross product of neighbouring normal texels**.
- Candid caveat: *"I'm not sure it's quite possible to create a perfect outline shader that works for all models and all camera angles at this low resolution."* **Low-poly models with clearly defined outer edges suit best**, and parameters need per-scene tuning.
- **The anti-crawl technique (from t3ssel8r), two steps:** (1) snap the camera to a **view-aligned, texel-sized grid** — kills pixel creep but makes motion stutter; (2) **shift the render output back in screen space by the snap error** — restores smooth motion.

**Dylan Ebert, "Texel Splatting: Perspective-Stable 3D Pixel Art", arXiv:2603.14587 (Mar 2026)** — https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.14587
- **Grid-snapping works under orthographic projection and fails under perspective**, because pixels at different depths drift at different rates and no single snap corrects them all.
- Texel splatting: render geometry into a **cubemap from a fixed world point**, splat each texel as a **world-space quad**. Cubemap indexing → rotation invariance; grid-snapping the origin → translation invariance.

**Practical upshot for a pixel-art 3D chess game: use an orthographic camera.** It is the difference between grid snapping working in ten lines and not working at all. FFT's 45°-locked diagonal yaw plus three discrete zoom steps is the same insight expressed as game design — constrain the camera so the pixel grid stays honest.
