# 2. Teardown (Dennis Gustafsson) — the richest technical source by far

Note this is the *counter-example*: physically-based raytraced voxels, not flat-shaded toy.

**Voxel size (primary, official):** one voxel is **0.1 m (10 cm)** at default scale. `GetShapeSize` returns "scale (number) – The size of one voxel in meters (with default scale it is 0.1)" — https://teardowngame.com/modding/api.html

**Authoring** (https://www.teardowngame.com/modding/):

- Palette is **255 indexed entries where the index *is* the material**: "Only the position in the palette is important from a material perspective. For example, the color at index 9 is always grass, no matter what actual color it is."

**Palette / material encoding** (https://blog.voxagon.se/2020/12/03/spraycan.html):
- 8-bit palette, up to 255 materials per volume, "the representation per voxel is then just a single byte to save memory."
- Each entry carries "roughness, emissiveness, reflectivity and physical material type (wood, metal, foliage, etc)."
- All palettes packed into a texture 256 wide × number-of-materials tall.
- Spraycan cost: two shades in four steps needs eight empty palette slots per material, "cutting the usable number of entries in the palette down from 255 to a mere 28."

**Lighting / AO / denoise** (https://blog.voxagon.se/2018/10/17/from-screen-space-to-voxel-space.html):
- Full raytracing **in voxel space**, not screen space.
- Shadow volume: "I chose a texture resolution of 5 cm," stored "eight neighboring voxels per byte in an octree fashion, so each bit represents one octant in a 10 cm cube." The shadow texture "is binary and knows nothing about materials."
- AO: **five rays per pixel**, ray origin offset by normal and ray direction to kill shadow acne.
- Soft shadows by jittering the light position (worked example: a light with a 30 cm radius); the jitter also hides voxel-grid artefacts.
- Budget: **~9 ms at 1080p on a GTX 1080** for all AO + lighting + fog + reflections including denoising.

**Frame breakdown** (Steven Wittens, https://acko.net/blog/teardown-frame-teardown/):
- One draw call per voxel object, **36 vertices / 12 triangles = a box**; the shader raymarches the 3D volume texture inside it.
- **2 extra MIPs** at half and quarter resolution to skip empty 2³ / 4³ blocks; object dimensions must be multiples of 4.
- **1-bit volumetric shadow map over the whole play area.** Marina level: a 1752×100×1500 3D texture, "a 262MB chonker"; each 8-bit texel packs 2×2×2 voxels, so effectively 3504×200×3000 voxels.
- AO: cosine-weighted hemisphere sampling, **2 samples per pixel**.
- Denoise: spiral blur weighted by distance, attenuated by depth and normal, then blended with the reprojected previous frame — "at least 4 times per frame" across lighting passes.
- **TXAA** with a tiny per-frame camera jitter.
- Emissive voxels do NOT self-illuminate; lights are placed manually (hemisphere, sphere, capsule, spot).
- Reflectivity is separate from metallicness; transparency via 50% screen-door / blue-noise thresholding.

Teardown's design-notes post is gameplay only, no art content: https://blog.voxagon.se/2020/11/05/teardown-design-notes.html

---

# 3. Minecraft — the canonical "smooth lighting" AO

**Official description** (https://minecraft.wiki/w/Light):
- "Smooth lighting is a lighting effect that blends light levels across block faces and darkens corners using ambient occlusion to add semi-realistic shadows and glowing from light sources."
- "For each corner of a side, the game checks diagonally for full blocks and determines the corner's brightness based on the found full blocks, with no full blocks meaning full brightness and both sides diagonally being full blocks meaning the darkest level possible." Values are then blurred and applied to the block texture.
- Minimum/Maximum smooth-lighting settings merged in Java 1.19.3 "because there is no difference between them."

**Exact numbers** (https://greyminecraftcoder.blogspot.com/2020/04/lighting-1144.html):
- Per vertex, sample "the three adjacent blocks plus the block which touches the face."
- "If all these four blocks are transparent, the 'Ambient Occlusion' light intensity will be **1.0**… if all four blocks are opaque the intensity will be **0.2**."
- "The Mixed Brightness for the vertex is calculated as the average of these four adjacent blocks." OpenGL then interpolates across the face.
- Code paths: `BlockModelRenderer::renderModelSmooth` vs `renderModelFlat`.

**Per-face directional shading** is real and documented as a concept, but the multipliers are not on the wiki. Block-model `shade`: "Defines whether the faces of this element should be shaded according to their orientation (true), or always shaded as if oriented straight up (false)." JE 26.3 adds `shade_direction_override`. https://minecraft.wiki/w/Model — the commonly cited constants (top 1.0 / bottom 0.5 / N-S 0.8 / E-W 0.6) are **unverified from a primary source**.

**The algorithm you actually implement** — Mikola Lysenko, who wrote the original Minecraft AO mod (https://0fps.net/2013/07/03/ambient-occlusion-for-minecraft-like-worlds/):

```js
function vertexAO(side1, side2, corner) {
  if (side1 && side2) return 0
  return 3 - (side1 + side2 + corner)
}
```
Returns 0 (max occlusion) to 3 (none). Then the mandatory anisotropy fix, or your quads shade differently depending on triangulation:
```js
if (a00 + a11 > a01 + a10) { /* generate flipped quad */ } else { /* normal quad */ }
```

**Meshing numbers** (https://0fps.net/2012/06/30/meshing-in-a-minecraft-game/): 8×8×8 solid cube — naive 3072 quads, culled 384, greedy 6. Other cases 690→22, sphere 4770→2100, noisy terrain 2198→1670. "The greedy mesh has no more than 8x as many quads than the optimal mesh." Critically, **merging is blocked by differing texture, light value, normal — and per-vertex AO**, so greedy meshing and vertex AO fight each other.

---

# 4. Townscaper (Oskar Stålberg)

**Verified** (https://www.gamedeveloper.com/game-platforms/how-townscaper-works-a-story-four-games-in-the-making):
- Grid: "taking a fixed hexagonal grid, breaking it up into quads, then breaking it up into quads again and then moving some of the points within the grid."
- "when a new piece is added, the Wave Function Collapse identifies the possible modules for that cell, and then afterwards it will decorate it."
- Marching-cubes-style: tiles are **corner segments**, not whole cells — "the Marching Cubes algorithm allows for tiles to be placed in ways that best fit the shape of the grid cells given it focuses on how to place the corners of buildings."
- Windows/doors are cut with the **stencil buffer**.

**Palette: 15 building colours + ground.** Voxel type 0 = red … 14 = white, 15 = ground. https://townscaper.fandom.com/wiki/List_of_colors and https://github.com/alvaro-cuesta/townsclipper

**Lighting:** a later update added a lighting panel for sun position; the night scenario auto-adds "cool warm orange lights inside houses." https://80.lv/articles/townscaper-adds-lighting-options-flying-towns

**Outlines: Townscaper DOES appear to use them** — the one game here that does. Community observation, not dev-confirmed: "It looks like the outlines are created from slightly enlarged geometry that's only visible from the backside" (classic inverted-hull). https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=29074015

**Brick texture trick** (same HN thread + https://reindernijhoff.net/2021/11/townscapers-rendering-style-in-webgl/): "Take a really low rez texture. Shrink every other pixel to the size of a single pixel on your screen. Now you got yourself a nice random brick texture. Townscaper does that dynamically in a pixel shader." Reinder calls it the "every odd pixel is a line" technique.

**AO technique: UNVERIFIED.** A phrasing circulates that the occlusion lives in a layered mesh reprojected to a texture on each change, blurred, then sampled in the vertex shader. I could not locate a primary source for it (Stålberg's tweets are not fetchable; his SGC21 "Beyond Townscapers" talk at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Uxeo9c-PX-w was not transcribable here). Treat it as a lead, not a fact.

---

# 5. Hytale — the most explicit *official* art-direction document I found

https://hytale.com/news/2025/12/an-introduction-to-making-models-for-hytale (verbatim quotes)

- **Geometry:** "We only use 2 primitives: Cubes (6 sides) Quads (2 sides)." No spheres, edge loops, triangles, or pyramids. Rationale: "This ensures all models are easy to make, unwrap, and animate, and don't require Weight Painting, rigging, or a 3D Art degree to get started."
- **Texel density:** textures are "non-square and must be multiples of 32px (32, 64, 96, 128, etc.)". **Characters/attachments 64px per unit; props/blocks 32px per unit.**
- **Stretch limits:** "avoid going under 0.7X and over 1.3X the stretch for a node in one axis."
- **Colour rule:** "Avoid pure white and pure black, as this will break lighting ingame." Shadows carry hue — "a hint of purple in the shadows" — rather than being desaturated.
- **Lighting:** "We paint lights and shadows inside textures and use real lights/shadows to bring everything together." No PBR: "we rely on in-house light propagation techniques."
- **Silhouette discipline:** "We work as simply as possible, then slightly increase geometry and polygon count when needed to improve the silhouette," so "players can read the world they navigate, regardless of how cluttered the space is."
- Shading modes are set **per node** and exported, though "Blockbench isn't able to display these shading modes yet."

Exact colour counts per texture, outline use, and AO specifics are **not stated**.

# 7. General technique — the part you can act on in three.js

### Why flat shading reads as "toy"
Flat shading evaluates lighting **once per polygon** from the face orientation, so each face is one uniform colour; the result is "sharp, pronounced edges characteristic of faceted surfaces" and specular highlights render badly. Gouraud interpolates vertex intensities; Phong interpolates normals per pixel. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shading

Each voxel face becomes a flat colour chip with a hard value step at every 90° corner. That value step *is* the readability — it is doing the job an outline would do, which is why these games do not need outlines.

### three.js: flat shading costs you nothing geometrically
three.js does **not** split vertices for flat shading. It derives the face normal in the fragment shader from screen-space derivatives:
```glsl
#ifdef FLAT_SHADED
	vec3 fdx = dFdx( vViewPosition );
	vec3 fdy = dFdy( vViewPosition );
	vec3 normal = normalize( cross( fdx, fdy ) );
#else
	vec3 normal = normalize( vNormal );
#endif
```
https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/dev/src/renderers/shaders/ShaderChunk/normal_fragment_begin.glsl.js

So you do **not** need `toNonIndexed()` + `computeVertexNormals()` just to get flat shading. Set `flatShading: true` and you are done.

- `Material.flatShading` — "Whether the material is rendered with flat shading or not." `@default false`. https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/dev/src/materials/MeshPhongMaterial.js
- `Material.vertexColors` — "If set to `true`, vertex colors should be used. The engine supports RGB and RGBA vertex colors depending on whether a three (RGB) or four (RGBA) component color buffer attribute is used." `@default false`. https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/dev/src/materials/Material.js

### three.js VOXLoader already does greedy meshing (this changed recently)
https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/dev/examples/jsm/loaders/VOXLoader.js — `buildMesh()` (`VOXMesh` is deprecated):
- Builds a `Uint8Array` volume of palette indices.
- Sweeps the 3 axes; a face exists only when exactly one side is solid (`behind > 0 && infront === 0`, or the reverse — sign encodes facing).
- Greedy-merges the mask into quads ("Find width" then "Find height" loops), keyed on the **colour index**, so merging stops at every colour change.
- Emits `position` + `index` + a `color` Float32BufferAttribute, one colour per quad, converted with `SRGBColorSpace`; palette entries come from the 256-entry `.vox` palette.
- Calls `geometry.computeVertexNormals()`, then `new MeshStandardMaterial()`. Because each quad owns its own four vertices, the normals come out flat regardless.

### MagicaVoxel / Qubicle export reality
- **MagicaVoxel OBJ export** produces `.obj` + `.mtl` + a **256×1 PNG palette** where "Each pixel maps to a color in the palette." It merges adjacent same-colour voxels (a 2×2×2 cube exports as 12 triangles, the theoretical minimum) but **cannot merge across a colour change on the same face**, which is the real triangle-count driver. A moderately complex character lands around **1,600 triangles**. https://luciopaiva.com/magicavoxel-threejs-howto/
- **Qubicle**: base edition exports *unoptimised* OBJ/FBX/Collada; the **Mesh Module DLC** "Unlocks low poly mesh optimization for FBX, Collada and OBJ." Voxel formats: QB, QEF, QBT, QMO, QBCL, VOX, Minecraft Schematic. https://store.steampowered.com/app/454550/Qubicle_Voxel_Editor/
- Practical consequence: **vertex colours beat a texture atlas** for this look. No UVs, no atlas bleed, no mip artefacts at phone size, and you can merge many objects into one draw call. The cost is that greedy meshing stops at every colour boundary.

### The canonical lighting model for the flat-shaded voxel look
Sean Barrett's `stb_voxel_render.h` states it compactly — https://github.com/nothings/stb/blob/master/stb_voxel_render.h

Vertex format: "per-vertex 'lighting' or 'ambient occlusion' value (**6 bits**)" and "per-face **5-bit normal** for lighting calculation."
Lighting: "ambient lighting: half-lambert directional plus constant, all scaled by vertex ao."

The actual shader lines:
```glsl
vec3 ambient_color = dot(normal, ambient[0].xyz) * ambient[1].xyz + ambient[2].xyz;
ambient_color = clamp(ambient_color, 0.0, 1.0);
ambient_color *= amb_occ;
lit_color = albedo * ambient_color;
```
with the uniform contract documented in the header: `ambient[0].xyz` = negative direction of the directional light for half-lambert, `ambient[1].rgb` = light colour scaled by NdotL, `ambient[2].rgb` = constant light added — "effectively light ranges from ambient[2]-ambient[1] to ambient[2]+ambient[1]."

That is the entire recipe: **one directional term (half-lambert, so nothing goes fully black) + one constant ambient + a multiplied per-vertex AO term, applied to a flat albedo.** No shadow map required.

### The written style rule for the flat look
https://www.gamedeveloper.com/art/voxelart-styles-in-video-games (Zach Soares) names four styles. The two that matter to you:
- **Pixelated Voxels (Flat Shaded):** "With any form of hard shadows applied the piece and style will be ruined." Because of the "minimal presence of shadows," "the style benefits from vibrant colors." Examples given: Fugl (Melodive), Voxelnauts (Retro Ronin).
- **Vector Voxel Art:** "uses only 90 degree bends when representing curves… a very clean style that is easy to read at varying scales." Example: Crossy Road.

Note the tension worth flagging: Crossy Road sits in the *vector* bucket (angled camera, real lighting, bends at 90°), not the *flat-shaded-no-shadows* bucket. If you want "Crossy Road," you want flat normals plus a directional light plus a hard shadow; if you want the pure flat look, you want flat normals, AO only, and no directional shadow at all. The article treats those as different styles.

### Outlines — direct answer
Of everything verified here, **only Townscaper shows evidence of outlines** (inverted-hull, community-observed, not dev-confirmed: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=29074015). Crossy Road, Minecraft, Teardown and Hytale have no outline technique documented in any source I could reach. The per-face value step from flat normals is what separates the forms.

### `@tweenjs/tween.js` — stale, and it has a leak footgun

26 months since the last npm release. The default branch's last commit is **2025-01-11**; the repo's recent `pushed_at` is feature branches and unmerged PRs, not releases. Open issues include *"Help wanted :)"* (closed Mar 2026) and **"Free project maintainer offer"** (open, Aug 2026). It is feature-complete and zero-dep, so it won't rot fast — but nobody is driving.

Current correct API (read from the shipped `dist/tween.d.ts`, v25.0.0), the global-group pattern is deprecated:

```ts
import { Tween, Group, Easing } from '@tweenjs/tween.js'

const tweens = new Group()                       // NOT TWEEN.update()
const t = new Tween(mesh.position)               // NOT new Tween(obj, group)
  .to({ y: 2 }, 300)
  .easing(Easing.Quadratic.Out)
  .onComplete(() => tweens.remove(t))            // ← REQUIRED, see below
tweens.add(t)
t.start()

// per frame:
tweens.update()                                  // defaults to performance.now()
```

**Verified footgun.** From the v25 source, `Group.prototype.update(time, preserve)` defaults **`preserve = true`**, and the removal branch is `if (tween.update(...) === false && !preserve) this.remove(tween)`. With the default, **finished tweens are never removed from the group**. A game that spawns a tween per move/capture grows `_tweens` unboundedly and re-allocates `Object.keys()` over the dead set every frame. You must `group.remove()` in `onComplete` yourself. The `preserve` param that would fix it is itself deprecated.

Also ES5-transpiled output (40 `prototype` refs, zero classes/arrows): 43KB raw, **~7.1KB gzip**.

> Verdict: don't. Stale, and it makes you hand-write the cleanup you were trying to avoid writing.

### Hand-rolled — the honest numbers

This is the whole thing. Not a sketch, not pseudocode:

```ts
type Ease = (t: number) => number
export const outQuad  = (t: number) => t * (2 - t)
export const outCubic = (t: number) => 1 - (1 - t) ** 3
export const outBack  = (t: number) => { const c = 1.70158; return 1 + (c+1)*(t-1)**3 + c*(t-1)**2 }
export const inQuad   = (t: number) => t * t

type Tw = { t: number; d: number; ease: Ease; step: (k: number) => void; done?: () => void }
const active: Tw[] = []

export const tween = (d: number, step: (k: number) => void, ease: Ease = outQuad, done?: () => void) =>
  active.push({ t: 0, d, ease, step, done })

export function updateTweens(dt: number) {
  for (let i = active.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
    const tw = active[i]
    tw.t += dt
    const finished = tw.t >= tw.d
    tw.step(finished ? 1 : tw.ease(tw.t / tw.d))
    if (finished) { active.splice(i, 1); tw.done?.() }
  }
}
```

**18 lines.** It has no leak (removal is unconditional, unlike tween.js), and it's `dt`-driven so it composes with your render loop and pauses for free.

Your hop is then one call:

```ts
tween(0.3, k => {
  mesh.position.lerpVectors(from, to, k)
  mesh.position.y += Math.sin(k * Math.PI) * 0.8   // the arc
}, outQuad)
```

Chain-capture lunges are `tween(...)` in a `done` callback. Screen-shake is a tween on `camera.position` with a decaying random offset. Glowing tiles are a tween on `material.emissiveIntensity`.

> **A dependency is not warranted.** 18 lines beats 7KB, 28KB, or a 4.7MB transitive dep — and the dependency-free version is the only one where you don't have to remember the cleanup rule.

| `three.quarks` | **0.17.1** | **2026-05-21** | MIT | Yes |

### `three-nebula` — not abandoned, the opposite

This is the finding that most contradicts your brief. It went through an intense development burst in the last six weeks:

- **13.0.0 (2026-08-22)** — deterministic seeded simulation; no longer touches global `Math.random`.

- **13.2.0 (2026-09-12)** — `RibbonRenderer` soft-edge polish.

> Verdict: healthy and modern, but it's a full VFX engine (behaviors, zones, JSON effect schema) for what you need to be eight flying cubes.

### `three.quarks` — solid, batched, has a visual editor

**0.17.1 (2026-05-21)**, MIT, 12.2K weekly downloads. **Peer dep `three: ">=0.182.0"`** — r186 is fine. TypeScript-native. Batched/instanced rendering, billboard + stretched-billboard + **mesh particles** + trails, emitter shapes, sub-emitters, force fields, Unity Shuriken import, and a WYSIWYG editor at `quarks.art/create` exporting JSON. 1.2MB unpacked.

> Verdict: the better pick *if* you were buying a particle engine — mesh particles suit voxel debris, and the editor is a real time-saver. You aren't buying one.

### Custom — `InstancedMesh`, and it's not close

For **chunky voxel cubes**, `InstancedMesh` wins outright. `THREE.Points` + ShaderMaterial renders camera-facing quads — to make those look like tumbling 3D cubes you'd write the cube projection in a shader. `InstancedMesh` just instances an actual `BoxGeometry`, so your debris rotates in 3D for free and matches the pixel-art blocks already in your scene. Confirmed present in r186 (`src/objects/InstancedMesh.js`, plus `BatchedMesh`, `Points`, `Sprite`).

Reusable burst emitter, complete:

```ts
const CAP = 300
const dummy = new THREE.Object3D()
const mesh = new THREE.InstancedMesh(
  new THREE.BoxGeometry(0.08, 0.08, 0.08),
  new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial(),
  CAP)
mesh.instanceMatrix.setUsage(THREE.DynamicDrawUsage)
mesh.count = 0
scene.add(mesh)

type P = { x:number;y:number;z:number; vx:number;vy:number;vz:number
           life:number; max:number; spin:number; c:THREE.Color }
const pool: P[] = Array.from({ length: CAP }, () => ({
  x:0,y:0,z:0,vx:0,vy:0,vz:0,life:0,max:0,spin:0,c:new THREE.Color() }))
let live = 0

export function burst(at: THREE.Vector3, n: number, color: THREE.Color, speed = 4) {
  for (let i = 0; i < n && live < CAP; i++) {
    const p = pool[live++]
    p.x = at.x; p.y = at.y; p.z = at.z
    const th = Math.random() * Math.PI * 2
    const ph = Math.acos(2 * Math.random() - 1)
    const s  = speed * (0.5 + Math.random())
    p.vx = Math.sin(ph) * Math.cos(th) * s
    p.vy = Math.abs(Math.cos(ph)) * s
    p.vz = Math.sin(ph) * Math.sin(th) * s
    p.life = 0; p.max = 0.6 + Math.random() * 0.4
    p.spin = (Math.random() - 0.5) * 10
    p.c.copy(color)
  }
}

export function updateParticles(dt: number) {
  for (let i = live - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
    const p = pool[i]
    p.life += dt
    if (p.life >= p.max) {                       // swap-remove
      pool[i] = pool[--live]; pool[live] = p; continue
    }
    p.vy -= 14 * dt
    p.x += p.vx*dt; p.y += p.vy*dt; p.z += p.vz*dt
    if (p.y < 0.04) { p.y = 0.04; p.vy *= -0.4; p.vx *= 0.8; p.vz *= 0.8 }  // bounce
    dummy.position.set(p.x, p.y, p.z)
    dummy.rotation.set(p.life * p.spin, p.life * p.spin * 0.7, 0)
    dummy.scale.setScalar(0.6 + (1 - p.life / p.max) * 0.4)
    dummy.updateMatrix()
    mesh.setMatrixAt(i, dummy.matrix)
    mesh.setColorAt(i, p.c)
  }
  mesh.count = live
  mesh.instanceMatrix.needsUpdate = true
  if (mesh.instanceColor) mesh.instanceColor.needsUpdate = true
}
```

**~45 lines.** One draw call, fixed allocation, no GC churn.

**Gotcha worth flagging:** per-instance colors are indexed by *slot*, not by particle. Because `updateParticles` swap-removes, particle↔slot binding changes between frames — so the color must be stored on the particle and re-written with `setColorAt` every frame, as above. Setting it only once in `burst()` produces colors that visibly jump between particles as others die. This is exactly the kind of bug that makes people reach for a library; it's four characters of fix once you know.

This same emitter covers **all** your effects: capture explosion (`burst` with piece color), kamikaze (bigger `n`, higher `speed`), arrow projectiles (a tween on a single mesh + a small trailing `burst`). 

### Other 2026 options
`partykals` (RonenNess) exists but is dormant and thin. Beyond that, the field has consolidated onto three.quarks and three-nebula — there is no new must-see entrant.

> **Verdict: custom InstancedMesh.** ~45 lines, exactly the voxel look you want, and both libraries would need roughly as much glue code to configure.

## 3. Audio

| Package | Version | Last npm publish | License | Maintained |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `howler` | **2.2.4** | **2023-09-19** | MIT | **No — last code commit 2023-09-19** |
| `zzfx` | **1.3.2** | **2025-09-17** | MIT | Yes (repo active 2026-09-11) |
| `jsfxr` | **1.4.1** | **2026-05-05** | **Unlicense (public domain)** | Yes |

### `howler` — your suspicion is correct

Three years stale. Commit log since v2.2.4: `Update readme` (2025-11-23), `Update BACKERS.md` (2024-06-23). That's it — **zero code commits since 2023-09-19**. 417 open issues. No `module`/`types`/`exports` fields in `package.json` (CJS `dist/howler.js` only); types come from community-maintained `@types/howler@2.2.13`, not the author. Still 708K weekly downloads on momentum.

> Verdict: **not the 2026 default.** Its reason to exist was papering over HTML5 Audio vs Web Audio and 2014-era codec bugs. Those are gone.

### `THREE.Audio` / `PositionalAudio`

Present in r186 (`src/audio/`: `Audio.js`, `PositionalAudio.js`, `AudioListener.js`, `AudioAnalyser.js`, `AudioContext.js`). They're thin wrappers over Web Audio — `THREE.AudioContext.getContext()` is literally a lazy `new (window.AudioContext || window.webkitAudioContext)()` singleton.

`PositionalAudio` costs you a `PannerNode` per sound plus per-frame listener matrix updates.

> Verdict: **skip.** A chess board is 8x8 in front of a fixed camera; 3D panning on a capture is inaudible. UI-style non-spatial sounds are correct here.

### Web Audio directly — the whole pattern

```ts
const ctx = new AudioContext()
const buffers = new Map<string, AudioBuffer>()

export async function load(name: string, url: string) {
  const res = await fetch(url)
  buffers.set(name, await ctx.decodeAudioData(await res.arrayBuffer()))
}

export function play(name: string, vol = 1, rate = 1) {
  if (ctx.state === 'suspended') return
  const src = ctx.createBufferSource()
  src.buffer = buffers.get(name)!
  src.playbackRate.value = rate                  // pitch variation, free
  const g = ctx.createGain()
  g.gain.value = vol
  src.connect(g).connect(ctx.destination)
  src.start()
}

// unlock — must run inside a real user-gesture handler
addEventListener('pointerdown', function unlock() {
  ctx.resume()
  removeEventListener('pointerdown', unlock)
}, { once: true })
```

**iOS rules, current state (verified 2026):**
1. **User-gesture unlock is still required and has not been relaxed.** An `AudioContext` starts suspended; `resume()` must be called from inside a click/touch/keypress handler ("sticky activation"). This is unchanged.
2. **The silent/ringer switch still mutes Web Audio on iOS** — HTML5 `<audio>` elements are exempt, Web Audio is not. This surprises people constantly.
3. **New in the 2025-26 window:** Safari has shipped the **Audio Session API**. Setting `navigator.audioSession.type = 'playback'` opts out of the ambient category and plays through the mute switch — no silent-buffer hack needed. Published as an **Editor's Draft as of Nov 2025, Safari-only**, and absent on iOS 16 and earlier. Feature-detect it:
   ```ts
   if ('audioSession' in navigator) (navigator as any).audioSession.type = 'playback'
   ```
   Fallback for older iOS is the classic silent-`<audio>`-tag trick (`unmute-ios-audio`, `swevans/unmute`) — but for a chess game, respecting the mute switch is arguably correct behavior anyway. I'd do the one-line feature-detect and skip the polyfill.

### 16-bit SFX generation — ZzFX is the lazier path, clearly

**`zzfx` 1.3.2 (2025-09-17), MIT.**
- `ZzFXMicro.min.js` is **1222 bytes raw / 870 bytes gzip** — the famous claim is real.
- Proper ESM: `import { ZZFX, zzfx } from 'zzfx'` (verified `export function zzfx(...)`, `export const ZZFX`, `export class ZZFXSound` in `ZzFX.js`).
- Play a sound in one line, no asset files at all: `zzfx(...[,,925,.04,.3,.6,1,.3,,6.27,-184,.09,.17])  // explosion`
- **Designer tool: https://killedbyapixel.github.io/ZzFX** — tweak knobs, hit a preset, copy the array, paste into your source. That's the entire workflow.
- Creates its own `AudioContext` (`zzfxX = new AudioContext`), so the same iOS unlock applies — call `zzfxX.resume()` on first gesture.
- **No TypeScript types shipped.** You'll want a one-line `declare module 'zzfx'`.

**`jsfxr` 1.4.1 (2026-05-05), Unlicense (public domain).**
```ts
import { sfxr } from 'jsfxr'
const sound = sfxr.generate('explosion')   // presets: pickupCoin, laserShoot,
sfxr.play(sound)                           // explosion, powerUp, hitHurt, jump,
                                           // blipSelect, synth, tone, click, random
```
Designer at **https://sfxr.me** — "serialize" gives you JSON to embed. 36KB raw / 8.7KB gzip. Also no types.

> **Lazier path: ZzFX.** 870 bytes vs 8.7KB, and a sound is a one-line array literal instead of a JSON blob. jsfxr's named presets (`explosion`, `hitHurt`, `laserShoot`) map suspiciously well onto your exact needs, so it's a fair alternative if you'd rather not fiddle with knobs — but ZzFX's designer gets you there in about the same time and costs 10x less. Both licenses are maximally permissive (MIT / public domain).

## Recommendation

| Need | Take | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Hops, slides, lunges, shake, tile glow | **Hand-rolled tween** | 18 lines |
| Explosions, debris, arrows, kamikaze | **Hand-rolled `InstancedMesh` emitter** | ~45 lines |
| SFX | **`zzfx`** — the only dependency | 870 B gzip |
| Audio playback | **Web Audio directly** + gesture unlock + `audioSession` detect | ~15 lines |

**Total: ~78 lines and one sub-kilobyte dependency.** The library alternatives run 7KB–28KB gzip (or a 4.7MB transitive dep) and would still need comparable glue code to configure.

- **`three-nebula` is not abandoned** — it published **yesterday (2026-09-12)** and has shipped a TypeScript rewrite, WebGPU renderer, seeded determinism, and nested emitters since August 2026. Peer range `>=0.122.0 <1.0.0` covers r186 cleanly; no pinning problem.

The `three.mjs` binding alone is 1.76KB gzip; the core engine it pulls in is substantially more.

# Voxel asset routes for King Down Chess — verified 2026-09-13

## Bottom line first

Three findings change the shape of the answer:

1. **three.js `VOXLoader` already greedy-meshes.** As of r182 (PR #32489, merged 2025-12-05) `buildMesh()` is a real greedy mesher, and PR #32488 added `.vox` scene-graph support so a multi-object `.vox` loads as a *named* `Object3D` hierarchy. Your premise ("mesh per voxel chunk, is it instanced?") describes pre-r182 three.js. **Add no npm voxel library.** Every candidate you listed is either dead, GPL, or nonexistent.
2. **MagicaVoxel on macOS is frozen at 0.99.6.2 (Sept 2020).** You're on darwin. Windows got 0.99.7.2; Mac did not. This is the single biggest argument against Route A as your primary editor.
3. **vengi `voxconvert` v0.5.0 does the whole of Route B in one command**, including palette snapping and interior fill — and it's the only tool in this list that is both current *and* covers STL→vox→glb end to end.

Recommended stack: **C day one → B as a tracing aid → A for the actual asset, exported to `.glb` offline, loaded with `GLTFLoader`.** Rigid-part rigs + tweens for animation. Palette baked offline, LUT in the pixelation shader only if you want live team-colour swaps.

Side note: your pinned versions are all current — `three@0.186.0` (2026-09-08), latest `vite@8.3.0`, `typescript@7.0.2`.

### `.vox` format limits (verified against the official spec)

- **Palette: 256 entries.** `RGBA` chunk is exactly 256 × 4 bytes. Index 0 is empty/air. Irrelevant to you — you want 32-64.
- **Model size: 256³ hard cap.** `XYZI` stores `(x, y, z, colorIndex)` as **one byte each**. Not a tool limit, a format limit. Larger scenes = multiple `SIZE`/`XYZI` models placed by `nTRN` transform nodes. At 32³ you have ~0.2% of the budget.

## Route B — voxelizing your STL/OBJ miniatures

### The winner: vengi `voxconvert`

| | |
|---|---|
| Version | **v0.5.0**, released **2026-04-18** (0.6.0 in development) |
| Repo activity | pushed **2026-09-03**, 1,408 stars |
| License | **MIT** (assets CC BY-SA 3.0) |
| Maintained | Yes, heavily — the 0.6.0 changelog is enormous |
| npm | **Does not exist.** `@vengi/*` and `vengi` are not on npm. Don't look for it there. |
| Homebrew | **No formula and no cask.** Install from GitHub releases. |

Reads and writes obj, stl, gltf/glb, ply, fbx **and** `.vox` — both directions, one binary.

**Install (macOS):**

```bash
cd ~/tools
curl -LO https://github.com/vengi-voxel/vengi/releases/download/v0.5.0/mac-vengi-voxconvert-app.zip
unzip mac-vengi-voxconvert-app.zip
xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine vengi-voxconvert.app      # Gatekeeper
VOXCONVERT="$PWD/vengi-voxconvert.app/Contents/MacOS/vengi-voxconvert"
"$VOXCONVERT" --version
```

> Flagged: the binary path inside the `.app` is inferred from standard macOS bundle layout, not verified by unzipping. Check with `find vengi-voxconvert.app -type f -perm +111`. There is also `mac-dmg.zip` (28 MB) with the full suite.

**The command you actually want — STL → 28-voxel-tall `.vox`, solid, snapped to your palette:**

```bash
"$VOXCONVERT" \
  -set voxformat_voxelsize 28 \
  -set voxformat_voxelizemode 0 \
  -set voxformat_fillhollow true \
  -set voxformat_createpalette false \
  -set palette "$PWD/kdc-palette.png" \
  --input sculpts/pawn.stl --output voxels/pawn.vox --force
```

**Batch over every sculpt (this is your "easy to add pieces" story — a flat folder + one loop):**

```bash
mkdir -p voxels glb
for f in sculpts/*.stl; do
  n=$(basename "$f" .stl)
  "$VOXCONVERT" -set voxformat_voxelsize 28 -set voxformat_voxelizemode 0 \
    -set voxformat_fillhollow true -set voxformat_createpalette false \
    -set palette "$PWD/kdc-palette.png" \
    --input "$f" --output "voxels/$n.vox" --force
  "$VOXCONVERT" -set voxformat_mergequads true -set voxformat_reusevertices true \
    -set voxformat_ambientocclusion false \
    --input "voxels/$n.vox" --output "glb/$n.glb" --force
done
```

**Key cvars (verified verbatim from `docs/Configuration.md` at tag `v0.5.0`):**

| cvar | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `voxformat_voxelsize` | **"The number of voxels on the largest axis (0 = disabled, use scale cvars instead). Single mesh exports only."** | `0` |
| `voxformat_scale` / `_x` / `_y` / `_z` | Scale vertices before voxelization (the fallback when `voxelsize` doesn't apply) | `1.0` |
| `voxformat_voxelizemode` | `0` = high quality (Sierpinski triangle subdivision), `1` = faster/less memory (direct rasterization, "may have gaps or holes with very large triangles") | `0` |
| `voxformat_fillhollow` | **"Fill the inner parts of completely close objects, when voxelizing a mesh format"** | see note |
| `voxformat_targetcolors` | **"Target number of colors after voxelization (0 = no limit)"** — this is your palette quantizer, new in 0.5.0 | `0` |
| `voxformat_createpalette` | `false` = snap to the `palette` cvar instead of deriving one from the mesh | `true` |
| `voxformat_rgbweightedaverage` | Area-weighted colour blend when several triangles hit one voxel | — |
| `voxformat_mesh_simplify` / `_ratio` | Decimate the input mesh *before* voxelizing — useful for your high-poly sculpts | `false` |
| `voxformat_voxelize_chunked` / `_chunksize` | For meshes too big to voxelize in one pass (16–512) | `false` / `128` |
| `voxformat_meshmode` | Export mesher: `0` cubes, `1` marching cubes, `2` binary, `3` greedy texture | `0` |
| `voxformat_mergequads`, `_reusevertices`, `_quads`, `_ambientocclusion` | Mesh-export optimization | — |
| `voxformat_transform_mesh` | Bake keyframe transforms into the exported mesh | `false` |

> Flagged: the docs site summary said `voxformat_fillhollow` defaults to `true`, the cvar table doesn't state a default. Set it explicitly.

### Python — `trimesh`

| | |
|---|---|
| Version | **5.1.0**, uploaded **2026-08-31** |
| Repo | pushed 2026-09-02, 3,678 stars, **MIT** |
| Install | `pip install "trimesh[easy]" numpy` |
| Maintained | Yes, very |

Exact API, read from `trimesh/voxel/creation.py` and `base.py` on `main`:

```python
voxelize(mesh, pitch, method: Literal['subdivide','ray','binvox'] = 'subdivide', **kwargs) -> VoxelGrid | None
voxelize_subdivide(mesh, pitch, max_iter=10, edge_factor=2.0)
voxelize_ray(mesh, pitch, per_cell=None)                 # needs pyembree to be quick
voxelize_binvox(mesh, pitch=None, dimension=None, bounds=None, **binvoxer_kwargs)
local_voxelize(mesh, point, pitch, radius, fill=True, **kwargs)
```

```python
import trimesh
m = trimesh.load("sculpts/pawn.stl", force="mesh")
m.apply_translation(-m.centroid)                 # centre first, or you get an asymmetric piece
m.apply_scale(28.0 / m.extents.max())            # 28 voxels on the tallest axis
v = m.voxelized(pitch=1.0)                       # shorthand for trimesh.voxel.creation.voxelize
v.fill(method="holes")                           # interior fill; also "base", "orthographic"
grid = v.matrix                                  # (nx, ny, nz) bool ndarray
v.as_boxes().export("pawn.glb")                  # one Box per voxel — NO greedy merge
```

- `VoxelGrid.fill(method="holes")` is the default; the three registered fillers in `trimesh/voxel/morphology.py` are `fill_base`, `fill_orthographic`, `fill_holes`. `hollow()` is the inverse.
- **`VoxelGrid.export()` only writes `binvox`.** There is no `.vox` writer in trimesh. Your export paths are `as_boxes().export("*.glb")` (fat, one box per voxel) or `.matrix` → hand-write `.vox`.
- `as_boxes()` on a solid 28³ piece emits ~22k boxes ≈ 264k triangles. Unusable directly. Call `.hollow()` first, or don't use this path.

**Verdict: trimesh is the right tool if you want the numpy grid** (procedural generation, tests, custom `.vox` writing). It is the wrong tool if you just want a `.vox` file — vengi does that in one line.

### Python — `open3d`

| | |
|---|---|
| Version | **0.19.0**, uploaded **2025-01-08** — 20 months old |
| Repo | pushed 2026-09-12 (main is active; releases are not) |
| Install | `pip install open3d==0.19.0` |

```python
import open3d as o3d
m = o3d.io.read_triangle_mesh("sculpts/pawn.stl")
m.compute_vertex_normals()
ext = m.get_max_bound() - m.get_min_bound()
m.scale(28.0 / max(ext), center=m.get_center())
vg = o3d.geometry.VoxelGrid.create_from_triangle_mesh(m, voxel_size=1.0)
# also: create_from_triangle_mesh_within_bounds(mesh, voxel_size, min_bound, max_bound)
```

**Don't use it here.** Surface-only — no interior fill, so your pieces come out as shells. No `.vox` export. Stale wheels (check Python 3.13/3.14 availability before committing). It's a point-cloud/reconstruction library that happens to have a voxel grid.

### Quality caveats — the honest answer

Yes, auto-voxelizing a miniature sculpt at 16–32 voxels tall produces mush. Concretely:

| Height | What happens |
|---|---|
| 8–16 | Abstract token. A Pawn is fine. A Maester with a staff, an Archer with a bow, a Beast — all read as the same lump. |
| **24–32** | **The realistic target.** Silhouette survives. Faces, fingers, armour trim, weapon detail do not. |
| 48–64 | Detail returns, but the result stops reading as "pixelized" and starts reading as "low-res 3D". Wrong side of your art direction. |

Specific failure modes on miniature sculpts:
- **Thin features vanish or break into noise** — sword blades, spear shafts, bow strings, capes, banner poles. `voxformat_fillhollow` doesn't help; they're below one voxel.
- **Heads become blobs.** A face needs ~6 voxels across to read at all; at 28 tall the head is ~5.
- **Asymmetry.** If the mesh's symmetry plane isn't aligned to a voxel boundary, the left and right sides come out different. Centre the mesh and nudge by half a voxel before voxelizing.
- **Colour is worse than shape.** Your sculpts are almost certainly untextured STL, so `voxformat_createpalette` derives nothing useful — every voxel comes out one colour. You will be painting these by hand regardless.

**So: manual cleanup is not optional, it's the whole job.** The realistic workflow is:

1. Voxelize at **2–3× target** (`voxformat_voxelsize 64` or `96`) to get an accurate volumetric reference.
2. Load that `.vox` as a reference layer in Goxel/MagicaVoxel.
3. **Hand-build the real piece at 28–32**, tracing the silhouette and exaggerating the identifying feature (Archer's bow, Paladin's shield, Maester's chain).

The voxelizer is a **tracing aid**, not an asset generator. Budget 1–3 h per piece first time, 30–60 min once you have a shared base/plinth and body block to copy. 12 pieces ≈ 1–2 weeks part-time.

And the thing that actually matters for chess: **pieces are read by silhouette from a near-fixed camera.** A hand-built 28-voxel piece with an exaggerated distinguishing feature reads better than a faithful 64-voxel auto-voxelization of the miniature. Fidelity to the sculpt is not the goal.

## Route C — procedural placeholders

This is your day one. Zero tools, zero pipeline, zero dependencies, ships this afternoon, and it's the only route that gets pieces on the board before you've decided anything else.

Two variants:

**Box-stack (laziest):** each piece is 3–6 `BoxGeometry` primitives merged into one geometry. Base cylinder-ish stack, body, head, one identifying feature. ~15 lines of data per piece in a `Record<PieceType, [x,y,z,w,h,d][]>` table. All 12 pieces fit in one ~80-line file. Merge with `BufferGeometryUtils.mergeGeometries()` (already in `three/addons`) so each piece is one draw call.

**Typed 3D array:** a per-piece `string[][]` where each character is a palette index — a 3D ASCII sprite. More faithful to the final voxel look, more typing. Roughly 32 lines of text per piece at 16³.

Go with **box-stack**, because the entire point of a placeholder is that you throw it away. The typed-array version is 80% of the work of just building the real thing in Goxel.

Crucially, the box-stack placeholder and the real `.vox` asset should live behind the *same* interface: `loadPiece(type): Promise<Object3D>` that checks for `glb/<type>.glb` and falls back to the procedural builder. Then you replace pieces one at a time, in any order, with no code change. That is also your "easy to add new piece models over time" answer — drop a `.glb` in the folder, done.

## Loading `.vox` at runtime in three.js

### The built-in loader, as of r186

```js
import { VOXLoader, buildMesh } from 'three/addons/loaders/VOXLoader.js';

const result = await new VOXLoader().loadAsync('models/pawn.vox');
scene.add(result.scene);           // Object3D hierarchy, node names preserved
// or: const mesh = buildMesh(result.chunks[0]);
```

What it actually does, read from `examples/jsm/loaders/VOXLoader.js` at tag `r186` (919 lines):

- **`buildMesh()` is a greedy mesher.** The source is literally commented `// Greedy meshing` and implements the standard per-axis mask-sweep with rectangle merging. It emits one `BufferGeometry` (position + index + `color`) per model chunk, with `computeVertexNormals()` and a `MeshStandardMaterial({ vertexColors: true })`. **Not instanced, not box-per-voxel.** Landed in PR #32489, merged 2025-12-05 → r182.
- **Scene-graph support.** Parses `nTRN` / `nGRP` / `nSHP`, decodes the rotation byte, converts VOX Z-up → three.js Y-up, and **sets `object.name` from the `_name` attribute**. PR #32488. This is important for your animation rig — see below.
- **`parse()` returns `{ chunks, scene }`**, not an array. Array-style access still works through a deprecation `Proxy` that logs a warning.
- **`VOXMesh` and `VOXData3DTexture` are deprecated** (PR #32491, r182). They now just wrap `buildMesh()` / `buildData3DTexture()` and `console.warn` on construction. Use the functions.
- Accepts `.vox` version **150 and 200**.

## Greedy meshing — and whether you need it

**What it is:** a naive voxel mesher emits 6 quads per solid voxel. The first optimization is face culling — skip any face shared with a solid neighbour. Greedy meshing goes further: for each of the 6 face directions, sweep slice by slice, build a 2D mask of exposed faces tagged by colour, then repeatedly grab the largest axis-aligned rectangle of identical mask values and emit it as **one quad**. A flat 10×10 wall face becomes 1 quad instead of 100.

**Typical reduction:** 5–20× on voxel art with flat regions, better on anything architectural, worse on organic/noisy models where adjacent voxels differ in colour (merging only happens across *same-colour* runs). Face culling alone already gets you the biggest win — greedy is the second-order gain.

**Do you need it at 32³? No. This is premature optimization at your scale.** Rough numbers for a solid 28-tall chess piece: a few thousand exposed faces → ~4–8k triangles naive, a few hundred to ~1.5k greedy. Multiply by 32 pieces on the board: ~256k tris naive worst case. A 2026 GPU does not notice 256k static triangles.

**What would actually cost you is draw calls, not triangles** — 32 separate meshes plus board plus post-process. Still nothing, but that's the number to watch if you ever profile. The fix there is instancing or merging per side, not meshing strategy.

The honest framing: **you get greedy meshing for free from the built-in loader whether you want it or not.** So the question is moot — just don't go shopping for a library to provide it.

## `.vox` → glTF offline: yes, this is the lazier path

Converting offline and shipping `.glb` means:
- Runtime loads `GLTFLoader` (which you almost certainly already have) and nothing else.
- No `.vox` parse + mesh build on the main thread at load.
- Draco / meshopt compression available if you ever want it.
- The output is inspectable in any glTF viewer, which makes "did the export break?" a 5-second check.

**Tools that do it:**

| Tool | Command | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **vengi voxconvert** (recommended) | `vengi-voxconvert --input pawn.vox --output pawn.glb -set voxformat_mergequads true -set voxformat_reusevertices true --force` | MIT, current, already in your pipeline for Route B |
| **Goxel** | GUI export; `.glb` binary export added in commit 2026-07-21, **not yet in tagged 0.15.1** (0.15.1 has `.gltf` only) | GPL-3.0 |
| **Blockbench** | Import `.vox` via the "Voxel Importer" plugin → export glTF/GLB | Needs the plugin; GUI only |
| **`@voxel-tool/cli`** | `npx @voxel-tool/cli` — `.vox` ↔ glb/gltf/obj/stl/ply/usdz/fbx, headless Node | MIT, but 1 star and weeks old. Only reach for it if you want this step inside `npm run build` with no native binary. |
| **Avoyd** | GUI, optimised glTF/GLB export | INDIE/PRO tiers only, paid |

**The one reason to keep `.vox` at runtime:** two-colour teams. A `.vox` is palette-indexed, so one file + two palettes gives you both sides for free. With `.glb` the colours are baked into vertex-colour attributes.

But that's solvable in ~5 lines on the `.glb` side — walk `geometry.attributes.color` at load and remap, or tint via the material. So: **ship `.glb`, do the team colour as a load-time remap or a material uniform.** Keep the `.vox` files in the repo as the editable source; they're the "PSD", `.glb` is the "PNG".

---

## Animation for voxel characters

The community recognizes three techniques, and the consensus maps cleanly onto your three options:

**(i) Per-frame model swaps** — export one `.vox` per frame, swap meshes. This is the native MagicaVoxel approach (it has no rigging), and it's what pixel-art-minded voxel artists do. It is also "laborious, particularly for enemies with many animation frames."

For you: 12 pieces × ~4 actions × 8 frames = **384 models**. Absurd for a chess game. **Reject.**

**(ii) Rigid-part rigs** — split the model into parts, parent each to a transform node, animate transforms with no vertex warping. This is the standard for voxel games (Crossy Road, Minecraft entities, Cube World). The community guidance: "with voxels you can do rigid body rigging between an object and the joint to avoid complicating your work," and use "variable-sized limbs (like a larger shoulder with a slimmer arm socketed inside)" so joints don't gap when they rotate. Known downsides: z-fighting between parts and mesh clipping at joints.

**In three.js this is nearly free given the r182+ loader.** Name your objects in MagicaVoxel/Goxel — `head`, `arm_l`, `torso` — and `VOXLoader` reads the `nTRN` `_name` attribute straight onto `object.name`. So:

```js
const rig = result.scene;
const head = rig.getObjectByName('head');
// animate head.rotation / head.position, or drive it with an AnimationClip
```

Export to `.glb` and the named hierarchy survives — `GLTFLoader` gives you the same `getObjectByName` handles.

**(iii) Tween-only, whole-piece** — position curves for the hop, `scale` squash/stretch on takeoff and landing, a rotation flourish on capture.

**Which to use:** **(iii) day one, (ii) when you want more.** Be honest about what a chess game needs: slide, knight L-hop, capture lunge, spawn, death. That is **five transform animations on a whole `Object3D`**, and rigging buys you nothing for any of them. The squash-stretch on a hop is the single highest-value animation you will write, and it's `scale.set()` on two keyframes.

Upgrade path when the game is fun and you want polish: name the parts in the source `.vox`, and (ii) unlocks itself with no pipeline change — the same file, the same loader, just more handles to animate. That's why (ii) is the right *ceiling* even though (iii) is the right *start*.

**Does skinned/skeletal animation make sense for voxel meshes? No.** Skinning blends each vertex across up to 4 bones by weight. Blending *warps* geometry — your cubes shear, faces stop being axis-aligned, and the blocky silhouette that is the entire point of the art style is destroyed. Worse, after greedy meshing your geometry has very few vertices sitting at merged-rectangle corners, so per-vertex weights are close to meaningless. Rigid parenting *is* the voxel equivalent of a skeleton — it's a skeleton with 1.0 weights and no blending. Community guidance agrees: voxel animation "requires custom rigs" and stock/traditional rigs "are generally designed to work with traditional 3d models."

If you want a rig authored in a tool rather than in code, **VoxEdit** is the one voxel editor with built-in rigging and animation.

## Palette quantization to a "16-bit" look

**First, a terminology correction worth making explicit:** "16-bit colour" technically means RGB565 / RGB555 — 5–6 bits per channel, i.e. **32–64 levels per channel, 32,768–65,536 total colours**. That is *not* what you want and it will not look retro. What people mean by "16-bit era look" is **a hand-picked 32–64-colour ramp**. Design for the ramp, not the bit depth.

### Offline (do this — it's the right place)

The `.vox` format is palette-indexed by design, so quantization is native, not a hack.

```bash
# Snap to a fixed palette PNG at voxelization time
-set voxformat_createpalette false -set palette "$PWD/kdc-palette.png"

# Or let vengi pick N colours for you (new in v0.5.0)
-set voxformat_targetcolors 48
```

This bakes the look into the asset, costs zero at runtime, survives the `.glb` export as vertex colours, and means the palette is a **single file you can iterate on** — change `kdc-palette.png`, re-run the batch loop, every piece updates.

Build the palette PNG from a Lospec palette (they export `.hex`, `.gpl`, `.pal` JASC, `.ase`, `.txt`, and PNG at 1x/8x/32x; there is a `/palettes/api` endpoint). vengi also ships `vengi-palconvert` in the same release for palette format juggling.

### Runtime LUT (only if you need live swaps)

Worth it only if you want: team colours switched at runtime, a "check" colour flash, a day/night or damage state. Otherwise it's a shader you maintain for nothing.

Implementation sketch:
- Upload the palette as an N×1 `DataTexture`, `minFilter`/`magFilter` = `NearestFilter`, `generateMipmaps = false`, `colorSpace = SRGBColorSpace`.
- In the fragment shader, either (a) nearest-colour search: loop the N entries, keep the minimum squared distance — a 48-iteration loop per pixel is nothing on any GPU at 1080p; or (b) store the palette *index* as a vertex attribute at build time and just index the LUT, which is exact and free but needs a custom material.

**One thing that will bite you:** do the quantization **after** the pixelation downsample, in the same post-processing pass. Quantize → blur/resample → and you've un-quantized. Your existing `RenderPixelatedPass` (`three/addons/postprocessing/RenderPixelatedPass.js`, already in three.js, `new RenderPixelatedPass(6, scene, camera)`) is the natural place to fold the LUT in — fork it, or add a quantize `ShaderPass` immediately after it.

### Standard tools

| Tool | Version | Install | License | Use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ImageMagick** | **7.1.2-31** (2026-09-03) | `brew install imagemagick` | ImageMagick licence | `magick in.png -dither None -remap kdc-palette.png out.png` — force an exact palette |
| **pngquant** | **3.0.3** | `brew install pngquant` | GPL-3.0-or-later AND HPND AND BSD-2-Clause | `pngquant 48 --nofs in.png` — derive an N-colour palette |
| **Lospec** | — | web | palettes are community-submitted | Pick the ramp, export `.hex`/`.gpl`/PNG |
| **vengi-palconvert** | v0.5.0 | same release zip | MIT | Palette format conversion |

Note these operate on *images*. Your pieces carry vertex colours, not textures — so ImageMagick/pngquant matter for **building `kdc-palette.png` itself**, and for any board/UI textures. `voxformat_targetcolors` is what quantizes the actual models.

Five fairy pieces:
1. ARCHER: moves 1 square orthogonally only (no diagonal step). Captures "from a distance" WITHOUT moving (rifle-style): may remove an enemy on any diagonally-adjacent square, or exactly 2 squares away orthogonally, even if pieces are in between (jumps). Gives check normally.
2. PALADIN: moves like a queen (any distance, 8 directions) but may JUMP over FRIENDLY pieces on its path (not enemy pieces). Captures by moving to the square. CANNOT capture a king (so never gives check). After capturing, the paladin itself is also removed from the board (kamikaze).
3. GUARD: moves 1 square in any direction to an EMPTY square only. Cannot capture anything. Cannot be captured by anything EXCEPT a king.
4. MAESTER: moves 1 square in any direction; if the target holds an enemy it captures; if it holds a FRIENDLY piece it SWAPS places with it. Additionally, if the maester and own king are both on their first rank, they may swap places as a move regardless of distance.
5. BEAST: moves 1 square straight forward only (to an empty square). Captures on any of the other 7 adjacent squares. After a capture, if it can capture another non-king piece from its new square, it MAY continue capturing in the same turn (chain).
Future rules to keep in mind (not needed now): per-king "army powers" (e.g. freeze an enemy piece for a turn, make a piece uncapturable for a turn, move a piece as a queen once, move one piece twice, teleport a piece within own half, swap a pawn with a captured piece, pawns move 2 always, pieces jump own pawns, king moves 2 & can't capture, king captures adjacent without moving, pawns move diagonally/capture forward) and later "card/spell effects".

**Recommendation: write the rules engine and AI yourself in TypeScript. Do not adopt or fork Fairy-Stockfish.**

All config-driven variant engines are move-generation DSLs, not rules DSLs. Your five signature mechanics are all "what happens on capture" rules. Fairy-Stockfish expresses **0 of 5** completely — rifle capture and chain capture are ruled out by the maintainer and by a `static_assert` showing the 32-bit move encoding is 30/32 full; uncapturable-except-by-king needs an unimplemented capture matrix (#1005); friendly-transparent sliders and swaps don't exist; kamikaze half-works via `petrifyOnCaptureTypes` but leaves a wall square.

Three numbers decide it: a Fairy-Stockfish NNUE for your 11 piece types would be **~94 MB** (their own formula; their FAQ caps loading at 80 MB); an equivalent "768-style" net is **~0.72 MB**; Lozza (MIT, pure JS) ships a complete NNUE engine in **291 KB gzipped** in a Web Worker. Plus the GPL-3.0 / SharedArrayBuffer cost of shipping their WASM.

Tiers: (1) TS mailbox engine + negamax alpha-beta, ~1–2 weeks; (2) optimise TS, port hot loop to Rust→WASM only if measured; (3) small NNUE trained in PyTorch on your own self-play, plain `Int16Array` inference — WebGPU loses at batch 1; (4) AlphaZero only via minizero, and only after a C++ port.

Key find: H.G. Muller's chessvariants Interactive Diagram already expresses ~4.5/5 of your pieces declaratively (`captureMatrix` `0` = kamikaze, `!` = relative ironhood, `mRcaibR` = rifle) **and** has `spell=freeze/protect/hide` matching your planned army powers. No licence header, so copy the taxonomy, not the code.

## 1. Elo, score, error bars

- **Elo from score — exact code Fishtest runs:** `def elo(x): return -400 * math.log10(1 / x - 1)` (with `x` clamped to `[1e-3, 1-1e-3]`), and inverse `L(x) = 1 / (1 + 10**(-x/400.0))`. Source: https://github.com/official-stockfish/fishtest/blob/master/server/fishtest/stats/stat_util.py
- Equivalent form on CPW: `Δ = 400·log₁₀(E/(1−E))`, `E = 1/(1+10^(−Δ/400))`. https://www.chessprogramming.org/Match_Statistics
- **Error bar, exactly as Fishtest computes it** (same file, `get_elo`): `mu_min = mu + Φ⁻¹(0.025)·stdev/√games`, `mu_max = mu + Φ⁻¹(0.975)·stdev/√games`, `elo95 = (elo(mu_max) − elo(mu_min))/2`, `LOS = Φ((mu − 0.5)/(stdev/√games))`. Note `stdev` here is the **per-game** σ derived from the pentanomial frequency array.
- `stats()` in that file: for a results array of length `2n+1`, `games = N·(count−1)/2`, `mu = Σ resultsᵢ·(i/2)/games`, `var = Σ resultsᵢ·(i/2 − (count−1)/2·mu)² / games` — i.e. pentanomial counts, variance expressed **per game**.
- **Normalized t-value / normalized Elo (Van den Bergh, the definition Fishtest now uses):** `tn := (µ − 1/2)/σ_pg`. In the trinomial case σ_pg is the per-game score SD; **in the pentanomial case σ_pg is the SD of the game-pair outcome distribution (scored 0, ¼, ½, ¾, 1) multiplied by √2**. Normalized Elo `eₙ := C_e/t · tₙ` with `C_e/t := 800/log(10) ≅ 347.43`. https://www.cantate.be/Fishtest/normalized_elo_practical.pdf
- Balanced book / trinomial: `σ_pg = ½·√(1−d)` (d = draw ratio) ⇒ **`eₙ ≅ e_l/√(1−d)`**. Conversion table from the same PDF: normalized Elo 5.00 corresponds to logistic Elo 5.00 / 4.18 / 3.54 / 3.16 / 2.74 / 2.24 / 1.58 at d = 0.00 / 0.30 / 0.50 / 0.60 / 0.70 / 0.80 / 0.90.
- Older 2018 definition (worth knowing, it is the one most forum posts mean): `t₀ = (ŝ−½)/σ̂₀`, with `σ(t₀) = 1/√N`, so 95% CI is `t₀ ± 1.96/√N`, and `t₀ ≅ 1.96·elo/(error·√N)`; also `t₀ ≅ 0.002878·elo/√(1−d̂)`. https://www.cantate.be/Fishtest/normalized_elo.pdf
- **Games needed (derived by me from `get_elo` above; constants verified numerically):** near µ=½, `d(elo)/dµ = 400/(ln10·¼) = 694.87`, so `elo95 ≈ 1361.9·σ_pg/√N`. For a balanced book, `elo95 ≈ 681·√(1−d)/√N`, i.e.

  **N ≈ 463,700·(1−d)/elo95²**

  | d | ±1 Elo | ±2 Elo | ±5 Elo | ±10 Elo |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  |0.0|463,725|115,931|18,549|4,637|
  |0.4|278,235|69,558|11,129|2,782|
  |0.6|185,490|46,372|7,419|1,854|
  |0.8|92,745|23,186|3,709|927|

  Sanity check against real data: Stockfish regression runs of 40,000 games report e.g. "Elo LTC 100.40 +-2.1" — formula gives ±2.4 at d=0.5. https://official-stockfish.github.io/docs/stockfish-wiki/Useful-data.html
- Note the direction of the draw effect: **higher draw rate lowers σ_pg, so it *shrinks* the Elo error bar for fixed N** — but it also shrinks the true Elo difference, which is exactly why normalized Elo exists.
- **Wilson score interval** (Wikipedia, verbatim): `p ∈ [1/(1+z²/n)]·( p̂ + z²/(2n) ± (z/(2n))·√[4np̂(1−p̂)+z²] )`. Wald for contrast: `p ≈ p̂ ± (z/√n)·√[p̂(1−p̂)]`. Wilson wins because it is asymmetric and "doesn't suffer from problems of overshoot and zero-width intervals that afflict the normal interval" — Wald collapses to zero width as p̂→0 or 1 and overshoots [0,1] when `p̂ < 1/(1+n/z²)`. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_proportion_confidence_interval
- Caveat for your use: a chess score is a **trinomial/pentanomial mean, not a binomial proportion**, so Wilson is the right tool for "fraction of games where piece X was never moved", not for the score itself. Use the pentanomial σ for the score.

## 2. Pentanomial vs trinomial

- Pentanomial = model the **game pair** (same opening, colours reversed) as one trial with 5 outcomes `{0, ½, 1, 3/2, 2}` (or normalised `{0, ¼, ½, ¾, 1}`), i.e. LL, LD, LW/DD, DW, WW. Fishtest: five outcomes "(e.g. ll, ld, dd/wl, wd, ww)", "leads to a substantial saving of testing resources". https://github.com/official-stockfish/fishtest/wiki/Fishtest-mathematics
- **Exact variance formulas — "The accounting identity", Van den Bergh** (https://www.cantate.be/Fishtest/accounting_identity.pdf). With Xᵢ,Yᵢ the two games of pair i, `S` the match score, `Zᵢ = (Xᵢ+Yᵢ)/2`:
  - trinomial per-game variance `V₃ := Σᵢ[(Xᵢ−S)² + (Yᵢ−S)²]/(2n)`
  - pentanomial per-game variance `V₅ := 2·Σᵢ(Zᵢ−S)²/n`
  - **Theorem (accounting identity): `V₃ − V₅ = (1/n)Σᵢbᵢ² + O(n^{−1/2})` = `E(b²) + O(n^{−1/2})`**, where `bᵢ` is the Elo-additive bias of opening i (`µᵢ = s+bᵢ`, `µᵢ° = s−bᵢ`). `√E(b²)` is the **RMS bias** of the book.
  - Consequence: with a *perfectly balanced* book the pentanomial saves nothing; the saving is exactly the book's bias variance. This is the whole reason UHO + pentanomial are used together.
- GSPRT paper states the two parametrisations explicitly: trinomial `(p₁,p₂,p₃)=(w,d,l)`, `a=(1, ½, 0)`; **5-nomial `(p₂, p_{3/2}, p₁, p_{½}, p₀)` with `a=(1, ¾, ½, ¼, 0)`, and N is the number of games divided by two**. Estimator: `φ̂ = Σaᵢp̂ᵢ`, `V(φ̂) = (1/N)(−φ̂² + Σaᵢ²p̂ᵢ)`. https://www.cantate.be/Fishtest/GSPRT_approximation.pdf
- Normalized-Elo pentanomial form: `t₀ = √2·(ŝ−½)/√(Σᵢ p̂ᵢ i² − 4ŝ²)` over `O={0,½,1,3/2,2}`. https://www.cantate.be/Fishtest/normalized_elo.pdf §4
- **Measured size of the saving (forum claim, Kai Laskos on TalkChess):** Komodo, 3moves_Elo2200.epd — normalized Elo trinomial vs pentanomial 0.784→0.803 (6s/3s), 0.571→0.609 (20s/10s), 0.564→0.603 (60s/30s), i.e. ≈2–7% better signal-to-noise on a *mildly* biased book; the gain is much larger on UHO books. https://www.talkchess.com/forum3/viewtopic.php?t=64358&start=50
- Trinomial's failure mode stated plainly: "The trinomial model overestimates elo confidence intervals" for paired reversed-colour games. https://github.com/AndyGrant/OpenBench

## 3. SPRT

- Fishtest runs a **GSPRT**: `LLR := L(θ̂₁,x) − L(θ̂₀,x)` with θ̂ᵢ the MLE constrained to `φ(θ̂ᵢ)=φᵢ`. "the test stops when LLR leaves the interval **[log(β/(1−α)), log((1−β)/α)]**". https://www.cantate.be/Fishtest/GSPRT_approximation.pdf
- **α = β = 0.05 ⇒ b = −a = log(19) = 2.94444…**, i.e. the familiar ±2.94. https://www.cantate.be/Fishtest/sprta.pdf
- Practical LLR formula Fishtest actually uses (normalized, works trinomial and pentanomial alike):
  **`LLR ≅ (N/2)·log( (1 + (t̂ₙ − tₙ,₀)²) / (1 + (t̂ₙ − tₙ,₁)²) )`**, with the linearised variant `LLR ≅ (N/2)(tₙ,₁−tₙ,₀)(2t̂ₙ − tₙ,₀ − tₙ,₁)` and the regularisation rule "LLR/N should be clamped to `[−(tₙ,₁−tₙ,₀)/2, (tₙ,₁−tₙ,₀)/2]`". https://www.cantate.be/Fishtest/normalized_elo_practical.pdf §4.2
- **Expected duration (worst case, actual Elo halfway between bounds):** `T = D/(eₙ,₁ − eₙ,₀)²` with `D := C_e/t²·log(19)² ≅ 1,046,535` ("close to 1,000,000, sufficiently accurate for back of the envelope"). Table from the paper: Δeₙ = 1/2/3/4/5/6 → 1,046,535 / 261,634 / 116,282 / 65,408 / 41,861 / 29,070 games. When the true Elo sits *on* a bound, replace numerator with `D′ = 9C_e/t²log(19)/5 ≅ 639,770`. Same PDF, (3.4).
  - So **SPRT[0.0, 5.0] ⇒ ≈41,861 games worst case; SPRT[−1.75, 0.25] (width 2.0) ⇒ ≈261,634 games worst case.** Both numbers are in *games*, not pairs.
  - General Brownian result behind it: `T = T(h_µ)/w²`, `w = (µ₁−µ₀)/σ`, `h_µ = (2µ−(µ₀+µ₁))/(µ₁−µ₀)`, `T(h) = (2b/h)·(1−e^{−hb})/(1+e^{−hb})`, `T(0) = −ab = b²`. https://www.cantate.be/Fishtest/sprta.pdf
- **Meaning of the Fishtest bounds:** `SPRT(0.0, 5.0)` = H0 "no gain" vs H1 "+5 **normalized** Elo", used for functional gainers; `SPRT(-1.75, 0.25)` = the non-regression/simplification bound, tolerating up to −1.75 normalized Elo. https://official-stockfish.github.io/docs/fishtest-wiki/Creating-my-first-test.html — the same doc gives STC 10+0.1, LTC 60+0.6, Hash 16 MB (STC) / 64 MB (LTC).
  - In *logistic* Elo those bounds are draw-rate dependent: 5.0 normalized ≈ 3.54 logistic at d=0.5, ≈2.24 at d=0.8 (table in §1 above). Older Fishtest bounds quoted as logistic were STC [0, 2.0] and LTC [0, 1.0].
- Normalization's payoff, stated by the wiki: "This normalization makes the expected duration of a test dependent only on the chosen bounds, independent of the specific draw ratio or opening book used." https://github.com/official-stockfish/fishtest/wiki/Fishtest-mathematics
- Tool-side: cutechess `-sprt elo0=E0 elo1=E1 alpha=<alpha> beta=<beta>`; fastchess adds `model=normalized|logistic|bayesian` (**default `normalized`**). https://github.com/cutechess/cutechess/blob/master/docs/cutechess-cli.6.txt , https://github.com/Disservin/fastchess/blob/master/man.md
- OpenBench: "`Bounds` and `Confidence` … format `[lower, upper]`", confidence = "type I and type II errors, refered to as alpha and beta", 0.05 recommended. https://github.com/AndyGrant/OpenBench/wiki/SPRT-and-Fixed%E2%80%90Game-Workloads
- Other bounds seen in the wild (CPW): gainers [0.5, 2.5], [0, 2], [0, 3], [0, 5], [0, 10]; non-regression [−1.75, 0.25], [−3, 1], [−5, 0], [−10, 0]. https://chessprogramming.org/Sequential_Probability_Ratio_Test

## 4. Opening books and randomisation

- **Why books at all:** deterministic engines replay the same game from the start position; the book supplies variety and lets the *same* opening be played twice with colours swapped, which is the precondition for pentanomial pairing.
- **Game pairs:** cutechess `-repeat` — "Play each opening twice (or n times). Unless the `-noswap` option is used, the players swap sides after each game." fastchess `-rounds N` — "Play N rounds of games where each game within the round uses the same opening." `-openings … order=[random|sequential] plies=N start=I policy=[default|encounter|round]`, `-srand SEED` for book randomisation. https://github.com/cutechess/cutechess/blob/master/docs/cutechess-cli.6.txt , https://github.com/Disservin/fastchess/blob/master/man.md
- **Fishtest's actual invocation** (verbatim, key flags): `-repeat -games 2 -rounds 10 -report penta=true -resign movecount=3 score=600 -draw movenumber=34 movecount=8 score=20 -openings file=UHO_Lichess_4852_v1.epd format=epd order=random plies=16 start=15619 -srand <seed>`. https://official-stockfish.github.io/docs/fishtest-wiki/Running-Fastchess.html
- **Books catalogue** (names, sizes, generation depth, cp-filter ranges): balanced `2moves_v1.epd` (40,457 pos), `8moves_v3.pgn`, `popularpos_lichess` (200k from real games); unbalanced UHO family filtered by engine eval, e.g. `4mvs_+90_+99.epd`, `8mvs_+90_+99.epd`, `UHO_4060_v1…v4`, `UHO_XXL`, `UHO_Lichess_4852_v1.epd` (2.6M positions, balanced W/B). https://github.com/official-stockfish/books/blob/master/README.md
- **Balanced vs UHO — what each measures.** UHO raises decisiveness (lower draw rate), raises normalized Elo per game, and therefore shortens tests; the cost is that it only measures skill *in the positions the book selects*. Forum/issue claims: PavelChess argued on the Stockfish repo that ~25% of UHO's first 500 positions are so skewed that a 2:1 search handicap still yields 416W–122L–462D, so "Gaining patches test needs much more games" and "Simplification patch can pass because a test shows less ELO loss than real"; vdbergh's reply was to build a better book and test it by the documented procedure, and Robertson Nurnberg: "For now we do not see an urgent need to change the book." https://github.com/official-stockfish/Stockfish/discussions/5079
- Counter-claim (forum, TalkChess): patches that only matter in balanced play score 0 under UHO and get rejected, so UHO systematically misses a class of improvements; UHO is a "stress-test opening method … should not be confused with a neutral measure of overall engine strength". https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?t=83573 , https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?t=85026
- Normalized Elo is the objective referee for this argument — it is *defined* as "a measure for the amount of games it takes to prove that one engine is stronger than another". Measured book sensitivities (Laskos, forum): 5ply_v1_40_50.epd 0.775±0.031, 3moves_Elo2200.epd 0.740, 2moves_v1.epd 0.739, a Stockfish-tuned book 0.873. https://www.talkchess.com/forum3/viewtopic.php?t=64358&start=50
- **Variants with no book:** neither cutechess nor fastchess generates random openings; the standard substitute is `-openings ... order=random plies=N` over a generated EPD, or generating your own N-random-legal-ply EPD set first. For your case: generate the position set once, keep it fixed across all comparisons (it is part of the "context" in Van den Bergh's §5 sense — change the book and every normalized Elo becomes incomparable), and always play each position as a colour-reversed pair.

## 5. Engine strength / time control vs measured balance

- **Draw rate rises with strength — hard numbers.** CCRL 40/15, 2,122,944 engine games: ≈22% draws at Elo 2000, ≈45% at 3000, ≈73% at 3500, ≈88.5% at 3650; fitted `logit p(Elo) = β₀+β₁E+β₂E²+β₃E³` with `E=(Elo−3000)/400`; extrapolated 99% draws at ≈Elo 3990. https://beuke.org/chess-engine-draws/
- **Draw rate rises with thinking time, and White's advantage falls.** AlphaZero self-play, 10,000 games at 1 s/move vs 1,000 games at 1 min/move: Classical 772W/8820D/409L at 1 s → 18W/979D at 1 min. Table 2, expected score for White: Classical 54.1% (end of training) → 51.8% (1 s) → **50.8% (1 min)**; Torpedo 57.0 → 56.8 → 54.0; Pawn-back 53.0 → 51.1 → 50.1. "across all variations the percentage of drawn games increases with longer thinking times". https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.04374
- **Direct implication for a variant-balance study: any White-advantage or draw-rate number you publish is a function of the engine strength and TC you measured it at, and it drifts toward (50%, all-draws) as either rises.** AZ's own framing: the increase in draws with time "seems to suggest that the starting position might be theoretically drawn in these chess variants".
- **Piece values are variant- and strength-dependent too** — AZ recovers per-variant piece values from the linear weights of the value head (Table 6), and finds them "quite different" in variants with increased pawn mobility. Same paper §3.8.
- **Elo compression at longer TC is *not* a law.** Stockfish's own 40,000-game measurements: SF7→SF8 "Elo STC 95.91 +-2.3, Elo LTC 100.40 +-2.1"; SF8→SF9 58.28→68.55; SF9→SF10 71.03→65.55, with the explicit remark "the common wisdom that increased TC causes elo compression is not always true". Speedup→Elo: `Elo_stc(x) = 2.10x`, `Elo_ltc(x) = 1.43x` (x = % speedup). https://official-stockfish.github.io/docs/stockfish-wiki/Useful-data.html
- **Same engine on both sides.** This is the *standard* method and it is deliberate — it holds everything but the tested change constant. Its known cost is shared blind spots: both sides mis-evaluate the same positions at the same depth, so a strategy that beats this engine's evaluation is invisible. AZ's mitigations, worth copying: (a) fix and report the "conditions of play" (move-selection rule, MCTS time) as part of the measurement; (b) **force diversity by sampling the first 20 plies proportional to MCTS visit counts** rather than playing deterministically; (c) compare across *two* time controls and report both, treating a metric that flips sign between them as unresolved. https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.04374
- Van den Bergh formalises the same caution as the **weak dependency hypothesis**: the ratio `NE_D/C(X,Y) = NE_D(X,Y)/NE_C(X,Y)` is assumed only "weakly dependent" on the engines X,Y — and he explicitly warns it "will be trivially false" in general, e.g. there can be "well scaling patches" and "badly scaling patches". Read: do not assume a balance result at one TC transfers to another. https://www.cantate.be/Fishtest/normalized_elo.pdf §5

## 6. Pitfalls

- **Adjudication — exact semantics and the conventional values.**
  - `-resign movecount=count score=score [twosided=true|false]`: "Adjudicate the game as a loss if an engine's score is at least `score` centipawns below zero for at least `count` consecutive moves." `twosided=true` additionally requires the winner's score ≥ `score` above zero for `count` consecutive moves (default false).
  - `-draw movenumber=number movecount=count score=score`: "Adjudicate the game as draw if the score of both engines is within `score` centipawns from zero for at least `count` consecutive moves, and at least `number` full moves have been played. **Captures and pawn moves will reset the counters.**"
  - https://github.com/cutechess/cutechess/blob/master/docs/cutechess-cli.6.txt
  - **Conventional Fishtest values: `-resign movecount=3 score=600`, `-draw movenumber=34 movecount=8 score=20`.** https://official-stockfish.github.io/docs/fishtest-wiki/Running-Fastchess.html
  - Direction of bias: aggressive draw adjudication (small `score`, small `movecount`, early `movenumber`) *raises* the measured draw rate and suppresses the long-grind wins that separate strong engines; aggressive resign adjudication truncates defensive resources and can convert real draws into losses. For a *new* variant, engine eval is uncalibrated, so a 20 cp / 600 cp threshold may mean something very different than in chess — validate by running a subset with adjudication off and comparing WDL.
- **Shallow-search repetition inflation:** with a shallow search neither side sees a way to make progress, so repetition draws are over-produced; this is a real risk for weak variant engines and is *exactly* the case where `-draw score=20` adjudication makes it worse, not better (a shallow engine's ±20 cp is noise). Prefer a higher `movenumber` and larger `movecount` when the engine is weak.
- **Tablebase adjudication:** cutechess `-tb <semicolon-separated paths>` (WDL files only), `-tbignore50` disables the fifty-move rule for adjudication. fastchess `-tbadjudicate` with `BOTH` (default) / `WIN_LOSS` / `DRAW`. **Not available for a new variant** — no tablebases exist — so expect longer games and a higher fraction of endgames decided by the engine's own (possibly wrong) evaluation. https://github.com/cutechess/cutechess/blob/master/docs/cutechess-cli.6.txt , https://github.com/Disservin/fastchess/blob/master/man.md
- **Ply cap / max game length:** cutechess `-maxmoves n` — "Adjudicate the game as **a draw** if at least n full moves have been played without result. Ignored if n equals zero (default)." fastchess `-maxmoves N` — "Enables draw adjudication if the game reaches N moves without a result." So **a capped game is silently scored ½–½ by both tools**. If you want to detect "the variant cannot force a result", you must count timeouts separately — the tool will not distinguish them from genuine draws.
- **Degeneracy detection — Browne's thesis** (Cameron Browne, *Automatic Generation and Evaluation of Recombination Games*, QUT 2008). His measured criteria, verbatim formulas:
  - `A_comp = (wins_W + wins_B)/G` — completion, ratio of games reaching a win/loss inside the move limit.
  - `A_bal = 1 − |wins_W − wins_B|/(wins_W + wins_B)` — balance; 1 = perfect.
  - `A_adv = |wins_1 − (wins_W+wins_B)/2| / ((wins_W+wins_B)/2)` — first-mover advantage; 0 = none, 1 = first (or second) mover always wins.
  - `A_draw = wins_0/G` — drawishness.
  - `A_tout = 1 − (wins_0 + wins_1 + wins_2)/G` — **timeouts, the separate count for games that hit the move limit; "An excessive number of timeouts indicate that a game may have serious flaws, such as goals that can never be reached."**
  - Duration: "useful for detecting pathological flaws in games in both direction; trivial games that end within a few moves, and excessively long games that are difficult to conclude."
  - His automated kill switch: **"If more than half of the match games fail to produce a winner before the move limit is reached then the game is deemed to be drawish. This indicates a serious flaw in either the rule set or the game's chosen policy and the child is discarded."** And the viability gate: `completion > 0.5 && balance > 0.5 && advantage < 0.5 && duration < 0.5`.
  - Available at https://eprints.qut.edu.au/17755/ (the full PDF is what these quotes are taken from).
- **Degeneracy in AZ's balance framework:** decisiveness and first-move advantage are inferred Bayesian-ly, not read off raw counts — Dirichlet posterior `p(π|G) = Dir(n_win+1, n_draw+1, n_lose+1)`, then Monte Carlo estimates of `p(π_draw^A < π_draw^B)` and `p(e^A > e^B)` where `e = π_win + ½π_draw`. Use this rather than point estimates when you compare many variants. They also flag a suspected **forced refutation by opening line** (a 100% score for one side in a specific line in Pawn-sideways) as preliminary until confirmed at longer TC — the right posture for "is there a forced win from move 1". https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.04374
- **Unmeasured-piece / dominant-opening detection:** no established literature. Practical instrumentation that falls out of the above: per-piece move counts and per-opening WDL, both with **Wilson intervals** (this *is* a binomial proportion, unlike the score), plus opening-tree entropy — AZ measures `H(t)` and average branching `M(t)` by sampling 10⁴ move sequences from `p(s)` and averaging negative log-probabilities, and reports that the most decisive variants (No-castling, Torpedo) had the *smallest* opening trees, "still of the same order of magnitude as that of Classical chess". A variant whose opening tree collapses by an order of magnitude is the signature of a dominant opening.

**Two things to carry into the simulation design:** (1) budget from `N ≈ 463,700(1−d)/elo95²` or `T = 10⁶/(Δeₙ)²` before running anything — a ±5 Elo balance claim at d=0.4 is 11,000 games, a ±1 Elo claim is 278,000; (2) always play colour-reversed pairs and record pentanomial counts, because `V₃ − V₅ = E(b²)` means a randomly-generated variant opening set (likely high bias) makes the trinomial error bar badly wrong in the *conservative* direction, and you will pay for it in games.
