Done. `docs/research/variant-balance.md`, 220 lines, 20 cited sources, only that file written.

**Summary**

1. **Protocol skeleton comes from the AlphaZero balance paper** (arXiv 2009.04374): expected White score `e = π_win + ½π_draw`, Dirichlet posteriors for comparing variants, 20-ply opening entropy, and piece values fitted as `tanh(wᵀd)` on piece-count differences — a method validated by recovering 3.05/3.33/5.63/9.50 for classical chess.
2. **The finding that reshaped the fun score:** `chess960.md` gives `corr(draw rate, White points) = −0.92` across 960 positions, and the AlphaZero paper saw the same. A decisive arrangement is usually just a White-favouring one, so decisive rate is now scored as a **residual** after regressing out `|White score − 0.5|`, never raw.
3. **Browne's PhD thesis is the only work validated against human preference**, and I pulled the equations from the primary PDF. His viability set alone correlates 0.59; all 57 criteria only 0.42; the famous 0.82 is fitted and evaluated on the same 79 games (0.65 held out).
4. **Two of his fitted signs are counter-intuitive and I followed them:** lead change is weighted **negative** (−0.277) and uncertainty-late dominates the ablation (48.8% error increase when removed). This contradicts the mid-range lead-change target the Risk study used; I sided with the human data.
5. **Metric definitions** are all reduced to one bounded lead signal `L_t = 2p_t − 1` from a fitted logistic squash of our centipawn eval, so Browne's two-player equations collapse to computable one-liners and mate scores cannot dominate.
6. **Statistics:** derived `N ≈ 463700·(1−d)/elo95²` from Fishtest's own error-bar code, plus normalized Elo, SPRT duration `T = 1046535/(Δeₙ)²`, Wilson intervals for genuine proportions, and the accounting identity `V3 − V5 = mean(bᵢ²)` — which matters a lot here because our "opening" is a random back rank, so unpaired error bars are badly wrong.
7. **Muller's method gives the sample sizes for piece values:** ~100 games per quarter-pawn, 800 games for ±0.09 pawn. His named failure mode is exactly ours — a seed value that inverts a plausible exchange makes self-play permanently blind, so the values must be iterated to a fixed point from our current Archer 430 / Paladin 470 / Guard 250 / Maester 330 / Beast 350.
8. **Protocol:** static depth-12–14 screen of every back rank (as Barthelemy did for all 960), cheap random-playout pre-filter, one frozen opening set, colour-reversed pairs, fixed nodes, sequential halving (512 arrangements / 200k games = 9 rounds, 43 games rising to 11k).
9. **Two implementation asks fall out of this:** `search()` needs MultiPV = 2 for the decision-cost metric, and capped games must be counted separately from draws — cutechess silently scores them ½–½.
10. **Honest caveats are in the doc, not buried:** the uncertainty-of-outcome hypothesis is unsupported by a 97-paper meta-analysis, BGG ratings are ~35% explained by complexity alone, Iida's refinement value cannot discriminate between our back ranks, and the weights must never be refit on our own simulation output.

# Engine evaluation vs. three.js r186 — pixelized-3D chess variant, web

**Verdict up front: none of the seven beats three.js r186 for this use case. three.js ships the exact effect and the exact asset loader you need, in the smallest bundle of any real-3D option. Stop looking.**

Nothing was written to the project. Bundle numbers below are my own measurements (esbuild `--bundle --minify --format=esm --target=es2022`, gzip -9 / brotli q11) built in the scratchpad and deleted afterward.

---

## The baseline you're trying to beat (measured, not remembered)

`three@0.186.0`, published 2026-09-08 ([npm registry](https://registry.npmjs.org/three)) — current as of today.

It already ships **both halves of your target look**, in both render paths:

| Path | File in `three/examples/jsm/` |
|---|---|
| WebGL / EffectComposer | `postprocessing/RenderPixelatedPass.js` (8.1 KB src) |
| WebGPU / TSL nodes | `tsl/display/PixelationPassNode.js` |
| Outlines | built into `RenderPixelatedPass` + `tsl/display/OutlineNode.js`, `SobelOperatorNode.js` |
| Palette / posterize | `tsl/display/Lut3DNode.js`, `postprocessing/LUTPass.js` |
| Dither-ish | `shaders/HalftoneShader.js`, `postprocessing/DotScreenPass.js`, `tsl/display/FilmNode.js` |
| **.vox** | `loaders/VOXLoader.js` (21.8 KB src) — MagicaVoxel parser, exports `buildMesh` / `buildData3DTexture` |

`RenderPixelatedPass` signature is literally your spec: `constructor(pixelSize, scene, camera, { normalEdgeStrength = 0.3, depthEdgeStrength = 0.4 })`, `setPixelSize()`, `NearestFilter` on both the beauty and normal render targets. The crisp outlines come free from normal+depth edge detection — you do not write that shader.

**Measured size:** 132 KB gzip / 110 KB brotli, *including* `EffectComposer` + `RenderPass` + `ShaderPass` + `Raycaster` + lights + `MeshLambertMaterial`. Bare renderer without post-processing is 130 KB gzip — the post-process stack costs ~2 KB.

---

## 1. Babylon.js — `@babylonjs/core@9.26.0`

- **Version:** 9.26.0 verified via npm. Babylon 9.0 shipped 2026-03-26 ([Windows Dev Blog](https://blogs.windows.com/windowsdeveloper/2026/03/26/announcing-babylon-js-9-0/), [forum announcement](https://forum.babylonjs.com/t/welcome-to-babylon-js-9-0/62940)). Headline features: Clustered Lighting, Volumetric Lighting, Frame Graph v1.
- **Bundle (measured, deep ES imports, best case):** minimal scene (Engine + Scene + FreeCamera + HemisphericLight + box) = **244 KB gzip / 197 KB brotli**. Realistic scene (ArcRotateCamera + StandardMaterial + DirectionalLight + `scene.pick` + one custom `PostProcess`) = **342 KB gzip / 263 KB brotli**. That is **2.6× three.js** for strictly less capability here.
- **Post-process pipeline:** strong and well-factored — 30+ core post-processes, plus a "thin" variant of each, plus the Frame Graph task system (`customPostProcessTask`, `colorCorrectionTask`, `fxaaTask`, …).
- **Built-in pixelation: NO.** I enumerated every class in `@babylonjs/core/PostProcesses/` and the whole `@babylonjs/post-processes` package (which contains only `asciiArt`, `digitalRain`, `edgeDetection`). There is a `PosterizeBlock` for **NodeMaterial** and a `geometryPosterizeBlock` — those are material-level, not screen-space post. There's a `bayerDitherFunctions` shader include, used internally for dithered transparency, not exposed as a dither post. `edgeDetectionPostProcess` is genuinely useful for your outlines; `colorCorrectionPostProcess` (3D LUT) gets you palette posterize. **Pixelation you write yourself.**
- **Voxel/.vox: NO.** `@babylonjs/loaders` has glTF/OBJ/STL/SPLAT. No `.vox`. `babylonjs-vox-loader` does not exist on npm. You'd bolt on `parse-magica-voxel` or `@voxel-tool/core` and build the mesh yourself.
- **WebGPU:** `@babylonjs/core/Engines/WebGPU/` exists; `WebGPUEngine` is opt-in, not the default `Engine`. Babylon's WebGPU path is mature (WGSL shader variants ship for every effect — that's most of the 652 `sideEffects` entries).
- **Mobile/iOS:** fine, same WebGL2/WebGPU story as three.
- **Main drawback:** 2.6× the bytes, and you still have to write the pixelation shader *and* the .vox loader. Tree-shaking is real but the floor is high — Babylon's `Scene` drags in a lot.

## 2. PlayCanvas — `playcanvas@2.22.2`

- **Bundle (measured):** barrel import of `Application` = **490 KB gzip / 382 KB brotli** — worst of the JS engines. Using the documented `AppBase` + explicit `AppOptions.componentSystems` tree-shaking path ([standalone docs](https://developer.playcanvas.com/user-manual/engine/standalone/)) gets it to **225 KB gzip / 173 KB brotli**. Still ~1.7× three.js, and that's before you add anything.
- **Post-processing:** the `CameraFrame` / `RenderPass` system is good: HDR bloom, SSAO, DoF, TAA, LUT color grading, vignette, fringing ([Post Effects docs](https://developer.playcanvas.com/user-manual/graphics/posteffects/)). Custom fullscreen passes via `RenderPassShaderQuad` / `camera.framePasses` ([Custom Render Passes](https://developer.playcanvas.com/user-manual/graphics/posteffects/cameraframe/custom-passes/)).
- **Built-in pixelation/posterize/dither: NO.** None in the effect list, none in the type definitions.
- **Voxel/.vox: NO.** Zero `vox` hits in `playcanvas.d.ts`.
- **WebGPU:** best-in-class here — single bundle ships `DEVICETYPE_WEBGPU` and `DEVICETYPE_WEBGL2` with a `deviceTypes: []` preference array, so one build falls back automatically. (three.js needs the separate `three/webgpu` entry point.)
- **Main drawback:** heaviest JS engine, effect library aimed at *cinematic* looks (bloom/DoF/TAA) — exactly the opposite of chunky-pixel — and the engine-only docs path is a second-class citizen next to the cloud editor.

## 3. Godot 4.x web export — **4.7.2-stable**

- **Version:** 4.7.2-stable, 2026-08-18; 4.8-dev5 in flight ([GitHub releases](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/releases)). The widely-quoted "4.6" is stale.
- **Size — I measured the actual shipping template.** I pulled `templates/web_nothreads_release.zip` out of `Godot_v4.7.2-stable_export_templates.tpz`:
  - `godot.wasm` = **37.68 MB raw**, **9.59 MB gzip -9**, **6.77 MB brotli q11**
  - `godot.js` 0.27 MB, plus audio worklets and html shell
  - **This is the engine alone, before your `.pck`.** Compare: the official 4.3 report said "around 40 MB uncompressed, and 5 MB compressed with Brotli" ([Godot blog](https://godotengine.org/article/progress-report-web-export-in-4-3/)) — so it has grown ~35% on brotli since 4.3.
  - **That is 60× three.js's brotli size for a chess game.**
- **Load time:** ~7 MB brotli of WebAssembly to download *and* compile before first frame. On a mid-range phone that is seconds, not milliseconds.
- **SharedArrayBuffer / COOP-COEP:** solved, correctly. Single-threaded export is **the default** since 4.3 — the docs say "it is the preferred and now default way to export your games on the Web" ([exporting_for_web](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/export/exporting_for_web.html)). No COOP/COEP headers needed. Threaded export still requires `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` + `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp`, and the PWA service-worker workaround exists. The threaded path's `coep:credentialless` fallback is "not supported by Safari or Firefox for Android."
- **iOS Safari in 2026 — improved but NOT clean.** The "single-threaded fixes Apple" claim is real and official. But the tracker disagrees that it's done. Open, current bugs (verified via GitHub API today):
  - [#116750](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/116750) "WebKit (Safari on iOS) page crash when playing audio during gameplay" — **open**, updated 2026-02-25, labels `platform:web` `platform:ios` `crash`
  - [#70621](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/70621) "WebAssembly maximum memory 2GB causes Out of Memory error on iOS Safari" — **open**, confirmed, updated 2026-06-01
  - [#120302](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/120302) invisible particles on WebKit — open, 2026-06-15
  - [#95941](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/95941) `InputEventScreenDrag/Touch` index bugs on iOS/iPadOS web — open, 2026-07-14 (touch input — relevant to you)
  - An earlier iOS audio crash, [#107390](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/107390), *was* fixed for 4.5. 47 open issues match `platform:web` + iOS.
  - Note: "use Chrome on iOS instead" is not a workaround — all iOS browsers are WebKit.
  - The docs still say: "Safari has several issues with WebGL 2.0 support that other browsers don't have."
- **Main drawback:** ~7 MB engine download for a board game, and iOS is a live bug surface, not a solved one.

## 4. Unity WebGL / Unity Web

- **Size:** best figures I could verify are Aras Pranckevičius' empty-project measurements ([gist](https://gist.github.com/aras-p/740c2d4f9977ce92b7de72b1394dd365)): **empty 3D/URP = 10.7 MB brotli** (3.7 data + 6.9 code); empty 2D = 7.7 MB; aggressively stripped 2D (Input System and uGUI removed, "disk size with LTO") = **2.0 MB**. ⚠️ **Flag: that gist is for Unity 6.0.23 (Oct 2024).** I could not find a credible 2026 re-measurement. Treat 10 MB as the realistic order of magnitude for a small 3D build.
- **Mobile web:** officially supported now. The 6000.7 manual states "iOS Safari 15 and newer" and "Chrome 58 and newer" for Android, requiring WebGL 2 + 64-bit + WebAssembly ([browser compatibility](https://docs.unity3d.com/6000.7/Documentation/Manual/webgl-browsercompatibility.html)).
- **WebGPU:** ⚠️ **could not verify.** The 6000.7 manual mentions WebGL 2 only, no WebGPU. SEO blogs claiming "Unity 6.6 moved WebGPU out of experimental" and "Unity 7 LTS ships WebGPU as default web target" are unsourced and those same pages also state demonstrably false things (e.g. "Safari 18.2" and "Firefox 130+" for WebGPU — both wrong per caniuse). Do not rely on them.
- **Main drawback:** proprietary, heavyweight, ~10 MB, and a full editor + C# toolchain for what is a few hundred lines of TypeScript. Disqualified on "minimal stack preferred" alone.

## 5. Phaser 4 — `phaser@4.2.1`

- **Version:** 4.2.1 (2026-07-09); 4.0.0 shipped 2026-04-10.
- **3D-capable: NO. Not at all.** npm keywords are literally `['2d', 'HTML5', 'WebGL', 'canvas', ...]`; the GitHub description is "a fun, free and fast **2D** game framework." Phaser 4's headline is a rewritten **WebGL** (not WebGPU) 2D renderer ([Phaser 4 Renderer](https://phaser.io/news/2026/04/phaser-4-renderer-faster-cleaner-and-built-for-modern-games)). Coverage explicitly says that for fully 3D games, other choices are recommended ([GameFromScratch review](https://gamefromscratch.com/phaser-4-released/)).
- **3D plugin state in 2026 — no maintained option exists:**
  - **enable3d** (`@enable3d/phaser-extension@0.26.1`) — last published **2025-03-08**, ~18 months stale. Peer-pinned to `three@0.171.0` (three is now 0.186.0) and `matter-js@0.17.1`. **Phaser 3 only.**
  - **Phaser3D** (the `Extern` GameObject + three.js injection approach) — announced for Phaser 3 ([Enable3D announcement, 2020](https://phaser.io/news/2020/04/enable3d)); I found no Phaser 4 port and no npm package.
  - `@number10/jsx-three` from the PhaserJSX ecosystem ([PhaserJSX, 2026-07](https://phaser.io/news/2026/07/phaserjsx-jsx-ui-framework-phaser-4)) is a UI-panels-onto-meshes bridge, **not** a 3D renderer for Phaser.
  - Net: every "Phaser 3D" path is "run three.js next to Phaser." At which point you are using three.js, with Phaser as dead weight.
- **Main drawback:** wrong tool. Eliminated.

## 6. Bevy + wgpu WASM — `bevy 0.19.1`

- **Versions:** `bevy` **0.19.1** (2026-08-13; 0.19.0 on 2026-06-19, [release post](https://bevy.org/news/bevy-0-19/)), `wgpu` **30.0.1** (2026-08-22) — both via crates.io API.
- **WASM size — I measured Bevy's own hosted example.** The official `3d-shapes` example (a genuinely small 3D scene) at `bevy-webgl2-examples.pages.dev`:
  - WebGL2 build: **21.6 MB raw wasm / 7.0 MB gzip -9**
  - WebGPU build: **21.7 MB raw / 7.0 MB gzip**
  - ⚠️ Flag: these are Bevy's CI example builds; I cannot confirm they use `opt-level="z"` + fat LTO + `wasm-opt -Oz`. A hand-tuned build would be smaller — but the [Bevy Cheat Book size-opt page](https://bevy-cheatbook.github.io/platforms/wasm/size-opt.html) gives techniques and **no numbers**, explicitly telling you to measure yourself. Secondary sources quote wildly inconsistent figures (3.5 MB to 30 MB); ignore them.
- **WebGPU vs WebGL2:** ⚠️ **you must pick one at compile time.** Bevy publishes two separate sites for exactly this reason, and [bevyengine/bevy#13168 "Support WebGL2 and WebGPU in the same WASM file"](https://github.com/bevyengine/bevy/issues/13168) is still the tracking issue. No runtime fallback. That means either you ship the WebGL2 build to everyone (losing WebGPU), or you ship ~7 MB twice and feature-detect.
- **iOS:** ⚠️ **could not verify** a first-party statement on Bevy WASM + iOS Safari. Safari 26 has WebGPU, so the WebGPU build *should* work, but with no runtime fallback you'd be shipping the WebGL2 build anyway — and Safari's WebGL2 is the historically flaky one.
- **Compile times / ergonomics:** ⚠️ I did not benchmark this. Known-bad by reputation for a hobby project: Rust + a full ECS + `wasm-bindgen` + `wasm-opt` in the loop, versus Vite HMR in milliseconds. Bevy also has no stable API — 0.19 in June 2026 landed "next-generation scenes (BSN)", a breaking rework.
- **Main drawback:** 7 MB and a Rust toolchain to render 32 pieces on a board. Also: no built-in pixelation or .vox loader — Bevy has render-graph nodes you'd write yourself.

## 7. Pixi.js v8 as 2.5D fallback — `pixi.js@8.20.1`

- **Version:** 8.20.1 (2026-08-26). v8.0.0 shipped 2024-03-05.
- **Size (measured):** **163 KB gzip / 134 KB brotli** for `Application` + `Sprite` + `Container` + `Assets` + `Spritesheet`. Marginally *larger* than three.js's 132 KB gzip **with** post-processing. Pixi does not save you bytes.
- **Renderer:** auto-detects with `renderPriority = ["webgl", "webgpu", "canvas"]` — WebGL is preferred by default, WebGPU opt-in via `preference`. Filter system (`FilterSystem`, custom `Filter` with WGSL+GLSL) makes a pixelate/posterize/dither screen filter trivial; `pixi-filters@6.1.5` has a ready `PixelateFilter`.
- **Voxel:** N/A by design — you pre-render `.vox` models to sprite sheets offline (MagicaVoxel itself, or a headless three.js + `VOXLoader` render rig).
- **Trade-offs vs. real 3D — the honest list:**
  - **Rotation:** dead. Every camera yaw needs a fresh pre-rendered sheet. 8 directions × 12 piece types × 2 colors × N animation frames is a combinatorial asset explosion, and you still can't rotate freely. If your chess variant ever wants to spin the board (and chess games always do, for the second player), this is a wall.
  - **Camera tilt:** locked at author time. The "tilted camera" in your spec becomes a baked property of the art, not a runtime parameter.
  - **Dynamic lighting:** gone. Baked only. No hover highlight that actually lights the piece, no shadow that follows a moving piece — you fake both with extra sprites.
  - **Depth sorting:** you hand-implement isometric painter's-algorithm sorting and it will bite you on tall pieces overlapping.
  - **Iteration cost:** every piece tweak means re-running the offline render pipeline. With real 3D you tweak a material and hit save.
  - **What you gain:** guaranteed-identical output on every GPU, trivially cheap on weak mobile, and pixel-perfect art control.
- **Verdict:** a legitimate fallback *only* if you commit to a fixed camera. For a chess variant, you almost certainly won't. And since three.js is smaller, "fallback for size" isn't a reason.

---

## WebGPU browser support, 2026

Source: [caniuse `features-json/webgpu.json`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Fyrd/caniuse/main/features-json/webgpu.json) (raw data, fetched today) cross-checked against the [W3C GPU for the Web Implementation Status wiki](https://github.com/gpuweb/gpuweb/wiki/Implementation-Status).

**caniuse global: 83.99% full support + 2.95% partial ≈ 86.9%.** (The rendered caniuse.com page reported 85.72% + 1.63% = 87.35%; use ~87% either way.)

| Browser | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Chrome desktop** | ✅ **113+** | caniuse note #9: "Support on Linux depends on hardware and drivers." Per gpuweb wiki: Linux Intel Gen12+ from Chrome 144, NVIDIA/Wayland from 147 |
| **Edge** | ✅ **113+** | |
| **Safari macOS** | ⚠️ **26.0+, PARTIAL** | caniuse note #7: "Partial support refers to only being enabled by default on macOS 26 Tahoe or later." On older macOS it's behind the `WebGPU` feature flag |
| **Safari iOS** | ✅ **26.0+, FULL** | This is the big 2026 change. iOS 18.x and earlier = flag-only |
| **Firefox desktop** | ⚠️ **partial** | caniuse note #8: "Only enabled by default on Windows as well as macOS 26 Tahoe or later on Apple Silicon." gpuweb wiki: Windows from **141**, macOS Apple Silicon (macOS 26+) from **145**, *all* macOS from **147**. Linux still Nightly — "Mozilla expects to ship on Linux in 2026" |

## Engine & library research — King Down Chess (verified 2026-09-13)

### Verdict up front

Nothing outside the Fairy-Stockfish family gives you a declarative way to express all five pieces. Every config-driven variant engine I checked is a *move-generator* DSL (where can this piece go), not a *rules* DSL (what happens when it gets there). Rifle capture, kamikaze, swap-on-capture and chain capture are all "what happens" rules. Plan on writing your own rules layer in TypeScript and treating any engine as an optional, separate AI process.

---

### 1. Sjaak II — dead since 2016, and the DSL can't express your pieces

Author's site lists **Sjaak II 1.4.1** as newest, no source or binary after it ([download page](http://www.eglebbk.dds.nl/program/chess-download.html); the site serves only over plain HTTP — HTTPS fails cert validation). Chessprogramming dates 1.4.1 to **December 2016** ([wiki](https://chessprogramming.org/Sjaak_(Glebbeek))). GPL, C. No upstream git host; the only GitHub presence is a third-party soft fork, [RMKirkpatrick/SjaakII](https://github.com/RMKirkpatrick/SjaakII) (created 2025-01-25, last push **2025-10-23**, 0 stars, GPL-3.0 — GitHub API). **Not maintained in 2026.**

The variant language is a self-documenting INI-ish text file, [`variants.txt`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RMKirkpatrick/SjaakII/master/variants.txt) (4164 lines). It has `Board:`, `Zone:`, `Piece:`/`Move:`/`Capture:`/`Flags:`, and three movement primitives — `slide (H,V,A,D)`, `leap (2,1)`, `step N` — plus `hop` and `aleap`. Against your five:

| Piece | Sjaak II |
|---|---|
| ARCHER (rifle capture) | **No.** The file states plainly: *"Currently, capture is replacement only."* |
| PALADIN (jump friendly, blocked by enemy; no check; kamikaze) | **No.** No friendly-transparent slider; `no_mate` exists but only blocks mate, not check; no kamikaze flag. |
| GUARD (uncapturable except by king) | **Partial.** `iron` = "may not be captured at all" — wrong semantics, no per-attacker exception. |
| MAESTER (swap with friendly, long-range king swap) | **No.** Castling is the only two-piece move, and it's rank-bound with fixed geometry. |
| BEAST (chain capture) | **No.** No multi-capture concept. |

Flags available are `royal, set_ep, take_ep, drop_no_check, drop_no_mate, drop_one_file, drop_dead, no_mate, shak, assimilate, no_retaliate, endangered, iron, capture_flag`. Rich for historical variants, useless for modern rule-invention. Skip.

### 2. ChessV — 2.2 from January 2020, and it explicitly can't add rules

[chessv.org](http://www.chessv.org/) (HTTP only; HTTPS presents a cert for `plesk8400.is.cc`) shows "Update 2020-01-22 — ChessV 2.2 released". No 2.3, no later news. C#/.NET 4.5.1, runs on Mono; GPL ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ChessV)). ChessV 0.9 is the legacy C# 1.x-era line; 2.x is the current rewrite with a `.cvc` scripting language whose syntax resembles C#.

The homepage's own wording is the whole answer: *"It supports combining existing pieces and rules, and even defining new pieces, but creation of new rules is not supported."* Wikipedia repeats it: the scripting language is stable but "creating new rules for new pieces is not supported yet." You could in principle subclass `Piece` in C# (the source zip is at `chessv.org/downloads/ChessV2.2-Source.zip`), but you'd be forking an unmaintained WinForms desktop app in a language you'd then need to bridge to a web stack. Skip.

### 3. Zillions, Ludii, Jocly, XBoard engines

**Zillions of Games** — [zillionsofgames.com](http://www.zillionsofgames.com/) is still up and still selling ZoG 2 (2.0.1). Last stable release is **2.0.1 from 2003** ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zillions_of_Games)). Closed-source, Windows-only, ZRF scripts. A download aggregator claims a "last updated 15 July 2026" — that's mirror metadata, **not verified** as a real release. Irrelevant for web.

**Ludii** — the most *expressive* option and the one you legally can't use. Latest release **v1.3.14, GitHub-published 2025-06-08** (GitHub API; [ludii.games/download.php](https://ludii.games/download.php) dates the same version 2025-02-20 — the two disagree, flagging it). Repo [Ludeme/Ludii](https://github.com/Ludeme/Ludii) last pushed 2026-05-31, Java, 165 stars. License is **[CC BY-NC-ND 4.0](https://github.com/Ludeme/Ludii/blob/master/LICENSE)** — non-commercial *and* no-derivatives. That kills it for a web game you might monetize, and forbids the forking you'd need anyway. Its ludeme grammar does have generic `(move Remove …)`, `(move Hop …)`, swap rules and `(then …)` consequences ([Language Reference PDF](https://ludii.games/downloads/LudiiLanguageReference.pdf)), so your pieces are *probably* expressible — I did **not** verify each ludeme, and it doesn't matter given the license. AI is general-purpose MCTS/alpha-beta over a general game API ([arXiv overview](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1907.00240)); fine for research, weak versus a tuned alpha-beta, and it's a JVM app, not a browser engine.

**Jocly** — moved from `mi-g/jocly` to **[aclap-dev/jocly](https://github.com/aclap-dev/jocly)**; last push **2024-06-06**, 77 stars. JS board-game library with 2D/3D UI and built-in AI. License is **AGPLv3** with a paid proprietary exception ([COPYING.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aclap-dev/jocly/master/COPYING.md)) — AGPL is worse than GPL for a hosted service. Games are hand-written JS model classes, so arbitrary rules *are* possible, but you'd inherit a two-year-stale codebase and an AGPL obligation. Skip unless you want to buy the exception.

**Musketeer Chess** — no independent engine; it's implemented as variants inside Fairy-Stockfish and the older [ianfab/Musketeer-Stockfish](https://github.com/ianfab/Musketeer-Stockfish). Nothing new to learn there.

**XBoard family** — [Fairy-Max](https://home.hccnet.nl/h.g.muller/CVfairy.html) (H.G. Muller) reads a self-documenting `fmax.ini`, but is capped at 15 piece types / 12x8 and is a pure Betza move-table engine — no rifle, no kamikaze, no swap. [HaChu](http://hgm.nubati.net/HaChu.html) is hard-coded for Chu Shogi family. Seirawan support exists in Sjaak II/Fairy-Max as fixed variants. All are native binaries speaking CECP over stdio — no WASM path, no rule extensibility. Useful only as a reference for Betza notation.

### 4. pychess-variants — the architecture to copy

[gbtami/pychess-variants](https://github.com/gbtami/pychess-variants), **AGPL-3.0**, 308 stars, last push **2026-09-12** — very actively maintained. Python 3.14 + aiohttp + MongoDB, TypeScript client (Snabbdom, esbuild).

The important structural lesson is the **single source of variant truth**: [`client/variantsIni.ts`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gbtami/pychess-variants/master/client/variantsIni.ts) is one big template string of Fairy-Stockfish INI, e.g.

```
[cwda:chess]
customPiece1 = d:BD
customPiece5 = g:fsRbK
```

That same text is loaded by the WASM engine in the browser and by the server, so client and server enforce identical rules by construction. Server dependencies confirm the split ([pyproject.toml](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gbtami/pychess-variants/master/pyproject.toml)): `pyffish==0.0.90` (Fairy-Stockfish Python binding) is the authoritative validator; the client uses `ffish-es6` WASM for instant legality/premove feedback plus `fairy-stockfish-nnue.wasm` for analysis; heavy analysis is offloaded to `fairyfishnet`. DeepWiki also claims the server uses a `bugchess` fork of python-chess — **not in pyproject.toml, unverified**.

Copy the pattern, not the code (AGPL): one rules module, compiled/shipped to both sides, server always re-validates.

### 5. Rules and board libraries (npm, verified 2026-09-13 via registry API)

| Package | Latest | Published | License |
|---|---|---|---|
| `chessops` | **0.15.1** | 2026-07-12 | GPL-3.0-or-later |
| `chessground` (legacy name) | 9.2.1 | 2025-05-15 | GPL-3.0-or-later |
| **`@lichess-org/chessground`** | **10.1.1** | 2026-03-27 | GPL-3.0-or-later |
| `chessgroundx` | **10.7.5** | 2026-05-12 | GPL-3.0 |
| `chess.js` | **1.4.0** | 2025-06-14 | BSD-2-Clause |
| `react-chessboard` | **5.12.1** | 2026-08-16 | MIT |
| `ffish` / `ffish-es6` | 0.7.10 | 2026-08-26 | GPL-3.0 |
| `fairy-stockfish-nnue.wasm` | 1.1.12 | 2026-08-26 | GPL-3.0 |

Note lichess **renamed** chessground to the scoped `@lichess-org/chessground` — the unscoped `chessground` is a year stale.

**chessops extensibility: effectively zero for new pieces.** [`src/types.ts`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/niklasf/chessops/master/src/types.ts) hard-codes `export const ROLES = ['pawn','knight','bishop','rook','queen','king'] as const`, and the whole library is 8x8 bitboards (`SquareSet`) with Hyperbola Quintessence attacks. Its variants (crazyhouse, atomic, KotH, 3-check, antichess, horde, racing kings) are subclasses that override *outcomes*, not the piece set. Adding a 7th role means forking the type union, the FEN parser, SAN, and every attack table.

**chessground vs chessgroundx** is the sharpest contrast in this whole report. Lichess's `Role` is the same frozen 6-item union. chessgroundx redefines it as a template literal type — `` type Role = `${'' | 'p'}${Alphabet | '_'}-piece` `` — so any letter a–z is a valid piece, rendered via a CSS class, on boards up to 16x16. **chessgroundx is genuinely piece-agnostic; chessground is not.** For a 5-fairy-piece 8x8 game, chessgroundx (GPL-3.0, active 2026-05) is the least-work board UI. `react-chessboard` 5.x (MIT) supports custom piece renderers and is the only permissively licensed option, but is 8x8/standard-oriented.

`chess.js` 1.4.0 is BSD-2 and the most permissive, but it's a monolithic 0x88 standard-chess generator with no variant or piece extension points — useful only if you want a clean reference implementation to copy ideas from.

### 6. Licensing — the part that actually constrains you

**(b) Fairy-Stockfish is GPL-3.0** (GitHub API on [fairy-stockfish/Fairy-Stockfish](https://github.com/fairy-stockfish/Fairy-Stockfish), last push 2026-09-06; README §"Fairy-Stockfish is free, and distributed under the GNU General Public License version 3"). All its npm artifacts (`ffish`, `fairy-stockfish-nnue.wasm`) are GPL-3.0.

**(c)** chessops, chessground, chessgroundx: GPL-3.0-or-later. chess.js: BSD-2-Clause. react-chessboard: MIT. Ludii: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Jocly: AGPLv3. pychess-variants: AGPL-3.0.

**(a) The Web Worker question — no clean answer, and the risk is real.** The FSF's own test ([GPL FAQ, MereAggregation](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-faq.html#MereAggregation)) turns on two things: *"Pipes, sockets and command-line arguments are communication mechanisms normally used between two separate programs"*, but *"if the semantics of the communication are intimate enough, exchanging complex internal data structures, that too could be a basis to consider the two parts as combined into a larger program."* A Web Worker talking UCI text over `postMessage` looks like the pipe case — separate address space, line-oriented protocol, no shared structures. That is the strongest argument available.

But three things cut against relying on it. First, **shipping WASM to a browser is distribution** — you must convey the engine's complete corresponding source (or a written offer) to every visitor, and GPLv3 §6 applies even though GPLv3 has no AGPL network clause. Second, I found **no statement from the Stockfish team or the FSF specifically addressing WASM/Web Worker deployment** — that is a genuine gap, flagged as unverified. Third, the Stockfish team has demonstrated willingness to litigate: they sued ChessBase in 2021 and the Munich court confirmed in the 2022-07-04 hearing that they could terminate the GPL grant; the [settlement of 2022-11-18](https://stockfishchess.org/blog/2022/chessbase-stockfish-agreement/) forced ChessBase to stop selling Stockfish-based products, appoint a Free Software Compliance Officer, and GPL its neural nets ([FSFE](https://fsfe.org/news/2022/news-20221212-01.en.html)).

Practical read: if you ship a GPLv3 WASM engine, plan to GPL the frontend, or keep the engine strictly server-side (GPLv3, unlike AGPL, imposes no source obligation for a network service you merely host), or write your own engine. Since your rules layer has to be custom anyway, the third option is cheaper than it sounds.

**Unverified / flagged:** Ludii ludeme-level expressiveness for your five pieces; Ludii's conflicting 1.3.14 dates; the pychess `bugchess` claim; the ZoG "2026 update"; any Stockfish/FSF statement on WASM specifically.

Research complete. Three families below, with real URLs and explicit "unverified" flags. Four of your premises turned out to be wrong — those are flagged inline and summarised at the end.

---

# A) Pre-rendered 3D-to-sprite pipelines

## Donkey Kong Country (Rare, 1994)

**Pipeline (verified).** Models built as NURBS in Alias PowerAnimator on SGI Challenge workstations (~£80,000 each, bought c. 1992), textured, boned, keyframed, rendered frame-by-frame, then compressed with Rare's proprietary "Advanced Computer Modelling" (ACM). A dedicated machine ran ACM with "a proprietary utility similar to Deluxe Paint." Renders took hours; artists left machines overnight. ROM 4 MB; team ~20; ~18 months. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donkey_Kong_Country, https://retromo.substack.com/p/donkey-kong-country-snes-1994

**The two conversion steps, in the artists' own words** (https://episodiccontentmag.com/2016/02/19/dkcountry1_chapter2/):
- Frame decimation — Steve Mayles: "If I handed Chris Sutherland a disk with a 16-frame walk animation, he'd probably only use every other frame." He adds it "would really wound you up when you made this great-looking animation, only for the programmers to chop it to pieces."
- Background tiling — Chris Sutherland: "taking a single pre-rendered background screen and then cutting it up into squares with the correct colour palettes that could replicate that image on the SNES," then "find places where pieces of the image could be repeated elsewhere to save video [memory] space."

**Pixels tall.** Donkey Kong idle ≈ **38×42 / 39×40 px**; Diddy ≈ **35×36**; Cranky 44×56; Expresso 45×65; Enguarde 62×49; Rambi 54×47. Measured from the asset files catalogued at https://www.mariowiki.com/Category:Donkey_Kong_Country_assets. On a 256×224 screen, DK is ~18% of screen height.

**Colours per character.** Hard hardware ceiling: SNES sprites are 4bpp — **16 entries per palette, index 0 transparent, so 15 visible colours**, chosen from 8 sprite palette slots (128 sprite colours total). Sprite tile sizes 8×8 / 16×16 / 32×32 / 64×64, two sizes selectable per game; 128 sprites in OAM, 32 per scanline. https://megacatstudios.com/blogs/retro-development/snes-sprite-engine-design-guidelines, https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/super-nintendo/

The important consequence: because the sprite is palette-**indexed**, you can re-upload CGRAM every frame and give each animation frame its own bespoke 15-colour palette. The Killer Instinct SNES patch community does exactly this — "dynamically refresh the player palette each frame to match the existing animation, as 15 colors are more than enough for one sprite frame" (https://www.zeldix.net/t2002p100-killer-instinct-arcade-mega-patch). That is the real answer to "how many colours per character" for this family: 15 *at any instant*, not 15 for the whole character.

**The quantise step.** PowerAnimator's colour quantiser reduced true-RGB renders to 256 colours before the platform-specific pass. This is repeated widely but only forum-sourced (https://www.neogaf.com/threads/the-making-of-donkey-kong-country-killer-instinct-pre-rendered-graphics.1607594/) — treat as **unverified**. Community accounts also say Rare scaled renders to the 8×8/16×16 tile grid and then hand-edited pixels on top (https://www.vg-resource.com/archive/index.php/thread-31192.html, 403s to automated fetch).

**What actually makes or breaks readability in this family.** The best single technical source is the pre-rendered/digitized chapter at https://nfgworld.com/grafx/games/NewBook/PreRendered/PreRendered.pdf. Concrete, quotable findings:
- **Quantisers allocate colours by pixel count**, so a feature occupying 10% of the image loses its colours to the 90%. Verbatim: "if 90% of the image needed red shades then the remaining 10% lost out. Usually this resulted in faces lacking detail, and *Donkey Kong's frickin' eye*." This is the characteristic failure mode of the whole pipeline — small high-salience features (eyes, hands, weapon tips) die in quantisation.
- **Fringing**: sprites are rendered against a matte colour, which "will forever be an inconsistent outline surrounding the sprite, unless it's carefully trimmed." Midway's fix was **rim lights on the models** — a highlight rather than a shadow at the contour, which both kills fringing and doubles as a readability outline.
- Hard palette-reduction numbers: **Primal Rage arcade sprite = 59 colours; SNES port = 14; Mega Drive = 11.**
- Frame-count economics: Cave's *Ketsui* pre-rendered ship uses **7 frames per turn direction**; hand-pixelled *Raiden* uses **2**, mirrored. *Mario vs. Donkey Kong* spends **8 frames on standing still**.
- Palette-swap trick: render **black-and-white sprites and add colour later** (used by Clay Fighter).

## Dead Cells (Motion Twin, 2017)

**Pipeline (primary source, Thomas Vasseur's own deep dive).** https://www.gamedeveloper.com/production/art-design-deep-dive-using-a-3d-pipeline-for-2d-animation-in-i-dead-cells-i-, full walkthrough mirrored at https://sudonull.com/post/14066-Dead-Cells-Using-3D-Pipeline-for-2D-Animation

1. Draw a **2D pixel-art model sheet** first (this step is usually omitted from summaries — the design is authored in pixels, not in 3D).
2. Build model + skeleton from that sheet in **3DS Max**, export **FBX**.
3. A **homebrew renderer** "renders the mesh in a very small size and without antialiasing, giving us that pixelated look."
4. Animate pose-to-pose on keyframes; interpolation frames added only "before or after the key frames. Never in-between."
5. Export each frame as **PNG + a normal map**; shade with "the simplest toon shader"; blend modes and hand-made VFX layered on top.

**Pixels tall: 50.** Vasseur, verbatim: "if the character's [height] in a game is only 50 pixels, then [spending] a heap of time [on the model is wasteful]."

**Your premise about a hand-clean pass is wrong.** Vasseur lists it as an *unsolved cost*, not a step. They could not kill "flickering pixels" automatically, they corrected manually only where forced, and they accepted "disappointing level of details" because hand-cleaning "contradicted their speed-focused workflow." Same sources.

**Colours.** There is **no indexed palette**. Backgrounds and decorations are hand-pixelled in Photoshop, then redrawn as **normal maps** so a dynamic 3D light system tints and reliefs them at runtime — "a torch on the left of a statue will light up the statue from the correct direction while respecting its base colours." Art direction is "saturated palette + Celtic architecture + alchemy." https://80.lv/articles/interview-with-the-developers-of-dead-cells. Per-character colour counts and total frame counts: **unverified**.

**Why it reads.** Runtime lighting, not the sprite, supplies contrast; a 50px silhouette with strong VFX for attack telegraphs.

## Octopath Traveler — this does NOT belong in family A

Octopath is not a 3D-to-sprite pipeline. It is **hand-drawn pixel art, rigged as an articulated puppet, then billboarded into a 3D scene.** Two Japanese primary sources say so explicitly:

- CGWorld, from the *Game Graphics 2019* book (https://cgworld.jp/feature/201908-gg2019-oct.html), verbatim: 「キャラクターの基本サイズは18×32となっており、子供、男性、大柄男性で幅と高さが数ピクセル変わっている。アニメーションの矩形範囲としては最大128×128だが、テクスチャパッキングする際に詰められている。」 — **base character size 18×32 px**, varying by a few pixels for child/male/large-male builds; **animation bounding box max 128×128**, packed at texture-pack time. Animation uses 「Photoshopのパペットワープ機能」 — **Photoshop Puppet Warp** — to reassign animation patterns instantly across differently-designed characters.
- Denfaminicogamer (https://news.denfaminicogamer.jp/kikakuthetower/231218g): pixel art is decomposed into a 「多関節モデル」 (multi-joint model), animated from the rig, then **pixel-level breakage is fixed by hand**. Acquire chose this because they are a 3D polygon studio, not a pixel-art studio.

Independent measurement of rips agrees: OT1 field sprite **16×34 px**, 27 colours/frame (sheet 81 colours, 8-bit indexed); OT1 battle sprite **34×51**; OT2 battle sprite **34×56 native**. https://www.spriters-resource.com/nintendo_switch/octopathtraveler/

**The 3D/effects half.** UE4. Verbatim from Square Enix's 4Gamer Business technical article (https://business.4gamer.net/article/1810/18101801/): 「UE4のPaper FlipBook機能により2D画像を2Dスプライトに動きアニメーションを使用している」 (Paper Flipbook drives the sprites); 「ポストプロセスエフェクトには、UE4の標準機能でColorGrading、Bloom、DOF、Bokeh、Lens Flares、Ambient Cubemap、Vignetteを使用している」 — the full post stack is **ColorGrading, Bloom, DOF, Bokeh, Lens Flares, Ambient Cubemap, Vignette**, via stock PostProcessVolume; Maya for prototyping. Tilt-shift plus point lights casting character shadows onto 3D terrain: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HD-2D

Producer Masashi Takahashi's own definition: "we left in a good amount of pixel aesthetic and compounded that with a three-dimensional environment, and we created this incredibly lush visual style that we call HD-2D." He also rejected the obvious alternative — simply making thicker pixels "ends up looking worse somehow." Pixel artist **Shizuka Morimoto**: "At first, I started using some techniques to add dramatic lighting to the 2D art, but Asano told me that wasn't enough… Once I started incorporating some 3D elements, it really gave the visuals a sense of depth." https://nintendoeverything.com/octopath-traveler-devs-on-character-origins-visual-style-initial-hd-rumble-plans-much-more/

**Scaling mechanism.** Sprites are nearest-neighbour textures scaled and rotated in a PBR renderer; **temporal AA** hides the resulting artifacts. This is why Octopath's "pixels" are not a consistent size on screen. https://www.neogaf.com/threads/the-last-night-dev-tim-soret-on-pixel-art-filtering-and-where-octopath-traveler-went-wrong.1463728/ Digital Foundry: native **720p docked / 1024×576 handheld, 30 fps** (https://nintendoeverything.com/octopath-traveler-technical-analysis/).

## Contrast cases: Blasphemous and Owlboy

**Blasphemous (The Game Kitchen).** Pure hand-pixelled, no 3D. Aseprite for drawing/animation, sheets imported into Unity; Photoshop and Pixaki/iPad Pro also used by pixel artist Andrey Gogiya (https://www.behance.net/gallery/85604481/Pixel-arts-and-animations-for-game-Blasphemous). Animator Raúl Vivar works by manipulating existing frames for fast iteration (https://www.gameanim.com/2021/02/19/blasphemous-pixel-art-animation-time-lapses/). Designer interview on the "purist" approach: https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-news/blasphemous-designer-purist-approach-games-pixel-art-style-1238370/ (paywalled). **Sprite dimensions, colour counts and frame counts: unverified** — no dev source publishes them. A Behance commenter guesses 64×64 for the Penitent One; unconfirmed.

**Owlboy (D-Pad Studio).** Nine years, 2007–2016, all pixel art hand-drawn in MS Paint then Photoshop CS3 (https://www.dpadstudio.com/presskitOwlboy.html). The studio **coined "hi-bit"** and defines it as "any pixel art game that operates beyond the limitations of the old 8/16/32-bit consoles" — their blog also names **640×360 as the emerging base resolution** for the category (scaling cleanly to 720p/1080p/4K), citing Hyper Light Drifter, Iconoclasts, Shovel Knight. https://dpadstudio.com/Blog/postHibit.html. Owlboy's own internal resolution is widely reported as 640×360 with Otus **39 px tall**, but the only source I could trace is a bachelor's thesis (Olli Heikkinen, *Hi-Bit Pixel Graphics*, Theseus 10024/501981, 403s to fetch) — **treat the 39 px as unverified**. Andersen's stated animation technique is sub-pixelling and in-between colours to imply motion between whole pixels.

---

# B) 32-bit isometric pre-rendered

## Diablo 1 (Blizzard North / Condor, 1996)

**Directions: 8.** The 1994 Condor pitch doc, verbatim: "The three-quarter perspective requires eight directions of movement, three of which can sometimes be flipped. Each monster will have multiple graphic deaths and will require at least 50 frames of animations." 640×480 SVGA. https://archive.org/stream/diablo_pitch/diablo_pitch_djvu.txt. Confirmed in the shipped engine: `enum class Direction { South, SouthWest, West, NorthWest, North, NorthEast, East, SouthEast }` (https://github.com/diasurgical/devilutionX/blob/master/Source/engine/direction.hpp).

**"3D Studio for Diablo 1" is unverified.** No primary source names the tool. It *is* verified for Diablo II — postmortem, verbatim: "Almost all of *Diablo II*'s in-game and cinematic art was constructed and rendered in 3D Studio Max," and "An in-house tool would render the files from many different angles (eight for all monsters, 16 for player characters)." 640×480, 8-bit colour. https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/postmortem-blizzard-s-i-diablo-ii-i-

**Sprite widths** (from the original data tables, https://github.com/diasurgical/devilutionX/blob/master/assets/txtdata/classes/warrior/sprites.tsv):

| class | stand | walk | attack | bow | death |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| warrior | 96 | 96 | 128 | 96 | 128 |
| rogue | 96 | 96 | 128 | 128 | 128 |
| sorcerer | 96 | 96 | 128 | 128 | 128 |

Monsters use **only three widths across all 112 rows**: 96 px (9), 128 px (69), 160 px (34) — https://github.com/diasurgical/devilutionX/blob/master/assets/txtdata/monsters/monstdat.tsv. **Frame heights are not stored** in CL2 (derived from decoded pixel count ÷ width), so "96×96 square" is an assumption, **unverified**.

Warrior frame counts: idle 10, walk 8, sword attack 16, axe 20, bow 16, block 2, death 20, cast 20, recovery 6.

**Tiles.** Base CEL frame **32×32 px**; floor/wall-bottom split into two 32×16 halves. Subtile ground layer **64×32**; full subtile **64×160** (10 frames) or **64×256** (16, Town/Hell). TIL megatile **128×192** (Town/Hell 128×288). https://github.com/savagesteel/d1-file-formats/blob/master/PC-Mac/CEL.md, .../MIN-TIL.md

**Palette handling — all of Diablo's colour work is index remapping.**
- PAL = 768 bytes, 256 colours, 3 bytes RGB; `offset = 3 × index`. .../PAL.md
- **TRN = 256 bytes, one index→index remap.** This is Diablo's team-colour analogue: monster variants are the *same art* plus a different TRN. Zombie / Ghoul / Rotting Carcass / Black Death all share `zombie\zombie` art with trn `—`, `bluered`, `grey`, `yellow`. Fallen One / Carver / Dark One share `falspear`. Skeletons: `skelaxe\white`, `\skelt`, `\black`. .../TRN.md plus the `trnFile` column of monstdat.tsv
- **Lighting is also remapping**: 16 levels × 256-entry tables (`LightsMax = 15`, `LightTableSize = 256`). https://github.com/diasurgical/devilutionX/blob/master/Source/engine/lighting_defs.hpp
- **Colour cycling is confined to low indices**: caves `CycleColors(1, 31)`; crypt lava `CycleColorsReverse(1, 15)` + glow `(16, 31)` — "Lava has 15 colors and the glow 16, so the full animation has 240 frames before it loops"; hive `(1, 8)` + `(9, 15)`. https://github.com/diasurgical/devilutionX/blob/master/Source/engine/palette.cpp

## Fallout 1/2 (Interplay)

**FRM format** (https://fodev.net/files/fo2/frm.html, https://github.com/falltergeist/libfalltergeist/wiki/Frm-file-format). Fixed **0x3E-byte header**: version, fps, action_frame, frames_per_direction, `int16 x_offsets[6]`, `int16 y_offsets[6]`, `uint32 data_offsets[6]`. Frame record: width, height, size, x, y, then one **palette index byte per pixel**.

**Directions: 6.** "Rotations use six directions: 0 northeast, 1 east, 2 southeast, 3 southwest, 4 west, and 5 northwest" (https://fodev.net/files/fo2/map.html). Critter art also splits into `.fr0`–`.fr5`. Equal consecutive `data_offsets` means that rotation reuses the previous one's frames — the engine's cheap mirroring.

The anchor is "the center of the bottom edge of the visible frame," and per-frame x/y are **motion deltas, not crop origins**. That is how feet stay planted while the bounding box changes size.

**Tile size 80×36 — verified from engine source, not a wiki.** `squareTileToScreenXY()` in https://github.com/alexbatalov/fallout2-ce/blob/main/src/tile.cc steps `+48/−12` on one diagonal and `+32/+24` on the other: 48+32 = **80** wide, 12+24 = **36** tall. Corroborated by `static int _intensity_map[3280]` = 80 × 41.

Two separate grids per elevation: **200×200 hex for objects, 100×100 square for floor/roof tiles.**

**Palette.** 256 entries, index 0 transparent, 255 black. Cycled ranges (https://fodev.net/files/fo2/fo_colors.html):

| indices | n | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 229–232 | 4 | green — radioactive slime |
| 233–237 | 5 | blue — computer screens |
| 238–242 | 5 | fire #1 |
| 243–247 | 5 | fire #2 |
| 248–253 | 6 | brown — shores/water |

Lighting is a 2D LUT: `intensityColorTable[colorIndex][intensity >> 9]`. **Fallout has no team/player colour system** — nothing reserved for faction tint.

**3D tool: unverified and probably not 3D Studio.** The NMA thread reports Lightwave plus Photoshop touch-up (https://www.nma-fallout.com/threads/what-was-the-technology-behind-fallout-1-2-s-graphics.218299/ — 403s to automated fetch; open manually before citing).

## Baldur's Gate 1/2 (Infinity Engine) — the richest palette-range system of the set

**BAM v1** (https://gibberlings3.github.io/iesdp/file_formats/ie_formats/bam_v1.htm). 20-byte header; frame count, **max 255 cycles**, compressed-colour-index byte. Frame entry carries width, height and **signed centre X/Y**. Palette = **256 RGBQUADs, BB GG RR AA order**. Transparency index = "the first occurrence of RGB(0,255,0)"; if absent, index 0. RLE: any non-transparent byte is literal; transparent index followed by `x` means `x+1` transparent pixels. **BG2 caps displayed frames at 256×256.** Actual avatar pixel size is per-frame variable — **no fixed sprite dimension; unverified.**

**Directions: 9 stored → 16 rendered.** "Most modern animation types use 9 base directions (S, SSW, SW, WSW, W, WNW, NW, NNW, N) with eastern directions calculated by the engine through mirroring." https://gibberlings3.github.io/iesdp/file_formats/ie_formats/ini_anim.htm

**The colour-range map, exact** (from NearInfinity's `SpriteDecoder`, the reference implementation: https://github.com/Argent77/NearInfinity/blob/master/src/org/infinity/resource/cre/decoder/SpriteDecoder.java):

```java
if (locationIndex >= 0 && locationIndex < 7) retVal = 4 + locationIndex * 12;
final int srcOfs = 4;  final int dstOfs = 88;
final int srcLen = 12; final int dstLen = 8;
palette[2] = 0xFF000000; palette[3] = 0xFF000000;
```

- **7 colour locations × 12 palette entries**, starting at index 4: `4–15`, `16–27`, `28–39`, `40–51`, `52–63`, `64–75`, `76–87`.
- **Indices 88–255 are auto-generated blend ramps** — all 21 pairs of the 7 ranges get an 8-entry interpolation. 88 + 21×8 = 256 exactly. This is why IE characters stay clean where two dyed materials meet.
- **Indices 2 and 3 forced to opaque black** (shadow).

Location meanings (opcode 51, https://gibberlings3.github.io/iesdp/opcodes/bgee.htm): `00` belt buckle/amulet, `01` **minor colour**, `02` **major colour**, `03` skin, `04` strap/minor trim, `05` armour, `06` hair. Equipment has its own blocks: weapon 16–22, shield 32–40, helmet 48–54. Values live in CRE header bytes `0x2c` metal, `0x2d` minor, `0x2e` major, `0x2f` skin, `0x30` leather, `0x31` armor, `0x32` hair (https://gibberlings3.github.io/iesdp/file_formats/ie_formats/cre_v1.htm), each selecting a gradient id from a 256-entry table (`00h–73h` valid everywhere, `78h–FFh` EE-only).

**Worth stating in your report:** IE areas are **painted backdrops cut into a 64×64 grid**, not a tiled isometric ground. TIS tiles are 64×64, **each with its own 256-colour palette**, 5120 bytes per tile (1024 palette + 4096 indices), index 0 transparent. https://gibberlings3.github.io/iesdp/file_formats/ie_formats/tis_v1.htm

## Age of Empires 2 (SLP) — the player-colour trick you asked about

**Verbatim from the openage format docs** (https://github.com/SFTtech/openage/blob/master/doc/media/slp-files.md):

> "In AoK and SWGB, blue player colors begin at index 16 in the palette, red at index 32, green at index 48, yellow at index 64, orange at index 80, cyan/teal at index 96, purple at index 112, and grey at index 128."
> "The real palette index is `player_color_palette_index + player * 16`, where `player` is the player ID you're drawing for (1-8)."

So **indices 16–143 are eight contiguous 16-entry player blocks.** The SLP stores only a **0–15 offset inside the block**; the artist paints a 16-step ramp and the engine picks the base. That is why AoE2 units keep full shading under any team colour. (AoE1:DE uses separate player-colour palettes, indices 0x00–0x7F.)

Commands:
- `0x06` player-colour draw, `0x0A` fill player colour
- `0x0B` shadow draw, against a **shadow palette that is a darkened copy of palette 50500**
- **`0x4E` Outline 1**, `palette_index = player * 16` — "the outline that surrounds a unit and is seen when a unit is obstructed, such as when it is behind a building or tree… Its color is determined by the team color of the player." **This is the single most explicit readability mechanism anywhere in the three families.**
- `0x6E` Outline 2, `palette_index = 243`

**Directions: 5 rendered → 8 shown.** "each animation has 10 keyframes and 5 directions. The other 3 directions are generated later by flipping the sprite on the y axis… 50 frames per SLP." Projectiles: 35 keyframes × 5 = 175 frames.

**Correct your 96×48.** openage's terrain doc gives a rhombus of **97 px across × 49 rows** (its diagram annotates the widest row as the 25th of 49); note the doc's prose labels are transposed and contradict its own diagram. `frame_id = (x % tc) + ((y % tc) * tc)`, `tc = 10` for the 100-tile terrains; terrain.drs holds 27 SLPs. https://github.com/SFTtech/openage/blob/master/doc/media/terrain.md

Per-frame `slp_frame_info` stores int32 width, height, hotspot_X, hotspot_Y — **sizes are per-frame variable, there is no single "unit sprite size."**

**AoE2 Definitive Edition.** Only sourced original-scale figure is **~100 px high** per unit, from the DE team. Verbatim from https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/rebuilding-a-classic-in-i-age-of-empires-ii-definitive-edition-i-: "Literally every asset in the game had to be remade"; "We didn't have any of the original assets. Those were all lost"; roughly **four times the fidelity**, worked from the old sprites as reference to preserve silhouettes so players still recognise "that unit as being a camel… 20 years later"; and "This game is still 2D. A lot of people think it's 3D now, but it's actually 2D sprites."

Format evolution:
- **SMX** (launch): up to 3 layers per frame — main graphic, shadow, outline — selected by a `frame_type` bitfield, per-frame `palette_number`. Still indexed. https://github.com/SFTtech/openage/blob/master/doc/media/smx-files.md
- **SLD** (build 66692+): **abandons indexed palettes.** DXT1/BC1 main + damage mask, DXT4/BC4 shadow + **player-colour mask**. Up to 5 layers. Player colour is now "technically greyscale images… treated as an index for looking up the actual player color value from a palette." https://github.com/SFTtech/openage/blob/master/doc/media/sld-files.md
- **32 directions** is an **AoE1:DE** figure, not AoE2 DE: "Where the original units would only turn in 8 directions, units now… 32 directions," and "every asset in the game has been rendered 3 times" for HD→4K. https://www.forgottenempires.net/age-of-empires-definitive-edition-is-it-a-3d-or-a-2d-game **Whether AoE2 DE also uses 32: unverified. Do not transfer the claim.**

## Heroes of Might & Magic III

**First, a correction: the HoMM3 adventure map is not isometric.** It is a square **32×32 px** grid (VCMI draws road halves as `Rect(0,16,32,16)` / `Rect(0,0,32,16)` — https://github.com/vcmi/vcmi/blob/develop/client/mapView/MapRenderer.cpp). Battles are a flat hex stage.

**DEF palette = 256 RGB triplets.** Per-sprite header carries format, width, height, fullWidth, fullHeight, leftMargin, topMargin — **per-frame variable, no fixed creature size (unverified)**. https://github.com/vcmi/vcmi/blob/develop/client/render/CDefFile.cpp

**Reserved indices, exact** (https://github.com/vcmi/vcmi/blob/develop/clientsdl2/render/ScalableImage.cpp, comment "First 8 colors in def palette used for transparency"):

| idx | magic RGB in the DEF | engine substitutes |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | (0,255,255) | full transparency |
| 1 | (255,150,255) | shadow border, α=64 (battle + map) |
| 2 | (255,100,255) | shadow border, α=64 (fog of war) |
| 3 | (255,50,255) | shadow body, α=128 (fog of war) |
| 4 | (255,0,255) | shadow body, α=128 (battle + map) |
| 5 | (255,255,0) | **selection / owner flag colour** |
| 6 | (180,0,255) | shadow body below selection, α=128 |
| 7 | (0,255,0) | shadow border below selection, α=64 |

**Player colour = indices 224–255** (https://github.com/vcmi/vcmi/blob/develop/client/render/Graphics.cpp):

```cpp
SDL_SetPaletteColors(targetPalette, palette, 224, 32);  // 32-entry owner ramp
SDL_SetPaletteColors(targetPalette, &color,   5,   1);  // single flag colour at index 5
```

The 32 colours come from `DATA/PLAYERS.PAL` — 8 players × 32 colours, 4 bytes each (4th byte is flags, not alpha), from file offset 24. Unowned uses `config/NEUTRAL.PAL`. Flat player colours: red `ff0000`, blue `3152ff`, tan `9c7352`, green `429429`, orange `ff8400`, purple `8c29a5`, teal `099ca5`, pink `c67b8c`, neutral `848484`.

Net: HoMM3 reserves **8 indices for transparency + two-level shadow, 32 for the owner ramp, 1 for the flag** — 41 of 256.

**3ds Max pipeline: unverified.** The best retrospective (https://www.gamedeveloper.com/production/heroes-of-might-magic-iii-remembering-erathia-15-years-later) names lead artist Phelan Sykes, assistant lead Rebecca Riel, illustrator George Almond, lead animator Adam McCarthy, and "over 10,000 pieces of artwork" — but no software, resolutions or frame counts.

## Disciples II

Weakest evidence of the six, and the weakest structural fit (flat 2D battle stage, 2D strategic grid). **3ds Max pre-render, sprite dimensions, colour counts, frame counts, team colour: all unverified.** GameSpot Designer Diary #9 is the right primary source but 403s: https://www.gamespot.com/articles/disciples-ii-dark-prophecy-designer-diary-9/1100-2801857/. Assets are in `.ff` archives; tools that could reverse the numbers: https://github.com/Vanosz/Disciples2-ROTE-Editor-Releases, https://github.com/VladimirMakeev/D2ModdingToolset. Reference sheets: https://www.spriters-resource.com/pc_computer/disciplesii/

## Facing-direction table

| game | rendered | displayed |
|---|---|---|
| Diablo 1 | 8 | 8 |
| Diablo II | 8 monsters / 16 players | same |
| Fallout 1/2 | 6 | 6 |
| Baldur's Gate | 9 | 16 (mirrored) |
| AoE2 | 5 | 8 (mirrored) |
| AoE1 DE | 32 | 32 |
| AoE2 DE | unverified | unverified |

## What actually keeps units legible on a tiled ground

Ranked by strength of evidence, all verified above:

1. **A dedicated outline layer in the owner's colour** (AoE2 `0x4E`, carried forward into SMX and SLD as a first-class layer). The only mechanism in the whole set documented *as* a readability feature.
2. **A dedicated shadow channel.** AoE2 `0x0B` against a darkened palette; HoMM3 bakes shadow into indices 1–4 at 25%/50% black so the artist paints shadow *as index* and the engine controls opacity.
3. **Team colour as a reserved ramp, never a flat colour.** AoE2 128 indices (16–143), HoMM3 32 + 1, Infinity Engine 84 base + 168 auto-blended.
4. **Lighting by index remap.** Diablo 16 levels × 256 tables; Fallout `intensityColorTable[colour][intensity>>9]`. Quantised contrast bands preserve silhouette edges at small size.
5. **Silhouette preservation as an explicit remaster constraint** (AoE2 DE).

**Explicitly not verified:** top-lighting conventions, fixed key-light angles, outline-width rules, or any written silhouette guideline from any of these six teams. The per-direction sprite sets *imply* a fixed camera and fixed light, but no document I reached says so. Do not invent one.
