# C) HD-2D and modern chunky pixel

Numbers marked **[measured]** come from pixel-measuring community rips (bounding box per frame, unique RGB per frame, edge-pixel histogram, integer-upscale test). Rips may be post-render captures, so colour counts are softer evidence than dimensions.

## Octopath Traveler I / II

Covered in full under family A above (18×32 authored base size; **[measured]** field 16×34 / battle 34×51, OT2 battle **34×56 native**, ~10% taller — which matches director Miyauchi's stated reason: raising character height was needed because "if we only increased the resolution of the background, the characters would look strange," and combat presentation changes a lot with height. https://nintendoeverything.com/octopath-traveler-ii-devs-on-the-games-evolved-use-of-hd-2d-and-more/).

**[measured] outline.** Dominant edge colour `#181818` (RGB 24,24,24), with hue-shifted dark variants (`#301810` warm brown, `#2A1A18` red-brown) on warm regions — black outline with **selective colour-shifted outlining**. 72–77% of edge pixels below luminance 32; 88–96% below 64. That very hard contour is what lets a 16 px-wide sprite survive on a lit, bloom-heavy 3D diorama.

Producer Takahashi on why UE4: "UE4 is very good at both 3D environments and 3D graphics." Asano, 2026: "HD-2D, which was born with Octopath Traveler, has gained recognition over the past eight years" (https://www.dualshockers.com/square-enix-hd-2d-remakes-teased-by-octopath-traveler-asano/). Producers have said HD-2D "costs more than you'd think" (https://nintendoeverything.com/triangle-strategy-producers-say-hd-2d-costs-more-than-youd-think-internal-teams-shared-knowledge-to-help-with-its-implementation/).

## Triangle Strategy (Artdink / Square Enix)

The single most useful entry for your tactics-grid question, because the pixel artist gave literal numbers.

**Outline, verbatim** (Nintendo DREAM pixel-art interview, https://www.ndw.jp/trianglestrategy_pixelart-interview/): 「キャラクターを縁取るアウトラインの一番暗い色は真っ黒ではなく、RGB（※）すべての値が24の黒を使用しています。」 — **the darkest outline colour is not pure black; it is RGB(24,24,24).** Shadows use near-black greys rather than pure black.

**Directions, verbatim, same source:** 「最初に衣装を着せていないキャラクターを8方向分描き、Photoshop上でグルグル回して確認して違和感が出ないように調整しました。」 — base undressed characters drawn in **8 directions**, then rotated in Photoshop to check for discomfort. But: 「スケジュールや工数の都合で8方向のグラフィックを描いたのはセレノア・ロラン・フレデリカ・ベネディクトの4人だけなんです」 — **only four characters (Serenoa, Roland, Frederica, Benedict) actually shipped full 8-direction graphics**, for schedule reasons. Sole tool: Adobe Photoshop. Adding one pose meant duplicating it across every character.

**[measured]** unit sprites **17–22 px wide × 35–41 px tall** (typical 19×38), **29–48 unique colours per frame**, true 1× pixel grid (0.2% of 2×2 blocks uniform). Edge colours `#181818` plus heavy hue-matched dark outlines (`#3E1818`, `#562323` on Frederica's red dress) — more selective outlining than Octopath, because units must read against many ground types from four camera angles. https://www.spriters-resource.com/pc_computer/trianglestrategy/

**Why Artdink got the job**, and the design rule that falls out of it (https://nintendoeverything.com/triangle-strategy-devs-on-how-the-game-uses-accurate-hd-2d/): Square Enix had several studios make HD-2D demos; Acquire judged only Artdink's "accurate," because Artdink "prepared a deformed image at the writing material level, before adding realistic effects to 'build it up'." Asano: "If you reduce a photorealistic image, it looks as if you're simply lowering the image quality." And the explicit fidelity cap: **"As the proportions change to look more realistic, the resolution increases and the pixels become smaller, making them look more like illustrations rather than pixel art."** They capped sprite fidelity on purpose.

The rotatable camera was the hard part — Asano: "Octopath Traveler had a fixed camera, but in tactical RPGs, you need to be able to rotate the map 360 degrees." https://www.destructoid.com/triangle-strategy-interview-producers-asano-arai-square-enix-hd-2d-tactics-rpg/

**Grid takeaway: ~19 × 38 px is what Square Enix shipped as a readable unit on a rotatable tactics grid.**

## Live A Live remake (2022)

Best technical source is Square Enix's own **UNREAL FEST WEST '22** talk, written up at https://gamemakers.jp/article/2023_02_21_30973/. Concrete techniques:

- **Deliberately weaker DOF and vignette** than Octopath ("strong DoF + vignette + shallow tone colour"), because the camera moves backwards often and the game wants a hot, not dreamy, feel. Chromatic aberration added as a modern touch.
- **Boss silhouette trick:** the main dot art is displayed with **two additional enlarged copies of the same dot art stacked behind it** to strengthen the contour.
- **Grounding indoors:** no DirectionalLight indoors, so circular shadows are drawn as **decals**, intensity tuned per map.
- **Readability on the checker battle grid:** players could not tell which squares a monster occupied, so **the shadow cast on grid tiles was made part of the attack-valid range** — the shadow *is* the hitbox display.
- Pipeline: GrayBox → rough model/light using the original pixel art → final model + sprite after level sign-off, because HD-2D uniquely needs modellers and pixel artists on the same asset.
- Rendering: moved from **deferred to mobile forward** mid-project; **FXAA and screen percentage both held at 100%** to preserve dot fidelity.
- Scale: 560+ skills, 307 built from reusable subsequences across motion (99), effects (177), camera (111), hit lighting (68), screen effects (13), field lighting (3).

**[measured]** field/NPC sprites **19–23 × 27–32 px** (typical 20×28), **21 colours per frame**, 46 per character sheet, native 1×. Outline `#181818` plus warm dark variants. So Live A Live is the **chunkiest and lowest-colour** of the Square Enix HD-2D set, sitting *below* Octopath's field height. https://www.spriters-resource.com/nintendo_switch/livealive/

Tokita on why HD-2D over 3D: a full 3D remake "would have changed the look too much." https://nintendoeverything.com/live-a-live-dev-on-remakes-origins-why-its-hd-2d/ SNES-vs-remake pixel delta: **unverified**.

## Sea of Stars (Sabotage)

Sabotage's own press kit: "Our custom-made render pipeline allows the creation of a breathtaking world coming to life by pushing the limits of 2D pixel-art games," with full dynamic lighting. https://sabotagestudio.com/presskits/sea-of-stars/

Thierry Boulanger: "With the bigger pieces, we really went full-on pixel art. No shortcuts." / "It's full screen, the pixel art is point by point." / animations "took weeks, they took over a month, each of them" / on lighting: "It gave volume to the environment." https://screenrant.com/sea-stars-interview-thierry-boulanger/ One engineer (Jeakim Hamel) owned dynamic lighting from 2018 onward, and "the pipeline and all production assets had to answer to the technical needs of the dynamic lighting." https://mobilesyrup.com/2023/09/11/sea-of-stars-level-design-sabotage-studio-thierry-boulanger-interview/ Art overview: https://www.megavisions.net/the-art-of-sea-of-stars-a-sea-of-pixels/

**Unverified and commonly mis-stated:** normal maps (every "Sea of Stars uses normal maps" source is inference; Sabotage only say "custom render pipeline" + "dynamic lighting"); **internal resolution** — the widely repeated **640×360 traces to Steam forum speculation, do not print it**; sprite dimensions and colour counts (no rips available).

## Eiyuden Chronicle: Hundred Heroes

Unity, fully 3D environments with 2D pixel characters. Producer/AD Junichi Murakami: they chose "an evolved pixel art style that does not depict everything in a realistic style," and Murayama insisted it read as "100% new artistic creation," not nostalgia. Character formats deliberately differ per character so personalities read distinctly. **Merging 2D sprites with 3D environments was "actually very, very, very hard" and took about two years**, because 3D camera angles must not break the 2D read. https://news.xbox.com/en-us/2024/04/23/talking-creative-minds-behind-eiyuden-chronicle-hundred-heroes/, https://www.cgmagonline.com/interviews/eiyuden-chronicle-hundred-heroes-murayama/

Suikoden lineage is literal: Murayama (design/scenario), **Junko Kawano** (character design, Suikoden I & II), Murakami, Komuta.

**Sprite resolution, colour count, outline: all unverified.** No rips, no dev figures.

## Tactics Ogre: Reborn — and the answer to "upscaled or redrawn"

**It is explicitly not HD-2D.** Producer Hiroaki Kato: "No, we didn't think about making it HD-2D." They considered 3D, rejected it, and kept the original's "really well-done pixel art," bringing "that sort of resolution and that sort of fidelity to new hardware." https://www.nintendolife.com/news/2022/09/tactics-ogre-reborn-producer-we-didnt-think-about-making-it-hd-2d Minagawa (AD) and Yoshida (character art) returned.

**[measured] — this settles it:**
- PSP *Let Us Cling Together* (2010) battle frames: **~14–18 × 26–27 px**, 21–32 colours/frame. https://www.spriters-resource.com/psp/tacticsogreletusclingtogether/
- Reborn battle frames: **60–68 × 100–112 px** (typical 64×104), **27–32 colours/frame**, 448–454 colours per full sheet. https://www.spriters-resource.com/pc_computer/tacticsogrereborn/
- Ratio is almost exactly **4× linear** — but **not** a nearest-neighbour 4× upscale: only **36% of 4×4 blocks are uniform**, while **84% of 2×2 blocks are uniform**. A naive 4× filter would score ~100% on the 4×4 test. Reading: the art sits on an effective **2× chunky pixel grid with a real minority of 1×-resolution detail and cleanup** — i.e. redrawn at higher resolution in the original style, exactly as claimed.
- **Outline is the interesting deviation:** edge pixels are overwhelmingly `#302820` (48,40,32) — a **dark warm grey-brown, not black**. Mean edge luminance 57–58 vs Octopath's 32–38. Reborn deliberately softens the contour relative to the HD-2D games.

Pre-release detail comparison: https://wccftech.com/tactics-ogre-reborn-early-comparison-highlights-redrawn-sprites-and-backgrounds/

## Into the Breach (Subset Games)

**Grid: 8×8 tiles per battle.** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Into_the_Breach The small board made 100 hand-designed maps cheaper than procedural generation: https://thinkygames.com/games/into-the-breach/

**Justin Ma on readability — the quotable material** (https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/-i-into-the-breach-i-dev-on-ui-design-sacrifice-cool-ideas-for-the-sake-of-clarity-every-time-):
- "As a game design principle, we would sacrifice cool ideas for the sake of clarity every time."
- "Our requirement that the player has to understand what's going on in any situation restricted our game design options considerably."
- On the playtest failure that forced it: "You could just see all these damage indicators all over the map. We were fine with that because we knew exactly what every enemy did… but it was very clear, as soon as we handed it to someone else, that we needed to make it very clear who was doing what."
- On animated tooltips: "I still think it's the most important decision we made about this. You could type out a hundred times, 'Damages a tile and pushes adjacent tiles,' but showing that little animation of them moving is a thousand times more effective."

GDC 2019 "Into the Breach Design Postmortem" (Matthew Davis) is paywalled: https://www.gdcvault.com/play/1025772/-Into-the-Breach-Design; free write-up https://80.lv/articles/gdc-2019-an-inside-look-at-into-the-breach

**[measured] mech sprite size** (bounding boxes from game-ripped PNGs via the wiki's MediaWiki API): **33–47 px wide × 26–50 px tall, typical ~42 × 36**. Combat Mech 42×35, Artillery 44×34, Siege 41×26, Jet 35×42, Electric 44×50; Vek: Beetle 39×33, Hornet 33×49, Scarab 36×39. **Colour counts and outline treatment unverified** (Cloudflare blocked downloads; assets live in `resource.dat`, extractable with the FTL unpacker: https://steamcommunity.com/app/590380/discussions/0/2650805212055481389/). Modder-practical figure: custom mechs built at 60×52, needing normal / no-shadow / hangar-highlight / idle / broken / water / broken-water variants (https://subsetgames.com/forum/viewtopic.php?t=32923).

**The design lesson, and it is the most transferable one here:** ITB puts a ~42×36 px unit on an 8×8 board and then puts *all* tactical state into overlays — arrows, damage previews, tile highlights, animated tooltips. The sprite only has to answer "which mech is this": silhouette plus one accent colour. The UI carries everything else.

## Unicorn Overlord (Vanillaware)

**Not pixel art.** Hand-painted parts animated as jointed puppets. Kamitani, in Gamasutra's "King of 2D" (https://www.gamedeveloper.com/business/king-of-2d-vanillaware-s-george-kamitani): the studio built a **proprietary character editor over about a year, "largely based off Flash and other well-known packages"**; complex creatures that look 3D use a hand-shaping method they call **"tebineri"**; and critically — **original artwork is drawn at roughly double display size and compressed down**, which is why moving to HD "wouldn't require substantial additional effort."

Unicorn Overlord specifics: conceived by **Takafumi Noma** in 2014, who was director, programmer and lead artist; ~10-year development. https://www.inverse.com/gaming/unicorn-overlord-interview-vanillaware, https://automaton-media.com/en/news/20240307-28225/

**Any pixel resolution figure for Unicorn Overlord: unverified.** The only defensible statement is Kamitani's "~2× display size, then compressed."

---

# Minimum pixels per character for silhouette readability

**There is no canonical industry rule.** I checked the canonical references directly and they give principles, not thresholds. Report it that way.

**What named artists actually say:**

- **Raymond Schlitter (SLYNYRD)** is the most concrete. His working standard is **16×32 px** — "1 tile wide by 2 tiles tall is one of the most common sprite sizes, and is the size I've chosen" — sized from the tile unit, because "basing the character size on tile units allows the sprite to naturally fit in the grid-like structure of the tile based world." Head takes **a third to half** of sprite height to keep expression readable. https://www.slynyrd.com/blog/2019/10/21/pixelblog-22-top-down-character-sprites His floor case runs an **8 px-tall figure** on an 8×8 tilemap, where "everything is there for basic readability… the sense of wonder is peaked by the lack of detail." https://www.slynyrd.com/blog/2023/11/26/pixelblog-47-tiny-pixels
- **Kiwi (2dwillneverdie)** gives the one hard threshold I found: **"When the sprite's under 50 pixels, don't draw leopard spots."** Below that the goal shifts from accuracy to instant recognition: "Use fewer details and more contrast. Use fewer colors that aren't close to each other." He calls ~120 px "an absolutely fantastic size" for fighter sprites. https://2dwillneverdie.com/tutorial/fix-my-sprite-volume-3/
- **Derek Yu**: start small, because "the hard part is learning how to cram a lot of detail into a few pixels," and "even large sprites never usually exceed 200 by 200 pixels." http://makegames.tumblr.com/post/42648699708/pixel-art-tutorial
- **"Pixel Parmesan"** refuses a number and gives a two-question framework instead: *what is the smallest necessary detail, and how many pixels does that detail need in this style?* Default heuristic: "if in doubt, go smaller." https://pixelparmesan.com/blog/choosing-the-right-resolution-for-your-pixel-art
- **Arne (androidarts)** — the most-cited pixel art tutorial — gives **no numeric minimum at all**. It is explicit about contrast instead: "it's possible to skip outlines all together and simply rely on color contrast to separate things." https://androidarts.com/pixtut/pixelart.htm
- **Cyangmou's "Readability – Pixel Art Style Possibilities"** is the one tutorial explicitly on this topic, indexed at https://lospec.com/pixel-art-tutorials/readability-pixel-art-style-possibilities-by-cyangmou — **the DeviantArt original is now 404**, so I could not read the chart and will not paraphrase it.
- **Michafrar, *Pixel Logic*** has a dedicated **Ch. 4 "Readability"**. https://pixellogicbook.com/

**The empirical anchor is stronger than any tutorial.** Shipped, verified numbers:

| use | size |
|---|---|
| readable tactics unit on a grid | **~16–22 × 27–41 px** (Octopath field 16×34, Live A Live 20×28, Triangle Strategy 19×38) |
| battle-scale pixel character | **~34 × 51–56 px** (Octopath) |
| chunky mech on an 8×8 board | **~42 × 36 px** (Into the Breach) |
| high-res tactics unit | **~64 × 104 px** (Tactics Ogre Reborn) |
| side-scroll action character | **50 px** (Dead Cells), **~38–42 px** (DKC), **39 px** (Owlboy, unverified) |
| historic tactics reference | FFT sheet **256×488**, body-part assembled |

Note that everything under 22 px wide is humanoid/biped. Into the Breach buys readability with a **wider, blockier mass** plus overlays, not with more pixels.

**From the strategy-art side (qualitative but well-sourced).** Blizzard artist Matt McDaid names readability as the single most important element and lists six sub-elements: **"Scale & proportions, Silhouette, Lighting, Color, Exaggeration, Composition."** His working method is consolidating high-frequency detail into low-frequency detail — "If you're texturing a 10 × 2 piece of wood… and it has 4 small nails hammered through the end, maybe just paint 2 larger, chunkier ones instead?" https://80.lv/articles/matt-mcdaid-mastering-the-stylized-art Riot states the silhouette test outright: "Silhouettes are the single most important thing for champion recognition in League. This is basically a champion's shadow: What do they look like shrouded in darkness?" — with one "defining primary characteristic that's unique to that champion" that never changes. https://www.leagueoflegends.com/en-us/news/dev/clarity-in-league/

**Do not cite** spritegen.io, sprixen.com, sprite-ai.art, pixnote.net, spritesheets.ai or generalistprogrammer.com. They dominate current search results for "minimum sprite size," have no named author, and confidently state fabricated figures like "6–12 colours per character."

---

# Shades per material

**Derek Yu gives the hard rule you were looking for:** "Use at most two shades of dark (dark and really dark), and two shades of light (light and really light) on top of your foundation color." That is a **5-step maximum ramp: base + 2 shadow + 2 highlight.** Plus: "The more colors you use, the more distracted your sprite will look. To make a sprite stand out, use only two or three main colors." No pillow-shading, no gradients. http://makegames.tumblr.com/post/42648699708/pixel-art-tutorial

**A step-count table with explicit use cases** (https://art-pia.com/guide-light-shadow-en.html — a studio guide, not a first-party game source, so weight it accordingly):

| steps | use | quoted |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | basic shapes | "splits into two faces; flat" |
| **3** | **standard** | "the minimum for volume" / "the standard for most motifs: characters, clothing, tools" |
| 4 | focal points | "the focal point of the picture, metal or ceramic surfaces" |
| 5+ | large subjects | "a large canvas showing a single subject" |

Its budgeting rule is the useful part: "the single highest-return color you can spend is the third step," and **"five motifs at three steps each will beat one motif at five steps."**

**Per-character limits from named artists.** Schlitter, for a 16×16 style: **"I limited the palette to 3 colors in addition to the outline per character"** (https://www.slynyrd.com/blog/2022/1/25/pixelblog-36-8-bit-adventure). Kiwi cites an artist holding **"no more than 5 different colors per palette"** on 48×48 sprites (https://2dwillneverdie.com/tutorial/fix-my-sprite-volume-3/). Saint11 keeps it non-numeric: "keep your color count low," ramps belong on rounded shapes while flat faces stay uniform to avoid banding (https://saint11.art/pixel_art_articles/article4/).

**Palette-construction ramps are a different number.** Schlitter's general-purpose palette uses **9 swatches per ramp, ~20° hue shift per step, 8 ramps, 128 colours** — but he adds "I never use a lot of colors for any one image." Do not confuse ramp length with per-sprite usage. https://www.slynyrd.com/blog/2018/1/10/pixelblog-1-color-palettes Arne: "Unless you are working with very small palettes (say, 3 colors), you probably need to set up color ramps," never build ramp ends from pure black/white, hue-shift instead — skin is "shadow a grayish warm purple… mid tone orange, and the light almost yellowish." https://androidarts.com/pixtut/pixelart.htm

**Cross-check against shipped work [measured].** A whole Octopath character sheet is **81 colours** across every frame and direction; one field frame uses **27**; Live A Live field frame **21**; Tactics Ogre Reborn 64×104 battle frame **27–32**; Triangle Strategy 19×38 unit frames **29–48**. So production sprites land at roughly **20–35 colours per whole character**, which across 5–8 materials is **3–5 shades per material** — Derek Yu's rule, confirmed empirically.

Curated named-artist shading tutorials: https://lospec.com/pixel-art-tutorials/tags/shading (ENDESGA's "Quicktip: Highlights" is specifically about shading changing per material).

---

# Four premises in your brief that are wrong

1. **Octopath Traveler is not a 3D-to-sprite pipeline.** It is hand-drawn pixel art, decomposed into an articulated puppet, animated with Photoshop Puppet Warp, hand-fixed at pixel level, then billboarded in UE4. Remove it from family A; it only belongs in C.
2. **Dead Cells has no systematic hand-clean pass.** Vasseur lists hand-cleaning as a cost they *refused*, accepting flickering pixels and reduced detail in exchange for speed.
3. **Tactics Ogre Reborn is explicitly not HD-2D** — producer Kato says so directly. It is also not an upscale: the 4×4 uniformity test (36%) rules that out.
4. **AoE2's tile is ~97×49, not 96×48**, and **HoMM3's adventure map is a square 32×32 grid, not isometric.** Also, Unicorn Overlord is not pixel art, and Diablo 1's "3D Studio" attribution is unverified (it is verified for Diablo II only).

**Sources that block automated fetching** and are worth opening in a browser yourself: the Unreal Engine Octopath II developer interview (https://www.unrealengine.com/en-US/developer-interviews/octopath-traveler-ii-builds-a-bigger-bolder-world-in-its-stunning-hd-2d-style), the NMA Fallout technology thread, the Disciples II Designer Diary #9, Square Enix's OT2 press hub, and the Hollywood Reporter Blasphemous interview.

# Academic metrics for board-game quality / interestingness / fun

Strength key: **[S]** peer-reviewed + explicit formula · **[M]** peer-reviewed, prose definition only · **[W]** blog/assertion/secondary.

---

## 1. Browne — LUDI (thesis 2008 + IEEE TCIAIG 2010)

Primary sources:
- Thesis PDF: https://eprints.qut.edu.au/17025/1/Cameron_Browne_Thesis.pdf (landing https://eprints.qut.edu.au/17025/). Criteria are **Ch. 8 §8.4, pp. 100–124**.
- Browne & Maire, "Evolutionary Game Design", IEEE TCIAIG 2(1):1–16, 2010. PDF: https://eprints.qut.edu.au/31909/1/c31909.pdf · DOI 10.1109/TCIAIG.2010.2041928
- Book: Springer, *Evolutionary Game Design*, ISBN 978-1-4471-2178-7 — http://www.springer.com/computer/ai/book/978-1-4471-2178-7
- Browne's site is **cambolbro.com** (not cameronbrowne.co.uk): http://cambolbro.com/

**57 criteria total: 16 intrinsic (from rules) + 30 quality (from play) + 11 viability (from outcomes)** [S, thesis p.100].

**Notation** (thesis §8.3, pp. 98–100): `G` = number of self-play trials; `M_g` = moves in game g; `M_gr` = number of *random* opening moves (variety is injected by playing the first R moves at random, not by eval noise); `M_gi` = intelligent (non-random) moves; `E(m_n) ∈ [0..1]` = board evaluation at move n (1 = win, 0 = no progress); **lead history** = eventual-winner eval minus eventual-loser eval per move, range `[-1..1]`; `E_co`/`E_oc` = current-over-opponent / opponent-over-current lead; `E_w`/`E_l` = winner/loser eval; `ES_c` = shallow (1-ply) eval, `ED_c` = deep (N-ply alpha-beta) eval. Nearly every quality criterion is a mean-over-trials of a per-trial mean.

### Quality criteria (verbatim formulas, transcribed to ASCII)

- **Branching factor** `A_bf = Σ_g min(1, [log10( Σ_{n=0}^{Mg-1} moves(m_n) / M_g ) + 1] / 2) / G` — "/2 to set a range limit of approximately 100 moves".
- **Response time** `A_rt` — same shape with `time(m_n)` seconds, `/2` → ~100 s limit.
- **Move effort** `A_me` — same shape with `nodes(m_n)`, `/6` → ~1,000,000 nodes limit.
- **Search penetration** `A_spen` — mean of `Σ_i depth(i)² / nodes(m_n)`, log10-normalised `/2`. Practical range only `[0..0.277]` for 4-ply search.
- **Clarity (variance)** `A_var = Σ_g [ Σ_{n=Mgr}^{Mg-1} VE_c(m_n) / (M_gi − 1) ] / G`, where `VE_c` = variance in evaluations of the moves available. Note: Browne found high clarity correlates with **low** variance + a few outliers, not high variance.
- **Clarity (narrowness)**: `narrowness(n) = count_{0≤r<moves(m_n)}( E_c(m_nr) > Ē_c(m_n) + 0.75 × (E_cmax(m_n) − Ē_c(m_n)) ) / moves(m_n)`; then `A_narr = Σ_g [ 1 − Σ narrowness(n)/(M_gi − 1) ] / G`.
- **Convergence**: linear-regression slope of branching factor vs move number; `A_conv = Σ_g (1 − (slope(g)/2 + 0.5)) / G`.
- **Uncertainty (overall / early / late)** — area between the lead plot and the "line of average certainty" from (0,0) to (M,1), sampled at `S = 100` points, `t = s/(S−1)`:
  - overall `A_unco = Σ_{s=0}^{S-1} [ min(1, (t − Σ_g E_co(m_{tMg})/G) / t) ] / S`
  - early `A_unce` = same but multiplied by `(1−t)/t` (weights the opening)
  - late `A_uncl` = same without the `/t` (weights the endgame)
  - Range `[-1..1]`, −1 = maximum certainty. Browne explicitly *rejected* Májek & Iida's [2004] entropy-based uncertainty as needing ~4,000 trials per measurement.
- **Drama (average)** `A_drav = Σ_g [ Σ_{n=Mgr+1}^{Mg-1} ( sqrt(E_l(m_n) − E_w(m_n)) if E_w < E_l else 0 ) / count(E_w(m_n) < E_l(m_n)) ] / G`. **Drama (maximum)** `A_drax` = same with `max` instead of the mean. "The square root of the lead difference is taken in each case to emphasise larger dramatic steps."
- **Killer moves** `A_km = Σ_g max_{Mgr≤n≤Mg-1}( [E_c(m_n) − E_o(m_n)] − [E_o(m_{n-1}) − E_c(m_{n-1})] ) / G` — the single largest *relative* swing per trial (a killer move = gain for mover **combined with** loss for opponent).
- **Permanence** `A_perm = Σ_g [ 1 − Σ_{n=Mgr+1}^{Mg-1} ((E_co(m_n) − E_oc(m_{n-1})) − (E_oc(m_{n-1}) − E_co(m_{n-2}))) / (M_gi − 2) ] / G` — measured over move *triplets*, so magnitude of both the hit and the correction counts.
- **Lead change** `A_lead = Σ_g [ Σ_{n=Mgr+1}^{Mg} (1 if leader(m_n) ≠ leader(m_{n-1}) else 0) / (M_gi − 1) ] / G` — zero-crossings of the lead plot.
- **Stability** `A_stab = Σ_g [ Σ_{n=Mgr+1}^{Mg-1} (|E_W(m_n) − E_W(m_{n-1})| + |E_B(m_n) − E_B(m_{n-1})|) / (M_gi − 2) ] / G`.
- **Coolness** `A_cool = Σ_g [ Σ_{n=Mgr+1}^{Mg-1} ( 0 if E_c(m_n) − E_o(m_{n-1}) ≥ 0 else |E_c(m_n) − E_o(m_{n-1})| ) / (M_g − 2) ] / G` — average forced self-harm (zugzwang-ish); Browne calls the pathology a "cold war".
- **Decisiveness threshold** `A_thr = max_{1≤g≤G, Mgr≤n≤Mg-1}( E_l(m_{n,g}) − E_w(m_{n,g}) )` — "the maximum lead that a player achieves *without* realising victory". Single value across all trials.
- **Decisiveness** `A_dec = 1 − Σ_g ((M_gd − M_g)/M_g) / G`, where `M_gd` = move at which the threshold is first reached.
- **Depth (discrepancy)** `A_disc = Σ_g [ Σ |ED_c(m_n) − ES_c(m_n)| / (M_gi − 2) ] / G` — deep vs 1-ply eval gap.
- **Board coverage** `A_bcov = Σ_g (cells_visited(g) / TotalCells) / G`.
- **Momentum (1/2/3)** `A_mom = Σ_g [ count_{Mgr+2≤n≤Mg-3}(E_co(m_{n-2}) < E_co(m_n) ∧ E_co(m_n) < E_co(m_{n+2})) / count(E_co(m_{n-2}) < E_co(m_n)) ] / G`. Momentum(2)/(3) require runs of 3 / 4 consecutive lead increases.
- **Correction (1/2/3)** `A_corr = − Σ_g [ Σ_{n=Mgr+2}^{Mg-2} (E_co(m_n) − E_co(m_{n+2})) / count(E_co(m_n) > E_co(m_{n-2})) ] / G`. Range `[-1..1]`. *Deliberately measured by value while momentum is measured by count*, so the two are not simple negations. (The user's "correlation" criterion = this **Correction**.)
- **Control** `A_ctrl = Σ_g [ Σ_{n=Mgr+1}^{Mg-1} ( narrowness(n) − (1 − A_narr) if E_co(m_n) > 0.1 else 0 ) / count(E_co(m_n) > 0.1) ] / G`. Range `[-1..1]`.
- **Foulup factor** `A_foul = Σ_g [ Σ_{n=Mgr+1}^{Mg-1} count(ES_c(m_n) ≥ ED_c(m_n)) / count(m_n) / (M_gi − 1) ] / G` — chance the obvious move isn't the best one.
- **Puzzle quality** `A_puzq = Σ_g [ better(m_n) / (moves(m_n) − 1) ] / G` — counter-intuitiveness of the solution (Sam Loyd criterion). Puzzles built by: play random to 75% of avg length → play depth≥3 to a win → step back 3 moves → full depth-3 expansion → minimax. Slowest criterion.
- **Puzzle potential** `A_puzp = Σ_g [ min(1, log10(moves(m_n))) / 2^(lines(m_n)−1) ] / G`.

### Viability criteria (all trivially computable)
`wins_W`, `wins_B`, `wins_1`, `wins_2`, `wins_0` (draws), `wins_E` (expected-player wins):
- **Completion** `A_comp = (wins_W + wins_B)/G`
- **Balance** `A_bal = 1 − |wins_W − wins_B| / (wins_W + wins_B)`
- **Advantage** `A_adv = |wins_1 − (wins_W+wins_B)/2| / ((wins_W+wins_B)/2)`
- **Drawishness** `A_draw = wins_0/G`
- **Timeouts** `A_tout = 1 − (wins_0 + wins_1 + wins_2)/G`
- **Duration** `A_durn = Σ_g |M_pref − M_g| / M_pref / G` — deviation from preferred length (`M_pref` = half max length; = 60 in the IEEE paper). *Larger = worse.*
- **Depth (skill level)** `A_skil = wins_E/G` with one player's search reduced by **one ply** (deliberately small, so the shallow player can still occasionally win).
- **Selfishness** `A_self = wins_E/G` vs an opponent evaluating only its own pieces.
- **Obstructive play** `A_obst = wins_E/G` vs an opponent evaluating only the opponent's pieces.
- **Resilience** `A_res = wins_E/G` vs a search-depth-0 (random) player.
- Intrinsic: **Complexity** `A_comp = min(1, log10(count(pieces) + 4·count(end) + 1)/2)` + 7 boolean movement types + 8 boolean goal types.

### The empirical result (this is the load-bearing part) [S]
79 sample games, 57 subjects, paired comparisons → human preference ranking; linear regression + leave-one-out CV. **Table 11.1 (thesis p.149):** corr_s / corr_r — All 57: **0.4172 / 0.4256**; Intrinsic 16: **0.0941 / 0.1145**; Quality 30: **0.4264 / 0.4366**; Viability 11: **0.5932 / 0.6086**; Best 17: **0.8208 / 0.8276**; Best 16: 0.7942 / 0.7986.

**Best-17 predictor set with signed weights** (Fig. 11.3, thesis p.150 — a raster figure, transcribed from the rendered page):
Goal(group) +0.0818 · Goal(stack) −0.0804 · Goal(block) −0.1055 · Piece capture +0.0585 · Convergence −0.0221 · **Clarity(variance) −0.3763** · **Uncertainty(late) +0.2023** · **Drama(average) +0.2167** · **Killer moves +0.3585** · Permanence +0.1027 · **Lead change −0.2769** · Decisiveness threshold +0.1311 · Momentum(1) +0.1244 · Correction(1) +0.1622 · Puzzle quality +0.0826 · Completion +0.0788 · Duration −0.0907 · **Bias −0.2576**.

**Ablation (Fig. 11.4, p.151)** — prediction error when each is removed (baseline 13.28%): Uncertainty(late) **48.79%** ≫ Lead change 36.45% > Permanence 28.09% > Completion 23.10% > Killer moves 23.09% > Duration 20.88% > Clarity(variance) 19.16% > Drama(avg) 17.06% > Goal(block) 16.98% > Decisiveness threshold 16.55% > Momentum(1) 16.42% > Piece capture 15.16% > Correction(1) 15.10% > Convergence 14.11% > Goal(group) 14.10% > Goal(stack) 13.83% > Puzzle quality 13.68% (least important; dropped → "best 16").

IEEE paper §VII names six standouts: *uncertainty; lead change (negative correlation); permanence; killer moves; completion; duration* — "participants appear to prefer stable games with uncertain outcomes that end within a reasonable number of moves, and in which strong moves are reasonably permanent."

Validation: mean score error 14.1% of range; mean ranking error 8.9/79 positions (11.2%). Synthesis: 1389 games evolved, 19 viable (98.7% attrition), predicted-vs-human correlation **−0.6491** [95% CI −0.851..−0.274] on the held-out evolved games. Yavalath ranked #2 of 19 by humans. **Viability thresholding (Table 12.1):** Duration is by far the strongest single viability filter; Completion alone is surprisingly weak.

**Caveat worth flagging:** n=79 games, 57 subjects, one rule language, criteria selected by search *on the same 79 games* then hand-tuned — so 0.82 is partly in-sample selection. The 19-game holdout at −0.65 is the honest number.

### Related: Browne, "Elegance in Game Design", IEEE TCIAIG 4(2):229–240, 2012
PDF: http://cambolbro.com/cv/publications/browne-elegance.pdf. Prose says elegance = **max**(simplicity, clarity, efficiency) and shibui = **min**(simplicity, clarity, efficiency, depth), but the typeset equations (1) and (2) print min/max **swapped** — an apparent erratum; §5.5.1 confirms elegance is "the maximum of". State-space complexity normalised as `C_ss(g) = log10(SS(g))/50` clamped to [0..1].

---

## 2. Iida — game refinement theory

**Derivation** (Nossal & Iida, IEEE GEM 2014, open author copy: https://dspace.jaist.ac.jp/dspace/bitstream/10119/12742/1/21333.pdf) [S]:
> "game progress x(t) will be given as a linear function of time t … `x(t) = (G/T)·t`" (1); the in-game model is `x(t) = G·(t/T)^n` (2); "acceleration … `x''(T) = Gn(n−1)/T^n · t^{n−2} = (G/T²)·n(n−1)`"; "we use its root square, **√G / T**, as a game refinement measure … We can call it **GR** value for short."

Board-game form (Li Siqi doctoral dissertation, JAIST 2025, supervisor Iida — https://dspace02.jaist.ac.jp/dspace/bitstream/10119/19922/2/paper.pdf, Eq. 2.1/3.1) [S]:
> `GR = √B / D = √(2G) / T = √a` — "B represents the average branching factor … D stands for game length, or the depth of the entire game tree. G is the average number of successful scores, and T is the average number of attempts per game. `√a` symbolizes the acceleration of game velocity."

Motion-in-mind reformulation (same source, Eqs. 2.2, 6.3–6.8; original = Iida & Khalid, "Using Games to Study Law of Motions in Mind", *IEEE Access* 8, 2020, CC-BY, DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2020.3012597, DOAJ record https://doaj.org/article/298bd2db7f01496295b74c09bf831e3b):
- velocity `v = B/(2D) = G/T = 1 − m` (m = "mass" = difficulty of solving uncertainty)
- acceleration `a = 2G/T²`, `GR = √a`
- jerk `j = 6G/T³ = 3B/D³`, `AD = ∛j`
- reward frequency `N = 1/v`; PRE(η) = η·T/N²; MEE = a/a₀ = √N

**Reported values** [S, dissertation Table 6.1 and Nossal & Iida Table III]:

| Game | B | D | GR (=√a) | AD (=∛j) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Chess | 35 | 80 | **0.074** | 0.059 |
| Shogi | 80 | 115 | **0.078** | 0.054 |
| Go | 250 | 208 | **0.076** | 0.044 |
| Basketball | — | — | 0.073 | — |
| Soccer | — | — | 0.073 | — |
| Badminton (old 15-pt side-out) | G=30.070 | T=45.154 | 0.121 | — |
| Badminton (current 21-pt rally) | G=46.336 | T=79.344 | 0.086 | — |
| Table tennis pre-2000 / post-2000 | 57.869/101.530, 54.863/96.465 | | 0.075 / 0.077 | — |
| Table tennis team event | 131.283 | 232.123 | 0.049 | — |

**"Sophisticated zone" = GR ∈ [0.07, 0.08]** — stated verbatim in both sources; the AD companion zone is [0.045, 0.06]. Note: the zone is an *observation over a handful of games*, not a derived result. The 0.07–0.08 claim is peer-reviewed but the causal/normative interpretation ("this range is fun") is **[W]** — it's an inference from ~6 games plus the sophistication-population paradox literature (https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-46100-7_28). Original INTETAIN 2014 derivation: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-08189-2_22.

Independent cross-reference worth knowing: DeepMind's chess-variant paper cites Iida et al. (2003) for the hypothesis that the number of *candidate* moves `m(s) ≈ √M(s)` where M is legal moves — the same √B that drives GR.

---

## 3. Ludii (Digital Ludeme Project) evaluation metrics

The authoritative list is the **source**, not a paper: https://github.com/Ludeme/Ludii/tree/master/Evaluation/src/metrics. All are `Metric` subclasses with a name, a one-line description and a declared range. UI: *Evaluation Dialog* (Shift+E), plus canned "Evaluation UCT 10/30/50 trials" — see https://ludii.games/downloads/LudiiUserGuide.pdf §on the Analysis menu.

**single/outcome** — Completion "Percentage of games which have a winner (not draw or timeout)" [0,1]; Drawishness "…end in a draw (not including timeouts)"; Timeouts; AdvantageP1 "Percentage of games where player 1 won. Draws and multi-player results calculated as partial wins"; **Balance** "Similarity between player win-rates" — implemented as `1 − maxDisc` where win credit per player is `(agentUtility+1)/2` and `maxDisc` is the largest pairwise win-rate gap; OutcomeUniformity "Inverse of the per-player variance in outcomes over all trials, averaged over all players".

**single/stateEvaluation** — **Lead Change** "Percentage number of times the expected winner changes" — per trial: count of states where the set of argmax-evaluation players differs from the previous state, ÷ number of real moves. **Stability** "Average variance in each player's state evaluation" (per-player variance of the eval series, summed over players, averaged over trials). **Clarity Narrowness** "The percentage of legal moves that have an evaluation value at least 75% above the difference between the max move evaluation value and average move evaluation value" — i.e. threshold `mean + 0.75·(max − mean)`; identical to Browne's 2008 narrowness. **Clarity Variance**. **Decisiveness Threshold** "Maximum state evaluation value achieved by non-winning player"; **Decisiveness Moves** "Percentage number of moves after a winning player has a state evaluation above the decisiveness threshold".

**single/complexity** — Decision Moves "Percentage number of states in the trial where there was more than 1 possible move"; Game Tree Complexity; State Space Complexity.
**single/boardCoverage** — Default / Full (cell+vertex+edge) / Used (auto-detected from rules): "Percentage of … board sites which a piece was placed on at some point".
**single/duration** — Duration Actions / Moves / Turns / Turns Std Dev / Turns Not Timeouts.
**single/stateRepetition** — Positional Repetition, Situational Repetition.
**multiple/metrics** (each emitted in **11 flavours** via `MultiMetricValue`: Average, Median, Max, Min, Variance, ChangeAverage, ChangeSign, ChangeLineBestFit, ChangeNumTimes, MaxIncrease, MaxDecrease) — **Drama** "Difference between the winning player's state evaluation and the maximum state evaluation of any player" (per-state series; so "Drama Average", "Drama Max", etc.); Branching Factor; Decision Factor ("number of possible moves, when greater than 1"); Board Sites Occupied; Move Distance; Move Evaluation; Piece Number; Score Difference; State Evaluation Difference.
**designer/** — Ideal Duration ("based on an ideal range"), Skill Trace.

Papers that use these: *Foundations of Digital Archæoludology* https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.13516 (strategic depth / drama / decisiveness / uncertainty as plausibility priors for reconstructing lost rule sets — **[M]**, prose only); *Measuring Board Game Distance* https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.03913; *General Board Game Concepts* https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.01078 (the `Concept.*` enum the metrics map onto).

---

## 4. AlphaZero chess-variant study (Tomašev, Paquet, Hassabis, Kramnik 2020)

https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.04374 · PDF https://arxiv.org/pdf/2009.04374 [S]

**Variants (Table 1):** Classical, No-castling, No-castling(10) (no castling for first 20 plies), Pawn one square, Stalemate=win, Torpedo (pawns move 1–2 anywhere; en passant anywhere), Semi-torpedo (double-step from 2nd *and* 3rd rank), Pawn-back (pawn retreats to 2nd/7th; pawn moves don't reset the 50-move rule), Pawn-sideways (lateral pawn moves; don't reset 50-move rule), Self-capture.

**Compute & protocol (§3.1):** one AlphaZero model per variant, **1M training steps, batch 4096, ~0.12 samples/position, Dirichlet(0.3) prior noise, 800 MCTS sims/move in training**, stochastic move selection for first 30 plies of training games. Evaluation: **N = 10,000 self-play games @ 1 s/move and N = 1,000 @ 1 min/move per variant**, diversity forced by sampling the **first 20 plies** proportional to softmax of MCTS visit counts, then top-move play. Plus N = 1,000 games from four fixed openings (Dutch, Chigorin, Alekhine, King's Gambit). No cross-variant baseline exists, so strength is not formally verified — they lean on Kramnik's qualitative review.

**Decisiveness / draw rate (§3.2):** posterior over outcome odds `π = (π_win, π_draw, π_lose)` with uniform Dirichlet prior + multinomial likelihood:
> `p(π|G) = Dir(n_win + 1, n_draw + 1, n_lose + 1)` (2)

then pairwise decisiveness is a probability, not a point estimate:
> `p(π^A_draw < π^B_draw) = ∫∫ I[π^A_draw < π^B_draw] p(π^A|G^A) p(π^B|G^B) dπ^A dπ^B` (3)

estimated by Monte Carlo sampling of pairs (they cite MacKay 2003 §37.1). Most decisive: Torpedo, Semi-torpedo, No-castling. Expected score for White (Table 2, training / 1 s / 1 min): Classical 54.1/51.8/50.8%, Torpedo 57.0/56.8/54.0%, No-castling 55.7/53.3/51.3%, Pawn-back 53.0/51.1/50.1%. Draw rate rises with thinking time across all variants.

**Opening diversity (§3.5)** — entropy of the *prior policy* over move sequences, "average information content of the first T = 20 plies":
> `H(s_t) = − Σ_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1}|s_t) log p(s_{t+1}|s_t)` (6) · `m(s_t) = exp(H(s_t))` (7) — the effective number of *candidate* moves ("de Groot's objective freedom of choice"; cites Iida et al. 2003 for `m ≈ √M`)
> `H(t) = − Σ_{s_{1:t}} p(s_{1:t}) log p(s_{1:t}) = E_{s_{1:t}}[−log p(s_{1:t})]` (8) · `M(t) = Σ p(s_{1:t}) m(s_t) = E[m(s_t)]` (9)

Table 3 (nats over 20 plies, with "equivalent 20-ply games"): No-castling 27.65 (1.02e12) · Torpedo 27.89 · Self-capture 27.94 · No-castling(10) 27.97 · **Classical 28.58 (2.58e12)** · Stalemate=win 29.01 · Semi-torpedo 31.63 · Pawn-back 32.30 · Pawn-sideways 34.16 · **Pawn one square 38.95 (8.24e16)** · uniform-random baseline 64.96 (1.63e28). **Key empirical claim: opening breadth is inversely related to decisiveness.**

**Material values (§3.8):** a linear probe, not the network. Feature vector `d = [1, d_p, d_N, d_B, d_R, d_Q]` of piece-count differences; `g_w(s) = tanh(wᵀd)` (16); minimise `ℓ(w) = E_{(s,z)∼games}[(z − g_w(s))²]` (17) on the 10,000 1 s/move games; normalise `w` by `w_p`. Table 6 (p/N/B/R/Q): Classical 1/3.05/3.33/5.63/9.50 · No-castling 1/2.97/3.13/5.02/9.49 · Torpedo 1/2.25/2.46/3.58/7.12 · **Pawn-sideways 1/1.80/1.98/2.99/5.92**. The Classical row reproducing ~3/3.3/5.6/9.5 is the sanity check for the method.

---

## 5. Other relevant work

- **GAVEL** (Todd et al., NeurIPS 2024) https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.09388 — LLM + MAP-Elites over Ludii games. Cheap filter: 100 *random*-policy playouts; reject if first/second win-rate gap > 0.5 or if < half of states have >1 legal move. Then **10 MCTS self-play games, 0.25 s/move, 50-move cap**. Metrics verbatim: "1. **Balance**: the largest difference in winrates between any pair of players. 2. **Decisiveness**: The proportion of games that do not end in a draw. 3. **Completion**: the proportion of games that reach an end state. 4. **Agency**: the proportion of turns for which the player to move has more than one legal move. 5. **Coverage**: the proportion of board sites … occupied by a game piece at least once"; plus **Strategic Depth** = proportion of games MCTS wins vs random over n=10. Aggregation: **harmonic mean** (deliberately, to punish one catastrophic metric), floored at 0.01 per metric. Fitness ladder −3 (won't compile) / −2 (unplayable) / −1 (fails filter). [S]
- **Evolutionary Tabletop Game Design: Risk** (Lara-Cabrera et al. 2023) https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.20008 — GA over Risk rule/map parameters, fitness = **`fitness_v = Σ_{i∈I} |v_i − o_i|` (minimisation, distance to a target vector)**, with Table 1 optima: Completion 1, Duration 0 (games end in 24 turns), Advantage 0, Branching factor 0.5 (~50 moves/turn), **Drama 0.5, Killer moves 0.5, Lead change 0.5** — note the interesting design choice that drama/killer/lead-change targets are *mid-range, not maximal*: "too much lead changes make the game too unpredictable or chaotic". 100 rule-based-agent matches per candidate, 48-turn cap. Criteria lifted from Browne. [S]
- **Mangeli & Xexéo**, "Measuring Aesthetics of Game Behavior", SBGames 2018 https://www.sbgames.org/sbgames2018/files/papers/ArtesDesignShort/188357.pdf — reworks Browne's criteria for multiplayer turn-based games; introduces a **Maximum Drama Path (MDP)** normalisation (drama = 1 iff the winner's path was the MDP) and a fuzzy aggregate. [M]
- **Suspense/surprise, formal** — Ely, Frankel & Kamenica, "Suspense and Surprise", *JPE* 123(1), 2015 https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/abs/10.1086/677350: **suspense at a period = variance of next period's beliefs; surprise = distance between current and previous belief.** This is the cleanest formal cousin of Browne's uncertainty/drama and is directly computable from an engine's win-probability trace — arguably a better-founded substitute. [S]
- **Uncertainty-of-outcome hypothesis (sports economics)** — the honest read is that it's *weakly* supported. Collins & Humphreys, "Contest Outcome Uncertainty and Fan Decisions: A Meta-Analysis", *J. Sports Economics* 23(6), 2022 https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/15270025221091544: >500 specifications across 97 papers, **no consensus**, results slightly favour *loss aversion* over outcome uncertainty. Also https://arxiv.org/pdf/1507.00634 (competitive-balance measures) and https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11151-023-09899-w. Treat "uncertainty ⇒ enjoyment" as a plausible prior, not an established law. [S but negative]
- **BoardGameGeek ratings** — no peer-reviewed predictive study surfaced; what exists is careful blog analysis. Vatvani, "Complexity bias in BGG" https://dvatvani.com/blog/bgg-analysis-part-2: **R² ≈ 0.35 of rating variance explained by complexity (weight) alone**, i.e. BGG ratings partly measure *heaviness* and audience self-selection, not enjoyment. Also https://blog.recommend.games/posts/debiasing-boardgamegeek-ranking/ and https://phenrickson.github.io/bgg_reports/reports/adjusting_bgg_ratings.html. All **[W]** — useful as a warning that any human-rating ground truth you regress against is confounded by complexity, recency and rating-count.

---

## Practical bottom line for a chess variant

The two things with real evidential weight and low implementation cost:
1. **Browne's viability four** (completion, balance/advantage, drawishness, duration) — best cost/benefit, and his own ablation shows *duration* is the single strongest viability filter while *completion alone* is nearly useless.
2. **A lead-history trace + {uncertainty(late), lead change (negatively weighted), permanence, killer moves}** — the four quality criteria that dominate his ablation. You need only a per-move eval series from self-play, which a chess engine already gives you.

Skip: Iida's GR as a *target* (n≈6 games, and √B/D is nearly determined by board size and game length, so it barely discriminates between variants of the same game). Use it as a descriptive sanity check at most. Prefer Ely–Frankel–Kamenica suspense/surprise over Browne's uncertainty if you have calibrated win probabilities rather than raw evals. Follow the DeepMind protocol (10k games/variant, first-20-ply sampling for diversity, Dirichlet posterior for draw-rate comparison, linear probe for piece values) if you need anything publishable about material or decisiveness.

## 1. AlphaZero / Lc0 training cost — and the minimum viable scale

**The headline numbers (primary source)**
- AlphaZero chess: **700,000 steps, mini-batch 4,096, on 5,000 first-gen TPUs for self-play + 64 second-gen TPUs for training**. https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1712.01815
- Chess run: **9 hours wall-clock, 44 million self-play games** (Table S3). Shogi 12h/24M, Go 34h/21M. Same URL.
- Surpassed Stockfish **after 4 hours (300k steps)**. Same URL.
- Training MCTS used **800 simulations/move, ~40 ms thinking time per move** in chess. Same URL.
- At play time AlphaZero searched **80k positions/sec vs Stockfish's 70M** — ~1000× fewer nodes. Same URL.

**Dollars**
- No credible public dollar figure for AlphaZero chess itself. The best-anchored estimate is for AlphaGo Zero: **$2,986,822 for the 3-day run and $35,354,222 for the 40-day run**, at an assumed **$6.50/TPU/hr** Google Cloud rate (March 2018). https://www.yuzeh.com/data/agz-cost.html
- "Tens of millions of dollars" for AlphaZero is asserted (not derived) in https://arxiv.org/html/2504.07757v1 — treat as [unverified] secondary.

**Lc0's actual distributed scale**
- Community estimate: **"a strong Leela takes about 60 million games of training (or more)"**. https://groups.google.com/g/lczero/c/vibJiUO1R5I
- Throughput per GPU on that thread: **RTX 2080 Ti ≈ 14 games/min ≈ 20,000 games/day**; RTX 2070 ≈ 12,000/day; RTX 2080 ≈ 14,500/day. Same URL.
- **Do the division: 60M games ÷ 20k/day = 3,000 GPU-days ≈ 8.2 GPU-years on one 2080 Ti.** The thread's own framing: **100× RTX 2080 Ti for 1 month ≈ $15,000** at Vast.ai rates, and the dollar cost stays ~$15k whether you use 100 or 5,000 GPUs — only wall-clock shrinks. Same URL.
- Lc0 has since played **>500 million self-play games, ~1 million/day** [unverified — encyclopedia secondary, not an lczero.org primary]. https://encyclopedia.pub/entry/30569

**Minimum viable single-GPU AlphaZero — the honest ceiling**
- The most candid single-GPU chess implementation targets **RTX 3090 (24 GB)** and states **~1500–2000 Elo from scratch, "realistically a couple of days"** wall-clock, with an explicit disclaimer: *"not a promise of grandmaster strength on a laptop."* https://github.com/yurit04/alpha_chess
- Its measured throughput on an untrained 128ch×10-block net: **~102,000 evaluated positions/sec, ~24,000 games/hour**, 77 evals/ply with playout-cap randomisation, forward pass ~121,000 pos/sec at batch 1024. Same URL.
- Default self-play search is **200 sims/move** (vs AlphaZero's 800) — a 4× cut that is itself a scale concession. Same URL.
- Graph-net AlphaZero variant, 8×8 chess from scratch: **500 iterations = 13 days 16 hours on 6–8 RTX A5000s**, reaching ~1876 Elo. https://arxiv.org/html/2410.23753v1
- **Takeaway: one GPU buys you ~2000 Elo of chess in days, not superhuman play.** Superhuman self-play chess is a 1,000–10,000 GPU-day problem regardless of framework.
- Sebastian Lague's chess work is handcrafted-eval + search, not a learned eval. The relevant NN data point from his 2023 tiny-bot contest: **"NNBot" reached 2246 Elo with a very small compressed net inside a 1024-token limit** [unverified — contest leaderboard, no primary writeup found]. https://sebastian.itch.io/tiny-chess-bots

## 2. The cheaper alternative: supervised value net / NNUE (this is the actual answer)

**Elo gains people report from a first net**
- **Leorik 3.0** (C#, HCE → NNUE): **~350 Elo**. CCRL Blitz **3277 (+359)**, CEGT **3124 (+358)**, independent 4300-game test at 30min **+309 Elo**. Net was **(768→256)×2→1, 622M positions, trained with `bullet`**. https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?t=79049&start=430
- **Prokopakop**: **+200 Elo over the non-NNUE version — "equivalent to all previous search optimizations combined"** (from ~1800 baseline). Arch **768→128×2→1 with SCReLU, 8 output buckets, int16 QA/QB**. https://slama.dev/prokopakop/nnues-and-where-to-find-them/
- **chess-inator** (Rust, small hobby engine): NNUE vs material-count baseline = **667 wins / 7 losses / 32 draws, "a few hundred Elo"**, on only **"a few million" positions** the author calls *"drastically little."* https://www.dogeystamp.com/chess6/
- **Stockfish 12's own NNUE gain over classical eval: "over 80 Elo on fishtest"** — the low end, because Stockfish's HCE was extremely mature. https://stockfishchess.org/blog/2020/introducing-nnue-evaluation/
- **The variant numbers are far larger** — see §5.

**How many positions**
- Community floor: **"I initially failed with only 15M positions so I'd recommend 100M+"** — Martin Sedlak. https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?t=83944
- Counter-evidence at the small end: a pure-JS **768→128→1 net trained on ~8M positions was "about on par with Lozza's eval (~2700 CCRL)"** — i.e. 8M positions bought parity with a mature hand-tuned eval. https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?t=83958
- Negative data point worth heeding: one dev with **40M positions was still 200–300 Elo *behind* his own HCE** across nets from 768×8 to 768×256. https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?t=84777&start=30
- Production scale for reference: Lozza's shipped net = **~600M positions**; Prokopakop **~500M generated (~32% unique after dedup)**; Leorik **622M**. https://github.com/op12no2/lozza · https://slama.dev/prokopakop/nnues-and-where-to-find-them/

**Data generation — the real cost, and it's CPU not GPU**
- Standard recipe (Sedlak): **"play a couple of random plies then let the engine play on (fixed nodes, 5–10k)"**, filtering out positions where side-to-move is in check or best move is a capture. https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?t=83944
- Prokopakop's concrete cost: **~500 positions/sec, ~11.5 days of self-play for ~500M positions**, fixed depth 8–12, first 1–6 moves randomised. https://slama.dev/prokopakop/nnues-and-where-to-find-them/
- Minic: **~2 weeks on 8 cores to generate 2B positions at depth 8**, then **~1 week on a GTX 1060 to train**, plus a week of testing — **~1 month per net end-to-end**. https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?t=76552
- Sable 1.6 (2026, ~3200 CCRL): all self-play data generated on **one i7-11700K + RTX 3070**, **4 self-play generations** (each regenerating data with the previous stronger net), **built over about a week**. Arch **768→512×2→1, clipped ReLU, int16, AVX2 incremental**. https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?t=86419&start=10
- **Bootstrapping shortcut that removes most of that cost**: Lozza and Cwtch both started from **public labelled EPD sets (`quiet_labeled.epd`, `lichess-big3-resolved.epd`)** and only then iterated with self-play. https://github.com/op12no2/lozza

**Tooling**
- `bullet` (Rust, jw1912) is the de-facto standard trainer for hobby engines: *"generally used for training NNUE-style networks for many of the strongest chess engines."* https://github.com/jw1912/bullet — its own docs tell beginners to start at plain **`768 -> N -> 1`** and explicitly warn that Stockfish-style architectures *"require significant effort, amounts of data, and/or training time/complexity."* https://github.com/jw1912/bullet/blob/main/docs/1-basics.md
- **`bullet`'s throughput in positions/sec and wall-clock for a 768→256 net is [unverified]** — I found no published benchmark; it lives in the Engine Programming Discord `#bullet` channel.
- Smallest net anyone reports as viable: **"N can be as small as 16 and already be competitive with a handcrafted eval"** — Lithander. https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?t=83170

## 3. Value-net + alpha-beta vs policy+value MCTS

- **Node-efficiency, measured**: Stockfish+NNUE needs **~81,000 PVS nodes to match Leela's strength**, far fewer than Stockfish+HCE needed. https://webdocs.cs.ualberta.ca/~mmueller/ps/2023/ACG_2023_Stockfish.pdf [figure via search index — the PDF itself would not text-extract for me]
- Endgame accuracy is near-parity, so the AB advantage is not evaluation quality: **Stockfish errs on 1.47% (winning) / 1.67% (drawing) positions; Lc0 errs on 1.32% / 1.07%.** Same paper, https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-54968-7_3
- **Why AB wins at low nodes**: alpha-beta cuts the effective branching factor **from ~35 to under 2**, so a fixed node budget buys depth 30–40 plies with the net only at the leaves. https://dev.to/djinn/why-stockfish-is-so-good-and-how-you-could-write-a-chess-engine-2lck
- **MCTS's structural failure mode for chess-likes**: *"UCT is unable to identify such traps in Chess and spends a great deal of time exploring much deeper game play than needed"* — shallow traps. And DrCliche: tactical sequences involve moves *"assigned low intrinsic weight by the policy head"*, so *"that sequence will never be explored enough for the algorithm to realize the truth."* https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?t=74798
- **The policy net is not optional for MCTS** — MCTS efficiency is entirely a function of policy quality, which means a variant MCTS agent needs you to train *two* heads well, not one. Same thread.
- Counter-evidence, and the one case for MCTS: **a0lite at just 400 nps with UCT scored points against engines searching 7 orders of magnitude more nodes** — when each eval is expensive and high-quality, MCTS amortises it better. Dietrich Kappe, same thread.
- TCEC at equal-effort hardware (43 Xeon cores vs 2× RTX 2080 Ti), S14 superfinal: **Stockfish 50.5–49.5 (+10 =81 −9)** — the closest ever. Stockfish then widened it: S19 **+18 −9 =73**, S20 **+14 −8 =78**. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TCEC_Season_17 · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TCEC_Season_19 · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TCEC_Season_20
- **Conclusion for a browser variant engine: value-net-in-alpha-beta is the right call.** You get one head to train instead of two, a policy-quality dependency removed, and the paradigm that's proven at low node counts — which is exactly the browser's regime.

---

## 4. Browser deployment at batch size 1 — your colleague is right

**WebGPU at batch 1: corroborated, with numbers**
- Measured WebGPU **API dispatch overhead: 24–36 µs on Vulkan, 32–71 µs on Metal** across 4 GPU vendors / 3 backends / 3 browsers. *"The dispatch overhead, not kernel quality, is the bottleneck at batch size 1."* https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08730
- Small-model, batch-1 head-to-head on an M2 MacBook Air: **WASM median ~8–12 ms vs WebGPU ~15–25 ms**; GPU buffer upload + dispatch + readback exceeds the compute itself. https://www.sitepoint.com/webgpu-vs-webasm-transformers-js/
- **A 768→256→1 net's forward pass is ~200k MACs. At 24–71 µs of dispatch overhead alone, WebGPU is pure loss here.**

**onnxruntime-web WASM: also too heavy for this**
- Documented **11–17× slower than native**: MobileNetV2 at **~45 ms (ORT-web) vs ~12 ms (tfjs with SIMD+threads) vs ~4 ms (native ORT)** on a 2019 MacBook Pro. https://github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime/issues/11181
- Framework overhead is per-operator kernel dispatch, which *"becomes substantial as actual kernel execution time reduces"* — i.e. worst exactly at your model size. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.05099
- **I found no published benchmark of a hand-written int16 JS NNUE vs onnxruntime-web on an identical net. That comparison does not appear to exist — mark it a gap, not a settled result.**

**The incremental-accumulator argument, quantified**
- A move changes **at most 4 input features (castling), average below 3**; only those columns are added/subtracted into the accumulator. https://github.com/fairy-stockfish/variant-nnue-pytorch/blob/master/docs/nnue.md
- **My arithmetic, from that structure**: full refresh on a 32-piece board into 256 lanes = **8,192 int16 adds**. A quiet-move incremental update = 2 features × 256 = **512 ops**. That's a **~16× reduction per eval**, and it is the entire reason NNUE exists. A `forward()` call into ORT or WebGPU throws this away by construction — there is no API to hand it a delta.
- Caveat that bites for variants: **king-bucketed feature sets (HalfKP/HalfKA) force a full refresh whenever the king moves.** A plain 768-input net never refreshes. For a variant with a mobile or unusual king, **stay on plain 768-style inputs.** Same URL.
- Even paying this cost, NNUE runs at **~80% of the HCE nodes/sec** and still wins massively. https://github.com/lichess-org/stockfish-nnue.wasm

**Quantisation constants you can copy**
- Current standard (2024): **SCALE = 400, QA = 255, QB = 64**, int16 weights and biases. With SCReLU, intermediates reach **QA² = 65,025** — overflow handling is required. https://chessprogramming.org/NNUE
- **My arithmetic on net size**: 768→256 int16 feature transformer = 768×256×2 = **393,216 B ≈ 384 KiB**; 768→128 = **192 KiB**; 768→32 = **48 KiB**. All trivially embeddable in a JS bundle.

**WASM SIMD from hand-written Rust: yes, reachable**
- `v128` and the **`i16x8` dot-product instruction `i32x4.dot_i16x8_s`** are in the core spec — exactly the primitive an int16 accumulator wants. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/WebAssembly/Reference/SIMD/arithmetic/dot_i16x8_s
- From Rust: `core::arch::wasm32` intrinsics, enabled by `#[target_feature(enable = "simd128")]` or `-C target-feature=+simd128`. https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/core/arch/wasm32/index.html · https://github.com/rust-lang/stdarch/blob/main/crates/core_arch/src/wasm32/simd128.rs
- Browser support is now universal across Chrome/Firefox/Edge/Safari. https://v8.dev/features/simd
- Scale of the prize: Lithander measured **~12× from SIMD** in his NNUE, and says *"you really want to use SIMD or otherwise your NNUE implementation is going to be too slow to be viable."* https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?t=83170
- Cost warning for the JS↔WASM boundary: WASM only wins on matmul **above roughly 128×128** because data marshalling dominates below that. **This does not apply if you keep the board, accumulator and net entirely inside WASM linear memory and cross the boundary once per search, not once per eval.** https://dev.to/ndesmic/fast-matrix-math-in-js-2-wasm-3mbn

**JS/TS reference implementations worth copying**
- **Lozza — the best reference, and it's pure JavaScript with no WASM at all.** *"a simple quantised 768→(256×2)→1 squared ReLU architecture, trained on about 600M positions"*, net embedded as one base64 line, `src/bullet.rs` included as the trainer reference. https://github.com/op12no2/lozza
- Lozza 4.0 is rated **CEDR 2847** [note: CEDR, not CCRL — I could not verify a current CCRL figure]. https://chessengines.blogspot.com/2024/12/new-version-chess-engine-java-lozza-40.html
- **Cwtch** — the same author's experimental JS NNUE engine; thread documents the whole bootstrap from a 768×1 material-only net upward, output scaled by 143, sigmoid stretched to `-x/100`. https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?t=83958
- **spareduck** — NNUE + alpha-beta in the browser via WebAssembly (C), if you want the wasm route. https://github.com/hang-sun1/spareduck
- Precedent that this ships at scale: lichess runs **stockfish-nnue.wasm** in-browser; an early SIMD NNUE build measured **60 knps**. https://github.com/lichess-org/stockfish-nnue.wasm

---

## 5. When the rules change

**The single most important table for your project**
- Fairy-Stockfish hosts **200+ variant NNUE nets, each with a measured Elo gain over that variant's handcrafted eval**: **3check +200, antichess +200, capablanca +354, seirawan +359, losers +368, racingkings +374, horde +490, kingofthehill +644, atomic +719, xiangqi +914, janggi +1128, crazyhouse +1136, shogi >+1000, grasshopper +2574.** https://fairy-stockfish.github.io/nnue/
- **Read that as your business case.** Standard chess gets +80 from NNUE because its HCE had 20 years of tuning. **A novel variant's HCE is untuned, so the learned eval is worth 200–2500 Elo, not 80.** Same URL.
- Also note **most of those 200+ nets were produced by two individuals** ("belzedar_ in discord" and Fabian Fichter) — this is provably a one-person, one-machine job. Same URL.
- Fairy-Stockfish generalised the architecture *"so that it can be used for different board sizes, arbitrary piece types, variants without kings, as well as variants with piece drops"* — i.e. the infrastructure for your case already exists. https://fairy-stockfish.github.io/about-nnue/
- Its trainer supports **`--resume_from_checkpoint`**, so warm-starting from an existing net is mechanically available. https://github.com/fairy-stockfish/variant-nnue-pytorch
- **How many positions per variant net, and how long: [unverified].** Not published; the default epoch size is 20M positions / 1M validation, which is a parameter not a recommendation. Same URL.

**Does fine-tuning across a rule change actually work? Yes — one good measurement**
- AlphaGateau pre-trained on **5×5 chess only** (100 iters, 2d 7h), then evaluated on **8×8 chess with zero 8×8 exposure: 807 ± 46 Elo**. After **100 fine-tuning iterations on 8×8 (5d 15h): 1876 ± 47 Elo.** https://arxiv.org/html/2410.23753v1
- Compare: the same-size model trained on 8×8 **from scratch took 500 iterations / 13d 16h**. **So 100 fine-tune iterations ≈ 500 from-scratch iterations — roughly a 5× saving, and the transferred net started well above random.** Same URL.
- The mechanism is architectural: graph nets handle *"differently-sized input graphs,"* letting one model span board variants without architecture changes. Same URL.

**The contrary data point — DeepMind didn't bother**
- The DeepMind variant study trained **9 chess variants plus classical**, and *"trained AlphaZero from scratch for each of the rule alterations... with the same set of model hyperparameters"* — **1M steps, batch 4096, 800 sims/move, per variant. No transfer, no fine-tuning.** https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2009.04374
- Read that as compute abundance, not evidence against transfer: at 5,000 TPUs, retraining is cheaper than thinking about transfer. **You are not in that position.**

**Rule-agnostic features — the strongest precedent, and it's tiny-scale**
- **Giraffe (Matthew Lai, 2015)** used **363 features** deliberately abstracted away from piece identity: side to move, castling rights, material configuration, piece lists, **sliding-piece mobility** (how far each slider can go in each direction), and **attack and defend maps** (the lowest-valued attacker and defender of each square). https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1509.01549
- Its cost: **72 hours on a 2×10-core Xeon E5-2660 v2 — CPU only, no GPU — on ~175M positions**, reaching **approximately FIDE International Master level** (STS 9641/15000). Same URL.
- **This is your architecture template.** Mobility and attack/defend maps are computed *from the move generator*, so they are automatically correct when a piece's movement changes — no input-plane redesign, no re-indexing, and the net's learned weights stay meaningful. Contrast with 768-style piece-type-×-square inputs, where adding a piece type or changing its movement invalidates the feature semantics.
- Independent support for the idea: attack/defend maps let a net *"learn concepts related to board control, which is difficult to derive from piece lists because piece lists are piece-centric rather than square-centric."* https://www.chessprogramming.org/Neural_Networks
- **Cost of the rule-agnostic choice**: attack/defend maps are *not* cheaply incrementally updatable — one move changes many squares' attacker sets. **You lose the 16× accumulator saving.** A hybrid (768-style incremental core + a small non-incremental mobility head recomputed per eval) is the obvious compromise, but I found no published engine doing this — that's an untested design, not a cited one.

**The supervised-on-a-variant precedent**
- **CrazyAra** learned crazyhouse from **569,537 human lichess games (Jan 2016–Jun 2018)** in **1.5 days of training**, plus 121,571 Stockfish games. It then **beat the reigning crazyhouse world champion Justin Tan 4–1**, and beat 12 of 13 entrants in the 2017 Crazyhouse Computer Championships. https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1908.06660
- The authors are explicit that they chose supervised learning *"due to limited computational resources, avoiding the expensive reinforcement learning approach used by AlphaZero."* Same URL.
- Move prediction accuracy 60.4%, mate-in-one 95.5%, value sign accuracy 68.9%; the mobile-optimised variant hit **28.4 ms inference on an Intel i5, up to 3× faster on CPU** than baseline. Same URL.
- **The catch for your project: CrazyAra had 570k human games of an existing variant. For a brand-new variant you have zero. Your substitute is self-play labelled by your own alpha-beta searcher — exactly the §2 recipe.**

If it matters, it's a half-day experiment worth running yourself.

# HD-2D / chunky-pixel art research

**Method note.** Where a dev source gave no number, I measured community sprite rips from The Spriters Resource with Python/PIL (bounding box per animation frame, unique RGB per frame, edge-pixel colour histogram, and an integer-upscale test = % of 2×2/4×4 blocks that are uniform). These are marked **[measured]** and carry the caveat that rips can be post-render captures. Anything I could not verify is marked **unverified** — I invented no numbers.

## 1. Octopath Traveler I & II (Square Enix / Acquire, UE4)

**Official meaning of HD-2D.** Square Enix's own press copy: OT2 "takes the series' HD-2D graphics, a fusion of retro pixel art and 3DCG, to even greater heights" — https://press.na.square-enix.com/OCTOPATH-TRAVELER-II/Focus/Pixel-Art . Square Enix coined and trademarked "HD-2D" in 2018 for Octopath; the style is "traditional 2D elements, such as pixel art and billboard sprites, with fully three-dimensional environments," with tilt-shift, depth of field, bloom, volumetric light/fog, particles, parallax, dynamic point lights casting character shadows, built in UE4 — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HD-2D

**Dev statements**
- Asano (CBU II) on the style's origin and spread: "HD-2D, which was born with Octopath Traveler, has gained recognition over the past eight years" — https://www.dualshockers.com/square-enix-hd-2d-remakes-teased-by-octopath-traveler-asano/ ; president Matsuda pushed for more HD-2D titles — https://automaton-media.com/en/news/20220221-9826/
- Cost: Asano told 4Gamer HD-2D "costs more than you'd think" — https://nintendoeverything.com/triangle-strategy-producers-say-hd-2d-costs-more-than-youd-think-internal-teams-shared-knowledge-to-help-with-its-implementation/
- Takahashi (OT2 producer) on the engine choice: "UE4 is very good at both 3D environments and 3D graphics," leading to the 2D-pixels-in-3D-environment concept — https://nintendoeverything.com/octopath-traveler-ii-devs-on-the-games-evolved-use-of-hd-2d-and-more/
- Miyauchi (OT2 director) on **taller sprites**: raising character height was needed because "if we only increased the resolution of the background, the characters would look strange"; the main driver was combat — "Increasing the characters' height changes the presentation in combat a lot… there are different animations for every skill." Same source. Also: "Everyone has rose-tinted glasses on for old pixel art," so they had to beat the remembered version; reference point was '90s high-fidelity pixel art (Chrono Trigger's trial scene). Secondary write-ups: https://nintendowire.com/news/2022/10/31/octopath-traveler-ii-devs-on-presentation-and-not-succumbing-to-pure-pixel-art-nostalgia/ , https://www.nintendolife.com/news/2022/10/octopath-traveler-ii-devs-aimed-to-make-its-hd-2d-visuals-picture-perfect
- The Unreal Engine developer interview (has the billboarding/point-light/shadow detail) is at https://www.unrealengine.com/en-US/developer-interviews/octopath-traveler-ii-builds-a-bigger-bolder-world-in-its-stunning-hd-2d-style — **it 403s to automated fetches**; the billboarding + point-light-shadow summary I could only confirm second-hand via https://nintendoeverything.com/octopath-traveler-technical-analysis/ . Treat the UE page as a source you should open in a browser yourself.

**[measured] sprite numbers** (rips: https://www.spriters-resource.com/nintendo_switch/octopathtraveler/ and https://www.spriters-resource.com/nintendo_switch/octopathtravelerii/)

| | frame size | unique colours / frame | notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| OT1 Olberic, **field** sprite | **16 × 34 px** (action frames widen to ~54 px) | 27 (25 above 0.5% of pixels) | whole 512×512 sheet = 81 colours, 8-bit indexed |
| OT1 Olberic, **battle** sprite | **34 × 51 px** | 62 (49 significant) | whole sheet = 71 colours |
| OT2 Hikari, **battle** sprite | **34 × 56 px native** | 31 significant (439 raw) | the rip is a clean 2× upscale (100% of 2×2 blocks uniform), so native = 34×56 |

So the OT2 "taller sprites" claim checks out numerically: 51 px → 56 px battle height, ~10%. The 400-colour raw count on OT2 almost certainly comes from the rip capturing lit/filtered frames — **treat OT2 colour count as unverified**; the 34×56 dimension is solid.

**[measured] outline.** Octopath uses a near-black outline of `#181818` (RGB 24,24,24) as the dominant edge colour, with dark hue-matched variants (`#301810` warm brown, `#2A1A18` red-brown) on warm regions — i.e. **black outline with selective colour-shifted outlining**. 72–77% of all edge pixels are below luminance 32; 88–96% below 64. That is a very hard, very dark contour — the thing that lets a 16 px-wide sprite survive on top of a lit, bloom-heavy 3D diorama.

## 2. Triangle Strategy (Artdink / Square Enix)

- **Why Artdink:** Square Enix had several studios make HD-2D demo footage; Acquire judged Artdink's the only "accurate" HD-2D, because Artdink "prepared a deformed image at the writing material level, before adding realistic effects to 'build it up'," rather than shrinking photoreal renders — Asano: "If you reduce a photorealistic image, it looks as if you're simply lowering the image quality." — https://nintendoeverything.com/triangle-strategy-devs-on-how-the-game-uses-accurate-hd-2d/ , https://www.gonintendo.com/contents/4132-triangle-strategy-producer-talks-about-recreating-an-accurate-hd-2d-style
- **Rotatable camera is the hard part:** Asano — "Octopath Traveler had a fixed camera, but in tactical RPGs, you need to be able to rotate the map 360 degrees." Arai — "It took a lot of resources to make the map observable from all sides." Asano again, in Destructoid: it was hard "to find that balance between moving the camera around… but having your characters created by dots" — https://www.destructoid.com/triangle-strategy-interview-producers-asano-arai-square-enix-hd-2d-tactics-rpg/
- **Explicit resolution-vs-style rule (very relevant to your report):** Asano — "As the proportions change to look more realistic, the resolution increases and the pixels become smaller, making them look more like illustrations rather than pixel art." The team deliberately capped sprite fidelity to keep them reading as pixel art. Same NintendoEverything link.
- Asano also described the look as "a diorama or a vignette-like object" (realistic light on deformed characters).

**[measured]** (https://www.spriters-resource.com/pc_computer/trianglestrategy/) Frederica and Erador unit sprites are **17–22 px wide × 35–41 px tall** per frame (typical 19×38 / 22×40), **29–48 unique colours per frame** (~29–35 significant). Not upscaled (0.2% of 2×2 blocks uniform → true 1× pixel grid). Edge colours: `#181818` black plus heavy **hue-matched dark outlines** (`#3E1818`, `#562323` on Frederica's red dress) — more selective outlining than Octopath, presumably because units must read against many ground types from any of four camera angles.

Grid takeaway: **~19 × 38 px is what Square Enix shipped as a readable unit on a rotatable tactics grid.**

- Art director Hiroshi Minagawa and character artist Akihiko Yoshida returned — https://www.rpgfan.com/review/tactics-ogre-reborn/
- Pre-release comparison noting *added detail* (e.g. Lanselot's sword) as evidence of redrawing rather than filtered upscaling — https://wccftech.com/tactics-ogre-reborn-early-comparison-highlights-redrawn-sprites-and-backgrounds/

**[measured] — this is the strongest evidence on "upscaled vs redrawn"**
- PSP *Let Us Cling Together* (2010) battle frames: **~14–18 × 26–27 px**, 21–32 colours/frame — https://www.spriters-resource.com/psp/tacticsogreletusclingtogether/
- Reborn battle frames: **60–68 × 100–112 px** (typical 64×104), **27–32 colours/frame**, 448–454 colours on a full character sheet — https://www.spriters-resource.com/pc_computer/tacticsogrereborn/
- Ratio is almost exactly **4× linear**. But it is **not** a nearest-neighbour 4× upscale: only **36% of 4×4 blocks are uniform**, while **84% of 2×2 blocks are uniform**. Interpretation: the Reborn art sits on an effective **2× chunky pixel grid** with a meaningful minority of 1×-resolution detail and cleanup — consistent with "redrawn at higher resolution in the original style," not with a filter pass. (A naive 4× upscale would score ~100% on the 4×4 test.)
- **Outline is the interesting bit:** Reborn's edge pixels are overwhelmingly a single colour, `#302820` (48,40,32) — a dark warm grey-brown, **not black**. Mean edge luminance 57–58 vs Octopath's 32–38. So Reborn deliberately softens the contour relative to the HD-2D games.
