## 9. Minimum pixels per character for silhouette readability

There is **no single canonical industry rule**. The closest thing to citable rules of thumb, from named artists:

- **Raymond Schlitter (SLYNYRD), the most concrete source.** His working standard is **16×32 px** character sprites ("1 tile wide by 2 tiles tall is one of the most common sprite sizes, and is the size I've chosen"), sized from the tile unit: "Basing the character size on tile units allows the sprite to naturally fit in the grid-like structure of the tile based world." Head takes **a third to half** the sprite height to keep expression readable — https://www.slynyrd.com/blog/2019/10/21/pixelblog-22-top-down-character-sprites
- Schlitter's **floor** case, on an 8×8 tilemap: characters built from a simple 8-px-tall figure, where "everything is there for basic readability… the sense of wonder is peaked by the lack of detail" — https://www.slynyrd.com/blog/2023/11/26/pixelblog-47-tiny-pixels (see also https://www.slynyrd.com/blog/2025/11/28/pixelblog-59-tiny-sci-fi-pixels)
- **Derek Yu's classic tutorial (2007)**, still the most-cited: start small, because "the hard part is learning how to cram a lot of detail into a few pixels," and "even large sprites never usually exceed 200 by 200 pixels" — http://makegames.tumblr.com/post/42648699708/pixel-art-tutorial
- **Cyangmou (Thomas Feichtmeir)** has the one tutorial explicitly about this topic, "Readability – Pixel Art Style Possibilities" (2018), indexed at https://lospec.com/pixel-art-tutorials/readability-pixel-art-style-possibilities-by-cyangmou — **but the DeviantArt original is now 404**, so I could not read the chart and will not paraphrase its contents. His index of resources: https://lospec.com/pixel-art-tutorials/author/cyangmou
- **Michafrar, *Pixel Logic: A Guide to Pixel Art*** has a dedicated **Ch. 4 "Readability"** (242 pages, chapters: intro, line art, anti-aliasing, colours, readability, dithering, game perspectives, clean-up, subpixeling, animation) — https://pixellogicbook.com/ , https://michafrar.gumroad.com/l/pixel-logic , overview at https://80.lv/articles/pixel-logic-a-pixel-art-tutorial-book
- **Arne (androidarts)** frames it as constraint rather than threshold: "Certain things are difficult to build out of LEGO bricks, and the same goes for pixels," and "you have to make every pixel count" — https://androidarts.com/pixtut/pixelart.htm

**Empirical anchor from the shipped games above, which is probably more useful than any tutorial:** readable tactical units cluster at **~16–22 px wide × 27–40 px tall** (Octopath field 16×34, Live A Live 20×28, Triangle Strategy 19×38), and readable *battle-scale* pixel characters at **~34×51–56 px**. Into the Breach's mechs at **~42×36** and Tactics Ogre Reborn's at **~64×104** are the upper end. Caution these are all humanoid/biped; ITB buys its readability with a wider, blockier mass on a huge 8×8 board plus overlays.

**Warning:** most top Google results for "minimum sprite size" right now (spritegen.io, sprixen.com, sprite-ai.art, pixnote.net, spritesheets.ai, generalistprogrammer.com) are AI-generated SEO pages with no named author. They confidently state things like "6–12 colours per character" and "16×16 once your silhouettes read reliably." **Do not cite them.** I excluded them from everything above.

---

## 10. How many shades per material

- **Derek Yu gives the hard rule you're looking for:** "Use at most two shades of dark (dark and really dark), and two shades of light (light and really light) on top of your foundation color" — i.e. a **5-step ramp maximum: base + 2 shadow + 2 highlight**. Plus: "The more colors you use, the more distracted your sprite will look. To make a sprite stand out, use only two or three main colors." And the two prohibitions: no pillow-shading, no gradients. http://makegames.tumblr.com/post/42648699708/pixel-art-tutorial
- **Raymond Schlitter (SLYNYRD)** gives a hard per-character number for a small-sprite style: "I used the general size of 16x16px, and limited the palette to **3 colors in addition to the outline** per character," chosen to mesh with 16×16 tiles — https://www.slynyrd.com/blog/2022/1/25/pixelblog-36-8-bit-adventure . His full-palette construction (9 swatches per ramp, ~20° hue shift per step, saturation peaking mid-ramp, brightness rising left to right, 8 ramps / 128 colours) is in https://www.slynyrd.com/blog/2018/1/10/pixelblog-1-color-palettes — note that's a *palette* ramp, not what one material uses in one sprite.
- **Pedro Medeiros (saint11)** keeps it minimal rather than numeric: "keep your color count low," "good pixel art eliminates all unnecessary detail," and ramps belong on rounded shapes while flat faces stay uniform (to avoid banding). Glossary distinguishes volume shadow / highlight / reflection highlight. https://saint11.art/pixel_art_articles/article4/ , index: https://saint11.art/pixel_articles/ (also mirrored on Medium's Pixel Grimoire)
- **Arne (androidarts):** "Unless you are working with very small palettes (say, 3 colors), you probably need to set up color ramps," never build ramp ends by mixing in pure black/white, and hue-shift instead — for skin, "shadow a grayish warm purple… mid tone orange, and the light almost yellowish." Avoid long ramps of fully saturated colour. https://androidarts.com/pixtut/pixelart.htm
- Curated named-artist shading tutorials (with source links) live at https://lospec.com/pixel-art-tutorials/tags/shading — notably ENDESGA's "Quicktip: Highlights," which is specifically about **shading changing per material**.

**Cross-check against shipped work [measured]:** a whole Octopath character sheet is **81 colours** across every frame and direction; a single field frame uses **27**; a Live A Live field frame **21**; a Tactics Ogre Reborn 64×104 battle frame **~28–32**; Triangle Strategy ~19×38 unit frames **29–48**. So real production sprites land at roughly **20–35 colours for a whole character**, which with 5–8 materials per character is right on Derek Yu's 3–5 shades per material.

---

## 11. Readability on a small tactical grid — the four levers, with evidence

1. **Hard dark contour.** Every Square Enix HD-2D game I measured uses `#181818` as the dominant outline colour, 72–77% of edge pixels under luminance 32, with hue-shifted dark variants on warm materials (selective outlining). Tactics Ogre Reborn deliberately breaks this, using a single warm `#302820` outline at roughly double the luminance.
2. **Colour separation over detail.** Asano's rule: raising resolution past a point makes sprites "look more like illustrations rather than pixel art" — they capped fidelity on purpose (https://nintendoeverything.com/triangle-strategy-devs-on-how-the-game-uses-accurate-hd-2d/). Schlitter's 3-colours-plus-outline is the same instinct at 16×16.
3. **Contrast against ground is bought with lighting, not the sprite.** HD-2D's DOF/tilt-shift blurs the fore/background bands so only the sprite plane is sharp, and point lights drop character shadows onto the 3D terrain (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HD-2D). Sea of Stars does the equivalent with its dynamic lighting: Boulanger — "It gave volume to the environment" (https://screenrant.com/sea-stars-interview-thierry-boulanger/).
4. **Push state into overlays, not into the sprite.** Into the Breach is the clean case: perfect information via arrows, damage previews and animated tooltips; Ma — "sacrifice cool ideas for the sake of clarity every time" (https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/-i-into-the-breach-i-dev-on-ui-design-sacrifice-cool-ideas-for-the-sake-of-clarity-every-time-).
